HAEMATOLOGY__Foundations of Haematology:
Overview — Coagulation Cascade & Clotting Tests
The coagulation cascade = a sequence of clotting factor activations (secondary haemostasis) that converges on thrombin, which turns fibrinogen → fibrin to stabilise the platelet plug. The exam skill = mapping the three pathways to the two clotting tests (PT and APTT) and reading the pattern.
The spine
Intrinsic (APTT) + Extrinsic (PT) → Common pathway → thrombin → fibrin. Then map deficiencies/drugs onto whichever test is prolonged.
Cross-ref: Haemophilia / VWD (intrinsic, ↑APTT), DIC (everything consumed), blood transfusion products (FFP/cryo replace factors), anticoagulation (warfarin/heparin/DOAC targets).
Primary vs Secondary Haemostasis — the context
Primary haemostasis
Platelet plug — vessel injury → vWF binds platelets to exposed collagen → platelet activation/aggregation. Tested by platelet count + platelet function testing (PFA/aggregometry) — the old skin bleeding time is no longer used in UK practice.
Secondary haemostasis
The coagulation cascade — clotting factors generate fibrin to stabilise the plug. Tested by PT + APTT.
vWF bridges the two: it mediates platelet adhesion (primary) and carries factor VIII (secondary) — which is why VWD can prolong the APTT.

Interpreting Prolonged PT vs APTT — the pattern table
Pattern Localises to Causes
↑ PT onlyExtrinsic (VII)Early warfarin, factor VII deficiency, early liver disease (VII has the shortest half-life)
↑ APTT onlyIntrinsicHaemophilia A (VIII) / B (IX), VWD (only when factor VIII is secondarily low — the APTT is often normal in mild VWD), heparin, antiphospholipid (lupus anticoagulant)

Mixing study: if a prolonged APTT corrects on mixing with normal plasma → factor deficiency; if it doesn't correct → an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor). The lupus anticoagulant paradox: it prolongs the APTT in the tube but causes thrombosis, not bleeding, in the patient — do not read that prolonged APTT as a bleeding risk.

Vitamin K-dependent factors = II, VII, IX, X (mnemonic "1972") plus the natural anticoagulants protein C & S. These are the warfarin targets.

  • Natural anticoagulants (keep clotting localised): antithrombin (inhibits thrombin + Xa), protein C & protein S (inactivate factors Va + VIIIa — the activated cofactors, which is why factor V Leiden makes Va resistant to APC), tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI)

Overview — Haemostasis
Haemostasis = the process that stops bleeding after vessel injury, balanced against keeping blood flowing — the pro-clotting vs anti-clotting equilibrium.
The three stages: primary (platelet plug) → secondary (coagulation cascade → fibrin) → fibrinolysis (controlled breakdown).
Why it matters: explains bleeding disorders (platelet vs clotting factor), antiplatelets, and the platelet-function vs clotting-factor testing distinction — cross-ref the coagulation cascade subtab (secondary haemostasis), bleeding disorders, antiplatelets, DIC.

Primary Haemostasis — the platelet plug
📷 Image placeholder — Platelet plug formation — adhesion (vWF bridging collagen to GpIb) → activation (granule release: ADP, TXA₂) → aggregation (GpIIb/IIIa–fibrinogen cross-links).
The vessel response: injury → vasoconstriction (immediate, limits blood flow) — then the platelets take over.
The three platelet steps
  • 1. Adhesion: platelets stick to exposed subendothelial collagen via von Willebrand factor (vWF) bridging to platelet GpIb receptors
  • 2. Activation: platelets change shape and release granule contents (ADP, thromboxane A₂, serotonin) → recruit more platelets
  • 3. Aggregation: platelets bind one another via GpIIb/IIIa receptors using fibrinogen bridges → the platelet plug

Secondary Haemostasis — the cascade (brief)
  • The coagulation cascade (intrinsic / extrinsic / common pathways) converts the platelet plug into a stable fibrin clot
  • PT/INR → extrinsic pathway; APTT → intrinsic pathway

Overview — Natural Anticoagulant System
Clotting must be localised to the injury and switched off once the job is done — otherwise a clot would propagate through the whole vasculature. The natural anticoagulant system is the body's built-in brake on coagulation.
The organising principle: haemostasis is a balance between pro-coagulant (the cascade) and anti-coagulant forces; these natural anticoagulants keep the cascade in check — and losing them tips the balance toward thrombosis (thrombophilia).
Why it matters: explains the inherited thrombophilias (factor V Leiden, protein C/S/antithrombin deficiency), how heparin works, the nephrotic-syndrome VTE risk, and warfarin-induced skin necrosis — cross-ref the coagulation cascade + haemostasis subtabs, anticoagulation, nephrotic syndrome, VTE.
Why the Brake Is Needed — the context
The coagulation cascade is a powerful amplifying system (a small trigger → massive thrombin/fibrin generation), so it needs equally powerful off-switches to:
  • Localise the clot to the site of injury (not spread)
  • Limit its size
  • Remove it once healing occurs (overlaps with fibrinolysis)
The balance concept: at any moment, pro-coagulant and anti-coagulant forces are in equilibrium — tip toward pro-coagulant → thrombosis; tip toward anti-coagulant → bleeding.
The Three Main Natural Anticoagulants — the spine

System Mechanism What it inhibits
Antithrombin III (ATIII)A circulating protease inhibitor that inactivates thrombin (IIa) + factor Xa (and others)Thrombin + Xa
Protein C + Protein SActivated protein C (with protein S as cofactor) inactivates factors Va + VIIIaThe two key amplifying cofactors (Va, VIIIa)

Antithrombin III — the heparin target (high-yield)
  • Mechanism: ATIII circulates and inactivates thrombin and factor Xa by binding them
The heparin link (key payoff): heparin (and LMWH) work by massively potentiating antithrombin III — heparin binds ATIII and accelerates its action ~1000-fold.
  • UFH potentiates ATIII against both thrombin + Xa; LMWH acts more selectively on Xa (cross-ref anticoagulation)
  • Antithrombin deficiency (inherited thrombophilia): less brake → thrombosis risk; also causes heparin resistance (heparin needs ATIII to work)
  • Acquired ATIII loss — nephrotic syndrome: ATIII lost in the urine → hypercoagulable → the VTE risk noted in the nephrotic syndrome topic (the cross-reference loop)
Protein C & Protein S — the warfarin / factor V Leiden link (high-yield)
Mechanism: thrombin (bound to thrombomodulin on intact endothelium) activates protein C → activated protein C (APC), with protein S as cofactor, inactivates factors Va and VIIIa → shuts down the cascade's amplification.
The elegant feedback: thrombin (the main clotting product) also triggers its own brake (via protein C) when it reaches healthy endothelium → the clot stays localised to the damaged area.
Both protein C and S are vitamin-K-dependent (like factors II, VII, IX, X) — the key to two high-yield clinical points:
Warfarin-induced skin necrosis
  • Warfarin lowers protein C faster than factors II, IX and X (protein C has a much shorter half-life) → a brief pro-thrombotic state at initiation → why heparin/LMWH cover is given when starting warfarin in acute VTE or other high thrombotic risk, but not routinely in AF (cross-ref anticoagulation). Factor VII actually has the shortest half-life of all, which is why the PT/INR moves first while the patient is not yet protected
Factor V Leiden (commonest inherited thrombophilia)
  • A mutated factor V that resists inactivation by activated protein C ("APC resistance") → the brake cannot switch it off → thrombosis risk
Protein C or S deficiency (inherited thrombophilias): less brake → VTE risk.
The Endothelium's Role — the surface that keeps blood flowing
  • Intact endothelium is actively anti-thrombotic: produces prostacyclin + nitric oxide (inhibit platelet activation / vasodilate), expresses thrombomodulin (activates protein C), and heparan sulfate (ATIII cofactor)
  • Damaged/dysfunctional endothelium loses this → contributes to thrombosis (part of Virchow's triad)

Overview — Haematopoiesis
Haematopoiesis = the production of all blood cells from a common haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) in the bone marrow — a continuous, tightly-regulated process replacing billions of cells daily.
The organising principle: a single pluripotent stem cell differentiates down two main lineages — myeloid and lymphoid — and where the process fails or goes wrong defines the cytopenias, leukaemias, and marrow failure syndromes.
Why it matters: explains why marrow failure causes pancytopenia, how leukaemias arise (lineage + maturation block), why EPO treats CKD anaemia, and the basis of stem cell transplant — cross-ref red cell/haemoglobin physiology, anaemia, leukaemias, CKD (EPO), the immune cells.
Where It Happens — changes with age
  • Fetus: yolk sac → liver + spleen (mid-gestation) → bone marrow (late)
  • Children: all bones
  • Adults: the axial skeleton — vertebrae, sternum, ribs, pelvis — plus the proximal ends of the femur and humerus (peripheral marrow becomes fatty)
  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis (liver/spleen reactivating) occurs in marrow stress/infiltration (e.g. myelofibrosis, thalassaemia) → hepatosplenomegaly
The Stem Cell Hierarchy — the lineage tree
📷 Image placeholder — Haematopoiesis lineage tree — pluripotent HSC → common myeloid progenitor (RBCs, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and common lymphoid progenitor (B, T, NK cells).
Pluripotent haematopoietic stem cell (HSC) → splits into two lineages:

MyeloidCommon myeloid progenitorRed cells, platelets (from megakaryocytes), granulocytes (neutrophils/eosinophils/basophils), monocytes

The two defining HSC properties: self-renewal (makes more stem cells, maintaining the stem cell pool — though the capacity is finite and declines with age) + differentiation (matures into all blood cell types — "pluripotent"; strictly multipotent in modern usage).
The maturation principle: cells become progressively committed (lose self-renewal, gain lineage specificity) as they mature → immature "blast" forms stay in the marrow; mature cells are released to blood.

Overview — Red Cell Physiology & Haemoglobin
Red blood cells (erythrocytes) exist to carry oxygen (and help with CO₂) — their structure, haemoglobin content, and lifecycle are all specialised for that single job.
The organising principle: the red cell is a biconcave, anucleate bag of haemoglobin optimised for gas transport and deformability — and the anaemias/haemoglobinopathies are best understood as failures of production, structure, or haemoglobin.
Why it matters: underpins the anaemias (by size), haemoglobinopathies (sickle cell, thalassaemia), haemolysis, and the bilirubin/jaundice link — cross-ref haematopoiesis, O₂ dissociation curve, anaemia, sickle cell, thalassaemia, bilirubin metabolism.
Red Cell Structure — form fits function
  • Biconcave disc: maximises surface-area-to-volume for gas exchange + allows deformability (to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself)
  • Anucleate (no nucleus/organelles in the mature cell): more room for haemoglobin + no mitochondria → relies on anaerobic glycolysis for energy (cannot use the O₂ it carries)
  • Flexible membrane (spectrin/ankyrin cytoskeleton): maintains shape + deformability → membrane defects cause abnormal shapes + haemolysis (e.g. hereditary spherocytosis)
  • Lifespan ~120 days: no nucleus → cannot repair → ages and is removed by the spleen (reticuloendothelial system)
Haemoglobin Structure — the oxygen-carrying molecule
📷 Image placeholder — Haemoglobin structure — 4 globin chains (2α + 2β in HbA), each with a haem group carrying a ferrous (Fe²⁺) iron and one O₂-binding site.
  • Structure: 4 globin chains, each with a haem group (an iron-containing porphyrin ring) → 4 O₂-binding sites per Hb (one per haem iron, in the Fe²⁺ state)
The iron point (high-yield): O₂ binds ferrous iron (Fe²⁺); if oxidised to ferric (Fe³⁺) → methaemoglobin, which cannot carry O₂ (methaemoglobinaemia).
Hb Chains Notes
HbA (97%)2α + 2βThe main adult haemoglobin
HbA2 (~2%)2α + 2δMinor; raised in β-thalassaemia trait
HbF (fetal)2α + 2γHigher O₂ affinity (left-shifted — pulls O₂ from maternal blood); replaced by HbA after birth
The chain logic (ties to haemoglobinopathies): α-chain problems → α-thalassaemia; β-chain problems → β-thalassaemia (presents after birth, as the HbF→HbA switch happens) and sickle cell (a β-chain point mutation).
Cooperative Binding & the Dissociation Curve
📷 Image placeholder — Oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve — the sigmoid shape from cooperative binding, with right shift (Bohr) unloading O₂ and left shift (HbF, CO).
  • The 4 haem groups show cooperativity (each O₂ bound eases the next) → the sigmoid O₂ dissociation curve (full detail in the respiratory oxygenation notes)
  • Shifts: Bohr effect (right shift unloads O₂ to tissues); HbF + CO are left-shifted
Red Cell Metabolism — why it needs protection (high-yield)
No mitochondria → relies on glycolysis for ATP, plus two protective pathways:
Pentose phosphate pathway → G6PD
  • Produces NADPH → glutathione → protects against oxidative damage; G6PD is the key enzyme
  • G6PD deficiency → oxidative haemolysis (triggered by infection, fava beans, drugs e.g. primaquine/sulfonamides; Heinz bodies, bite cells) — ties to the malaria primaquine + drug ADR notes
Pyruvate kinase (glycolysis)
  • Generates ATP for the membrane; PK deficiency → haemolysis
The Red Cell Lifecycle — production to breakdown (links to jaundice)
📷 Image placeholder — Red cell breakdown / bilirubin pathway — splenic macrophages split Hb into recycled globin + iron and haem → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin → liver → bile.
  • Production (erythropoiesis): in marrow, driven by EPO (kidney), needs iron, B12, folate as building blocks → reticulocyte → mature RBC
  • Lifespan: ~120 days
Breakdown — the bilirubin link (high-yield)
  • Old/damaged RBCs removed by the spleen/macrophages → haemoglobin split into:
  • Globin → recycled to amino acids
  • Iron → recycled (stored as ferritin, transported by transferrin)
  • Haem → biliverdin → bilirubin → unconjugated bilirubin → liver conjugates it → bile
The haemolysis logic: ↑red cell breakdown → ↑unconjugated bilirubin (pre-hepatic jaundice) + ↑LDH + ↓haptoglobin + ↑reticulocytes → the lab picture of haemolysis.

Overview — White Cells & the Immune Cells
White cells (leucocytes) are the cellular immune defence, produced in the marrow and circulating in blood. This note covers them as blood cells: what each does, the FBC differential, and the clinical patterns (which cell rises in which situation).
The organising principle: white cells split into the same myeloid vs lymphoid lineages as haematopoiesis, and each cell type rises in a characteristic situation — so the differential white cell count is a diagnostic clue.
Why it matters: explains interpreting the FBC differential, the response to bacterial vs viral vs parasitic infection, and the leukaemias/leucocytoses — cross-ref haematopoiesis (production), Immunity + Immunodeficiency notes (the immunological mechanisms — not repeated here), leukaemias, infection.

⚠ Red Flag — Safety Point
Unexplained IDA in men & post-menopausal women → bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy) [BSG]
To exclude GI malignancy — particularly colorectal or gastric cancer.
  • Use the 2-week-wait suspected-cancer pathway if aged ≥60, or younger with a positive FIT or alarm features [NICE]
  • Pre-menopausal women: treat menstrual loss + iron trial and scope only if ≥50, GI symptoms, FHx bowel cancer, or refractory

  • Ferritin is an acute phase reactant — it rises in inflammation

📷 Image placeholder — Duodenal enterocyte iron handling — gastric acid Fe³⁺→Fe²⁺, DMT-1 uptake, ferroportin export and hepcidin regulation; explains why PPIs/achlorhydria/H. pylori impair absorption.

Iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum. Gastric acid keeps iron in the soluble ferrous (Fe²⁺) form required for absorption via DMT-1. PPIs, post-gastrectomy, or H. pylori-related achlorhydria → Fe³⁺ (insoluble) → malabsorption.

Management
  1. Oral ferrous sulfate 200 mg once daily — first-line. (Current NICE/BSG practice: once-daily or alternate-day dosing is as effective as the older TDS regimen and better tolerated — frequent doses raise hepcidin and reduce fractional absorption.) Continue for 3 months after Hb correction to replenish stores.

    • Avoid if malabsorption is the cause
    • Recheck the FBC at 4 weeks — expect Hb to rise by about 20 g/L [NICE]

  2. IV iron infusion (ferric carboxymaltose / Ferinject, or ferric derisomaltose / Monofer) — if oral fails, is not tolerated, or malabsorption is the cause. Avoid during active sepsis — free iron feeds bacteria.

    • A raised threshold for chronic cardiovascular disease is not a NICE recommendation

The Logic — Why These Values?
IDA — body WANTS iron

Iron stores empty → body upregulates transferrin production to capture any available iron → ↑ TIBC. Stores depleted → ↓ ferritin.

"Empty shelves — more shopping trolleys sent out"

ACD — body HIDES iron

Hepcidin rises (acute phase reactant) → iron sequestered in macrophages → ↑ ferritin (stored away). Less transport needed → ↓ TIBC. Mechanism: starves bacteria of iron.

"Iron locked in the vault — no delivery trucks needed"

ACD causes: Chronic inflammation (RA, IBD, SLE), chronic infection (TB, HIV, osteomyelitis), malignancy, CKD (also ↓ EPO component).

Autosomal dominant — most common inherited haemolytic anaemia in Northern Europeans. Defect in RBC membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3) → sphere-shaped RBCs → fragile → destroyed in spleen.

HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Disease:
The decisive fork: HbS polymerises when deoxygenated. Deoxygenation → HbS polymerises → RBC sickles → two branches:
  • (1) haemolysis (fragile RBC → anaemia, gallstones, folate demand, aplastic vulnerability)
  • and (2) vaso-occlusion (rigid cell jams capillaries → infarcts, organ damage, crises)
  • Every complication lives on one of these two branches — with hyposplenism/functional asplenia as the third, clinically separate consequence of repeated splenic vaso-occlusion
  • Cross-ref Thalassaemia: same β-chain, same chr 11, but qualitative defect here vs quantitative there

  • Point mutation in β-globin (chr 11) → glutamate → valine at position 6 → HbS
  • Deoxy-HbS polymerises → RBC sickles; RBC lifespan 10–20 days (normal 120)
  • Sickling initially reversible on reoxygenation; becomes irreversible with repeated cycles → progressive organ damage
Epidemiology & genetics
  • Africa, Caribbean, India, Middle East
  • Heterozygote (trait) advantage — malaria protection → balanced polymorphism
  • Trait (HbAS): asymptomatic under normal conditions, and NOT the same as disease (HbSS) — but not entirely benign:
    • painless haematuria/papillary necrosis
    • hyposthenuria
    • splenic infarction at extreme altitude or hypoxia
    • and exertional rhabdomyolysis are recognised
  • Antenatal + newborn heel-prick screening (day 5)
The two-branch spine:
  • Haemolysis branch → anaemia, pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, aplastic crisis
  • Vaso-occlusion branch → stroke, ACS, AVN, priapism, CKD, retinopathy
  • Hyposplenism branch → functional asplenia → encapsulated-organism sepsis

📷 Image placeholder — Vaso-occlusion diagram — rigid sickled cells jamming a capillary → ischaemia/infarction; and dactylitis of the hands in a child.
Key discriminator: reticulocytes are HIGH in sequestration (marrow compensating) but LOW in aplastic crisis (marrow suppressed by parvovirus B19) — classic SBA.
CrisisMechanismKey discriminatorManagement
Vaso-occlusive (painful)Capillary occlusion → ischaemiaPain ± fever; dactylitis in children; clinical diagnosis
  • Strong opioid within 30 minutes plus regular paracetamol and an NSAID (unless contraindicated)
  • Warmth and hydration
  • Oxygen if SpO₂ is 95% or below on air, or below the patient’s own baseline — see the protocol section below

Acute chest syndromePulmonary vaso-occlusion/infarctNew CXR infiltrate (≥1 complete lung segment) plus any one of fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, wheeze, cough or new hypoxia — fever is not required — leading cause of death
  • Antibiotics (incl. atypical cover), oxygen titrated to SpO₂ >95%, analgesia, incentive spirometry, IV fluids without overload
  • Transfusion — simple top-up if Hb falling, urgent exchange if severe or deteriorating; ± NIV/ITU
  • Escalate early — urgent haematology/haemoglobinopathy team involvement and a critical-care review, because exchange and ventilatory support are decided there, not at the bedside
Transfusion logic:
  • Simple top-up transfusion for symptomatic anaemia, aplastic crisis, splenic sequestration and pre-operative optimisation
  • An uncomplicated painful crisis is NOT an indication to transfuse, and Hb should not be pushed above about 100 g/L (raising the haematocrit causes hyperviscosity and worsens sickling)
  • Exchange transfusion (rapid HbS% reduction, target <30%) for acute stroke, severe or deteriorating acute chest syndrome, and multiorgan failure
  • Acute splenic sequestration is treated with fluids and cautious small-volume simple transfusion, not exchange — the pooled cells are auto-transfused back as the spleen decompresses
  • Always use extended phenotype-matched (Rh and Kell) blood — alloimmunisation is common; chronic transfusion needs ferritin/T2* monitoring and iron chelation
The Acute Painful Episode — UK Protocol
The clock starts at the door.
  • Offer analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation to every patient attending hospital with an acute painful sickle cell episode (NICE)
  • The Royal College of Emergency Medicine tightens the emergency-department target to within 15 minutes
  • Then reassess pain every 30 minutes until pain is controlled, and at least 4-hourly thereafter, using an age-appropriate pain scoring tool
What to give
  • Strong opioid — morphine by a suitable route (oral / IV / SC), titrated to effect; patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) if repeated boluses are needed
  • Plus regular paracetamol AND an NSAID, by a suitable route, unless contraindicated — these adjuncts are recommended positively for all patients alongside the opioid (NICE)
  • Follow the patient's individualised care plan where one exists — many patients already know the regimen that works for them
  • Treat the precipitant and the basics: infection, dehydration, cold exposure, hypoxia; keep the patient warm
What NOT to do
  • Do not offer pethidine — an explicit negative recommendation (NICE). Its metabolite norpethidine accumulates in renal impairment (common in SCD) and is proconvulsant
  • Oxygen is not automatic.
    • Document SpO₂ on air, and give oxygen when saturations are 95% or below on air, or below the patient's own baseline (NICE)
    • Remember the reading itself can mislead: pulse oximeters overestimate true saturation in darker skin, so a borderline number in a patient with sickle cell disease may be hiding real hypoxaemia — treat the patient, and get a gas if you are unsure
  • Do not delay or dilute the opioid because a patient attends often, has a high tolerance, or “looks well” — the diagnosis is clinical and the pain is whatever the patient says it is
Monitoring while on opioids
  • Record pain score, sedation score, respiratory rate, SpO₂ and blood pressure — hourly for the first 6 hours, then at least 4-hourly once stable
  • Naloxone immediately available wherever the opioid is given
  • Prescribe routinely alongside the opioid: a laxative, plus antiemetic and antihistamine/antipruritic as required
  • Stay alert for evolving acute chest syndrome — new hypoxia, chest pain or breathlessness, classically 24–72 h into a painful crisis
Why this is examined — “No One's Listening” (APPG)
  • Inquiry by the APPG on Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia with the Sickle Cell Society into avoidable deaths and failures of care in secondary care
  • Found routine failure to meet the national standard on timely pain relief in A&E and on general wards
  • Patients disbelieved about their own pain and mislabelled as drug-seeking; low awareness of sickle cell among non-specialist staff
  • Concluded that these negative attitudes are underpinned by racism, compounded by chronic under-staffing of specialist services
Chronic Management

Ongoing therapies
  • Avoid triggers — dehydration, cold, hypoxia, infection
  • Folic acid — chronic haemolysis
  • Hydroxycarbamide — ↑HbF → fewer crises; first-line disease-modifying agent (indication, titration and monitoring in Hydroxycarbamide in Practice below)
  • Transfusion for severe anaemia
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant — potentially curative (best with an HLA-matched sibling donor, mainly in children)
  • Gene therapy — exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy): a CRISPR therapy approved in the UK (MHRA)
    • a world first that edits BCL11A to reactivate HbF
    • a newer potentially curative option for severe disease without a matched donor
  • No longer used:
    • crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin) no longer has a UK licence (MHRA) — it was withdrawn after a phase 3 trial failed to confirm benefit, and NHS supply has ended;
    • and voxelotor (anti-sickling) was withdrawn worldwide over safety concerns. Do not start either
Infection prophylaxis — functional asplenia
And the corollary: fever in a patient with sickle cell disease is an emergency, not a wait-and-see.
  • Assess urgently, take blood cultures and give broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly
  • Prophylactic penicillin does not exclude pneumococcal sepsis, and a hyposplenic patient can deteriorate within hours
  • Penicillin V (phenoxymethylpenicillin) TWICE daily
    • 500 mg BD in adults
    • in children 62.5 mg BD (<1 yr), 125 mg BD (1–5 yr), 250 mg BD (6–17 yr)
    • Started by 3 months of age and continued lifelong (erythromycin if penicillin-allergic)
  • Pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years
  • Meningococcal, Hib, annual flu vaccines
  • Rationale: recurrent splenic infarction → functional asplenia → encapsulated organism risk (Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis)
Stroke Prevention & Neurological Surveillance
Stroke is the one vaso-occlusive complication we screen for prospectively. Transcranial Doppler (TCD) finds the child whose cerebral vessels are already narrowed and high-flow, before the infarct — and starting transfusion at that point prevents most strokes.
The TCD screening programme
  • Who: children with HbSS or HbSβ⁰-thalassaemia (the genotypes with the highest stroke risk)
  • When: annually from age 2 until at least age 16
  • What is measured: the peak blood flow velocity in the middle cerebral and distal internal carotid arteries — a high velocity means a narrowed, high-flow vessel
  • TCD is a screening test: an abnormal value is confirmed on repeat before committing a child to a lifelong transfusion programme
Acute stroke in SCD — a different pathway
  • Sudden focal deficit in a patient with SCD is a haemoglobinopathy emergency: urgent imaging and an immediate call to the specialist haemoglobinopathy team
  • Treatment is urgent exchange transfusion to drop HbS rapidly — not the standard thrombolysis pathway used for atherothrombotic stroke
  • Secondary prevention is then an ongoing transfusion programme, because recurrence risk without it is very high
Normal velocityLow riskContinue annual screening
Borderline velocityIntermediateRepeat sooner than a year — an intermediate-risk group that may convert
Abnormally high velocityHigh risk of overt strokeChronic transfusion programme maintaining HbS <30% — this dramatically reduces the risk of stroke
Silent cerebral infarction:
  • MRI-visible infarcts with no focal deficit — the commonest form of brain injury in SCD, and easy to miss because nothing dramatic happens
  • They are associated with falling cognitive performance, school difficulty and a raised risk of later overt stroke, so declining school performance in a child with SCD is a reason to think about MRI, not just about the child
Hydroxycarbamide in Practice
Knowing that it raises HbF is only half the card. Finals and F1 prescribing ask who gets it, how it is titrated and what is monitored (BSH).
Who to offer it to
  • Offer to patients with HbSS or HbSβ⁰-thalassaemia who have recurrent vaso-occlusive crises or evidence of end-organ damage — and note that in children with HbSS/HbSβ⁰ it is offered from around 9 months of age irrespective of severity
  • Classic thresholds: ≥3 crises per year requiring hospital admission, or crises that interfere with daily life, schooling or work
  • Also used for recurrent acute chest syndrome and severe symptomatic anaemia
  • Titrate to the maximum tolerated dose (up to about 35 mg/kg/day) rather than settling for a low fixed dose — underdosing is a common reason for apparent “failure”
Monitoring — the numbers to know
  • FBC + reticulocyte count 2 weeks after starting and 2 weeks after every dose increment
  • Once on a stable dose, at least every 8–12 weeks for the duration of treatment
  • Stop treatment if the neutrophil count is ≤1.0 × 10⁹/L (restart at a lower dose once recovered)
  • A rising MCV is the practical marker of adherence and response — if the MCV has not moved, suspect the tablets are not being taken
Adverse effects
  • Myelosuppression — neutropenia, thrombocytopenia (dose-limiting, and the reason for the FBC schedule)
  • Skin and nail hyperpigmentation
  • Drug-induced leg ulcers — awkward, because SCD itself causes leg ulcers
  • Nausea, alopecia, rash
Pregnancy — the counselling point
  • Teratogenic — and reduces sperm counts
  • Stop at least 3 months before a planned conception, in both women and men
  • Discuss contraception at the point of starting, not at the point of a positive test
  • Unplanned pregnancy on treatment → stop the drug and refer urgently to a joint obstetric–haematology service

Priapism
An erection lasting more than 4 hours in sickle cell disease is a urological emergency , not an embarrassing inconvenience.
  • It is ischaemic (low-flow) priapism — a compartment syndrome of the corpora, with sickled cells obstructing venous outflow
  • Every hour of delay costs erectile tissue
Two patterns
  • Stuttering priapism — recurrent, self-limiting episodes lasting <4 hours, often waking the patient from sleep. A warning sign: it predicts major episodes
  • Major (acute ischaemic) priapism — a painful, rigid erection lasting >4 hours. The glans and corpus spongiosum are typically soft while the corpora cavernosa are hard
  • Ask about it directly — men frequently do not volunteer the symptom, and the commonest failure here is a consultation in which it is never raised
First steps (and what patients are taught at home)
  • Hydration (oral or IV) and prompt analgesia along the usual acute-episode pathway
  • Warm bath or shower, emptying the bladder, and gentle exercise such as walking
  • These are for the early episode only — they must never be used to run the clock past 4 hours
  • Educate patients to attend early: the message is “come in at 2–3 hours”, not “wait and see overnight”
If it persists beyond ~4 hours — urology, now
  • Corporal aspiration ± irrigation of the corpora cavernosa, followed by intracavernosal phenylephrine
    • an α-agonist that causes cavernosal smooth-muscle contraction and venous outflow
    • given in small diluted aliquots, repeated at intervals up to a stated maximum
    • with blood-pressure and pulse monitoring for hypertension and reflex bradycardia
    • Use the dose in your local urology/haemoglobinopathy protocol or the BNF.
  • Never irrigate with cold saline in sickle cell disease — cooling precipitates further sickling and can trigger a generalised painful crisis. Use body-temperature/warmed fluid
  • Failure of aspiration and sympathomimetic injection → surgical shunt
Where transfusion fits — and what happens if you wait
  • Exchange transfusion is adjunctive only.
    • It may be considered alongside urological treatment, but must never delay aspiration and injection
    • A classic exam trap is choosing “arrange exchange transfusion” over “refer immediately to urology”
  • Beyond roughly 24 hours, ischaemia gives way to corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction — damage that no later intervention reverses
  • After recovery, address recurrence: review hydroxycarbamide and the overall disease-modifying plan, and give the patient a written escalation rule

The decisive fork: Which globin chain, and how many genes are affected? Alpha is graded by number of defective alleles (1→4); beta by trait vs non-transfusion-dependent vs transfusion-dependent. Everything — severity, presentation, transfusion-dependence — falls out of gene dosage. Cross-ref Anaemia note: thalassaemia is a key microcytic cause.

What is thalassaemia?
  • Haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive
  • Reduced or absent globin chain production
  • Defect: alpha (chromosome 16) or beta (chromosome 11)
The disease mechanism

Reduced production of one chain → excess of the paired chain → unstable precipitates → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis → fragile RBCs → splenomegaly. It is the imbalance that causes disease.

Beta-Thalassaemia

Chr 11 mutation → reduced/absent beta chain → excess alpha chains precipitate → haemolysis + ineffective erythropoiesis.

Trait vs IDA discriminator (highest-yield SBA):
  • In thalassaemia trait, ferritin and iron stores are normal
  • The microcytosis is disproportionate to the degree of anaemia
  • IDA has ↓ferritin, ↑TIBC, low iron
  • HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis confirms beta-thalassaemia trait
  • But check iron status before you act on either result: co-existing iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask beta-trait, so a normal HbA2 in a microcytic patient with a low ferritin does not exclude it — treat the iron deficiency and repeat
  • And never start empirical iron in a microcytic patient without confirming deficiency first — a trait patient given iron they do not need is simply being iron-loaded
Bony abnormalities — marrow expansion
  • Extramedullary haematopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly
  • Marrow expansion → ↑fracture risk, enlarged maxilla, frontal/parietal bossing
  • “Hair-on-end” skull X-ray appearance (classic SBA image)
Alpha-Thalassaemia
📷 Image placeholder — Alpha-globin gene-dosage diagram — 1 to 4 defective genes mapping to silent carrier → trait → HbH disease → Hb Barts (hydrops fetalis).

Chr 16; 4 alpha-globin genes. Severity by number of defective alleles. Excess gamma chains (fetal) or beta chains form unstable tetramers (HbH, Hb Barts).

Alleles affectedNameClinical picture

Alpha thalassaemia trait often has a normal Hb electrophoresis — diagnosis requires genetic testing (or HPLC showing Hb Barts in neonates). In HbH disease, supravital staining with brilliant cresyl blue shows HbH inclusion bodies ("golf-ball" cells), and electrophoresis shows a fast-moving HbH band.

Management
Transfusion-dependent (major)
  • Regular transfusions every 3–4 weeks to keep the pre-transfusion Hb at 95–105 g/L — suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, prevents bony deformity and extramedullary haematopoiesis. Extended red cell typing before the first transfusion, then Rh- and Kell-matched units lifelong — alloimmunisation makes every future crossmatch harder and causes delayed haemolytic reactions (BSH)
  • Lifelong folic acid
  • Splenectomy for hypersplenism — vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, and annual influenza), ideally at least two weeks beforehand, then lifelong prophylactic penicillin V. And the corollary: fever in an asplenic patient is an emergency — blood cultures and prompt broad-spectrum antibiotics; prophylactic penicillin does not exclude pneumococcal sepsis (BSH)
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant — potentially curative (best in children before iron overload)
  • Gene therapy — exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy): a CRISPR therapy (approved in the UK (MHRA)) reactivating HbF — a newer potentially curative option for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia without a matched donor
Trait / mild disease
  • No treatment required outside pregnancy — but in pregnancy give high-dose folic acid 5 mg, from preconception through the first trimester
  • Genetic counselling — and formal carrier testing of the partner before any risk is excluded
  • Avoid iron unless deficiency is confirmed on iron studies
Iron overload — the central long-term problem
📷 Image placeholder — Iron-overload organ map — transfusional iron deposition in heart (cardiomyopathy, leading cause of death), liver, pancreas, pituitary and gonads.

Iron overload comes from two sources: repeated transfusion, and increased gut absorption (ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin) — so non-transfusion-dependent patients overload too. Iron accumulates in organs:

  • Heart → cardiomyopathy / cardiac failure — leading cause of death
  • Liver → cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Pituitary → growth failure, infertility
  • Thyroid / parathyroid → hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism
  • Pancreas → diabetes mellitus
  • Gonads → hypogonadism, delayed puberty

Iron chelation: subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox / deferiprone.

  • Deferiprone causes agranulocytosis — check the neutrophil count before starting and weekly on treatment, stop the drug if neutrophils fall below 1.5 × 109/L, and tell the patient to stop it and get an urgent FBC the same day for fever, sore throat or flu-like symptoms [BNF]
  • It is the most effective chelator at removing cardiac iron
  • Monitor serum ferritin plus T2* MRI to quantify cardiac and liver iron — cardiac T2* is what predicts the cardiomyopathy

Exam Pearls
Alpha thalassaemia trait — electrophoresis can be normal; needs genetic testing. Beta trait — electrophoresis shows ↑HbA2.
Disproportionate microcytosis + normal ferritin → think thalassaemia trait, not IDA. HbA2 >3.5% confirms beta-thalassaemia trait on electrophoresis.
Hb Barts (4 alleles) = hydrops fetalis, usually fatal in utero or soon after birth. HbH (3 alleles) = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia.
Transfuse to a pre-transfusion Hb of 95–105 g/L in major → suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis → prevents bony deformity and extramedullary haematopoiesis.
Curative option = allogeneic stem cell transplant. Splenectomy for hypersplenism — always vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and give the annual influenza vaccine.
Cardiac iron overload is the leading cause of death in beta-thalassaemia major. Treat with chelation (desferrioxamine / deferasirox / deferiprone), monitor ferritin and cardiac T2* MRI.
HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma:
Multiple myeloma = malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells → monoclonal paraprotein (usually IgG > IgA).
  • The dividing line from precursor states is end-organ damage: MGUS and smouldering myeloma lack CRAB; myeloma has it.
  • That discriminator is how the spectrum is usually examined — but note three myeloma-defining biomarkers now also diagnose myeloma and mandate treatment with no CRAB feature:
    • clonal marrow plasma cells ≥60%
    • involved:uninvolved serum free light chain ratio ≥100
    • or >1 focal lesion on MRI

  • B — urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains)
  • L — serum-free light-chain assay — essential
    • because in light-chain-only myeloma there is no intact paraprotein and serum protein electrophoresis can be completely normal
    • a serum-only screen will miss it, so urine Bence-Jones and serum free light chains must both be sent
  • I — serum immunoglobulins (paraprotein type)
  • P — serum protein electrophoresis — monoclonal band
📷 Image placeholder — Skull X-ray showing multiple punched-out lytic lesions ("raindrop skull"), the classic myeloma radiology.
Confirm: bone marrow biopsy
Clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma) — this is mandatory.
  • Combined with a myeloma-defining event = diagnostic of myeloma
  • a CRAB feature, or one of the biomarkers: clonal plasma cells ≥60%, free light chain ratio ≥100, >1 focal lesion on MRI
Imaging (preference order)
  1. Whole-body MRI — first-line
  2. Whole-body low-dose CT
  3. Skeletal survey (plain X-ray)
Classic signs
  • punched-out lytic lesions
  • raindrop skull
  • vertebral collapse
  • Isotope bone scans are NOT used — myeloma lesions are purely lytic with no osteoblastic reaction, so they show no tracer uptake
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Transplant-eligible pathway — Dara-VTd induction → autologous SCT → lenalidomide maintenance, versus the non-transplant regimen, with the thalidomide→VTE-prophylaxis flag highlighted.
Anti-myeloma therapy
  • Bortezomib + thalidomide + dexamethasone (VTD) — the classic triplet backbone
    • Current practice adds daratumumab (anti-CD38 monoclonal) → the “Dara-VTd” quadruplet is now standard first-line for transplant-eligible patients (deeper responses; recommended by NICE)
  • Newer relapsed/refractory options: anti-BCMA CAR-T (ide-cel, cilta-cel) and bispecific antibodies (e.g. teclistamab)
  • Autologous stem cell transplant in fit patients
  • Relapsing-remitting course; managed by haem-onc MDT
VTE prophylaxis — exam trap
The immunomodulatory drugs — thalidomide AND lenalidomide — are prothrombotic, especially combined with dexamethasone
  • Thromboprophylaxis must be co-prescribed: aspirin at standard risk, LMWH (or a DOAC) at higher risk
  • A classic MCQ distractor — and remember it applies to lenalidomide maintenance too
  • They are also highly teratogenic and are prescribed only inside the Pregnancy Prevention Programme — 28-day prescriptions, supervised pregnancy testing and effective contraception (MHRA)
Bone disease
  • Bisphosphonates (zoledronate) — suppress osteoclasts, reduce fractures
    • Zoledronic acid is offered to everyone with myeloma to prevent bone disease — not only to those who already have lytic lesions (pamidronate, then clodronate, are the alternatives)
  • Before the first dose: “consider immediate referral for dental assessment and treatment” — the risk being avoided is osteonecrosis of the jaw.
    • Check renal function/eGFR first — zoledronic acid is dose-reduced in moderate impairment and avoided below a creatinine clearance of about 30 mL/min
    • Denosumab where bisphosphonates are unsuitable, but correct any hypocalcaemia first, co-prescribe calcium and vitamin D and monitor the calcium — severe hypocalcaemia is commonest in exactly this renal-impaired group (MHRA)
  • Radiotherapy for localised bone pain
  • Orthopaedic stabilisation for pathological fracture
  • Vertebroplasty / kyphoplasty for vertebral collapse
Supportive care
  • Hypercalcaemia:
    • stop thiazides and any calcium/vitamin D supplements
    • then IV fluids (0.9% sodium chloride to restore volume)
    • then an IV bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid, dose-adjusted for renal function) once rehydrated — calcium falls over 2–4 days
    • Loop diuretics are NOT first-line; use them only for fluid overload during rehydration
  • Transfusion for symptomatic anaemia
  • Infection prophylaxis + vaccinations
    • and treat any fever in a patient on anti-myeloma treatment as neutropenic sepsis: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, without waiting for the neutrophil count (NICE)
  • Renal: avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins, dialysis if needed — but see Myeloma Kidney below: the definitive treatment of the AKI is urgent anti-myeloma therapy
Myeloma Kidney — Treating the AKI
The principle
  • in cast nephropathy the kidney is being injured by free light chains arriving from the marrow
  • Fluids and dialysis buy time, but the only way to stop the injury is to switch off light-chain production — so urgent anti-myeloma therapy is the definitive treatment of myeloma-induced AKI
Do
  • Start anti-myeloma therapy immediately — a bortezomib-based regimen is started without waiting for renal recovery; the exact regimen is a haematology decision
  • Aggressive rehydration — IV fluids to restore circulating volume and keep light chains moving through the tubules
  • Treat the hypercalcaemia — it is both a cause and an amplifier of the AKI, so it is part of the renal rescue
  • Stop ACE inhibitors / ARBs and NSAIDs; avoid iodinated contrast
  • Dialysis for the usual AKI indications only — a bridge while the anti-myeloma treatment takes effect
Do not
Do not do plasma exchange for myeloma-induced acute renal disease
  • Stripping light chains out of the plasma does nothing about the marrow that keeps making them — and the trials showed no renal benefit
  • Do not confuse the indications: plasma exchange is the treatment of symptomatic hyperviscosity, not of cast nephropathy
  • Same disease, different problem
Time-dependent: renal recovery — including coming off dialysis — is genuinely achievable if light-chain production is switched off quickly. Treat new renal impairment in myeloma as the emergency it is.
After Induction — Transplant, Maintenance, Relapse
The pathway: induction → is this patient transplant-eligible? → intensive arm (autologous SCT, then maintenance) or non-intensive arm → relapse → next line of therapy.
Transplant-eligible arm
  • Eligibility is fitness, not a birthday — judged on performance status, comorbidity (cardiac, respiratory, renal) and frailty
    • There is no hard age cut-off; the decision is an MDT one
  • Induction to maximum response, then stem cell mobilisation (G-CSF ± chemotherapy) and harvest by apheresis — the patient's own stem cells are collected and frozen
  • Autologous, not allogeneic — the graft is a rescue, not the anti-myeloma treatment
Transplant-ineligible arm

Patients not fit enough for intensive consolidation are treated with ongoing drug therapy rather than a fixed course plus transplant, chosen and monitored by the haematology team.

The bit students miss
Autologous SCT is not curative.
  • It deepens and prolongs the first remission — but relapse is expected
  • each relapse triggers the next line of therapy, with remissions typically getting shorter
Monitoring Response & Detecting Relapse
The tracking marker
  • The paraprotein on serum protein electrophoresis is the marker you follow — measured serially through treatment, its level tracks disease burden
  • Serum free light chains are followed instead where the disease is light-chain-only (no measurable serum paraprotein), and they move faster
  • A falling paraprotein = responding; a plateau = maximum response from that line of treatment
Surveillance intervals
  • Monitor at least every 3 months after treatment is completed — paraprotein (or serum free light chains) alongside FBC, U&E and calcium
  • MGUS is the contrast — monitored annually, because what is being watched for there is progression, not relapse
A rising paraprotein is the first sign of relapse — it usually climbs before symptoms return
  • Repeat it, reassess the patient for new end-organ damage, and take them back to the haem-onc MDT for the next line of therapy
  • Myeloma remains incurable: this monitoring exists to catch relapse early, not to declare cure
Complications
📷 Image placeholder — Myeloma emergencies at a glance — spinal cord compression (urgent MRI spine), acute hypercalcaemia, AKI/cast nephropathy and hyperviscosity.
Marrow / bone branch
  • Anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia
  • Recurrent infections (immunoparesis)
  • Pathological fractures
  • Spinal cord compression
  • Hypercalcaemia
Paraprotein branch
  • Renal failure (cast nephropathy)
  • Hyperviscosity syndrome
  • AL amyloid → cardiac, renal, peripheral neuropathy
  • Treatment-related neuropathy (bortezomib, thalidomide)
Exam Pearls
Transplant: eligibility is fitness, not age; lenalidomide maintenance follows; it is not curative.
CRAB = the diagnostic tetrad. Its presence separates myeloma from MGUS/smouldering — the single most important discriminator.
Waldenström's = IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease. Anaemia is normocytic normochromic; ESR and plasma viscosity raised.
Raindrop skull + punched-out lytic lesions = classic radiology. Whole-body MRI is now first-line imaging (more sensitive than skeletal survey).
Bence-Jones protein = urinary light chains. Urine dipstick is negative — dipstick detects albumin, not light chains. Must send urine electrophoresis.
Thalidomide or lenalidomide → VTE — always co-prescribe thromboprophylaxis (aspirin at standard risk, LMWH/DOAC at higher risk). A guaranteed MCQ trap.
The paraprotein is the tracking marker (serum free light chains if light-chain-only). Monitor at least every 3 months after treatment — a rising paraprotein means relapse. MGUS, by contrast, is annual.
Myeloma AKI: the treatment is the chemotherapy. Fluids, treat the calcium, stop the ACEi/NSAIDs — then start anti-myeloma therapy immediately. Plasma exchange is not indicated — a favourite negative stem.
Zoledronic acid is offered to every myeloma patient to prevent bone disease — not just those with lytic lesions
  • Dental assessment comes before the first dose (osteonecrosis of the jaw) — but it must not delay urgent myeloma treatment (NICE)
Over-60 + persistent back pain or unexplained fracture → screen for myeloma — FBC, calcium and plasma viscosity/ESR, with serum protein electrophoresis and serum free light chains.
  • If those are consistent with myeloma: very urgent electrophoresis and Bence-Jones urine within 48 hours, and refer on a suspected cancer pathway (NICE)
  • Do not attribute to mechanical or osteoporotic without checking

Hodgkin Lymphoma
📷 Image placeholder — Histology of a Reed-Sternberg cell — the large binucleate "owl-eye" cell (CD15+/CD30+) that defines Hodgkin lymphoma on lymph-node biopsy.
Risk Factors:
  • EBV (especially mixed cellularity subtype) · HIV · Immunosuppression
  • Note HIV raises NHL risk far more than HL risk (DLBCL, Burkitt, primary CNS lymphoma)
  • Other NHL associations:
    • H. pylori and gastric MALT
    • Sjögren's and Hashimoto's with marginal-zone lymphoma of the affected gland
    • and coeliac disease with enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma (EATL) — suspect it when a previously stable coeliac patient becomes refractory to a gluten-free diet with weight loss, abdominal pain or small-bowel obstruction/perforation
Histological subtypes — classical HL vs NLPHL
  • Classical HL accounts for the great majority of cases.
    • Its diagnostic cell is the Reed-Sternberg cell — a large binucleate cell whose two mirror-image lobes each carry a huge eosinophilic nucleolus, giving the "owl-eye" appearance
    • Immunophenotype CD15+ CD30+ CD20−
  • Classical HL has four histological subtypes:
    • Nodular sclerosis — the commonest classical subtype; typically a young adult, often a woman, with a mediastinal mass. Fibrous bands divide the node into nodules.
    • Mixed cellularity — the most strongly EBV-associated subtype; tends to affect older patients and those who are immunosuppressed or HIV-positive.
    • Lymphocyte-rich — uncommon; abundant background lymphocytes, few RS cells, generally a favourable outlook.
    • Lymphocyte-depleted — the rarest; sparse lymphocytes with many RS cells, seen in older and HIV-positive patients, and the most aggressive.
  • Nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL (NLPHL) is a separate entity, not a fifth classical subtype.
    • The malignant cell is the "popcorn" (LP) cell — a polylobated nucleus like a popped kernel — rather than a classical Reed-Sternberg cell, and its markers are the mirror image of classical HL: CD20+ CD30− CD15− (and CD45+)
    • It is indolent, usually presents early-stage, relapses late, and — being CD20+ — responds to rituximab
Presentation
  • Painless cervical lymphadenopathy — in UK primary care, unexplained persistent lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly warrants referral on the suspected cancer pathway (assessment within 2 weeks)
    • particularly with fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss, pruritus, breathlessness or alcohol-induced nodal pain
    • in a child or young person the same findings need very urgent assessment within 48 hours (NICE)
    • Check an urgent FBC at the same time
  • Mediastinal mass on CXR
  • B symptoms: fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months
  • BUZZWORD: Alcohol-induced nodal pain — the classic HL buzzword and effectively diagnostic in an exam stem, but present in only a few per cent of real patients, so its absence means nothing
Investigations
  • Excision (whole-node) biopsy is the diagnostic test — fine-needle aspiration is NOT adequate
    • because the diagnosis and subtype depend on the architecture of the node and the reactive cellular background around the malignant cells, and an aspirate yields cells without architecture.
    • Wherever lymphoma is a possibility, get the tissue before starting corticosteroids — steroids are lymphocytolytic and can render the histology non-diagnostic
    • A core biopsy is the acceptable alternative when the node is deep or inaccessible
    • Excision biopsy → Reed-Sternberg cells: large binucleate cells with owl-eye nucleoli (CD15+ CD30+, CD20−) — this marker profile defines classical HL; NLPHL is CD20+ and CD30−
  • PET-CT for staging
  • FBC: eosinophilia, lymphopenia in advanced disease
  • ESR: disease activity marker
  • LDH: prognostic (it is an IPI variable), and a marker of bulk, tumour lysis risk and transformation
  • HIV and hepatitis B and C serology before treatment — rituximab can reactivate hepatitis B, so HBsAg and anti-HBc are checked before any anti-CD20 antibody is given
Management — ABVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy
Adriamycin (doxorubicin)
Bleomycin
Vinblastine
Dacarbazine
  • Currency: for advanced-stage HL, brentuximab vedotin + AVD is now recommended for untreated stage 3–4 CD30-positive disease (NICE)
  • nivolumab + AVD has outperformed it in trials but is not yet recommended for NHS use.
  • ABVD remains standard for early-stage disease.
ABVD Toxicities
Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis
Adriamycin (doxorubicin) → cardiomyopathy
Vinblastine → peripheral neuropathy, constipation
Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
📷 Image placeholder — Burkitt lymphoma histology — the "starry-sky" appearance (tingible-body macrophages among sheets of lymphocytes); a classic buzzword image.
More common than HL — roughly six times as common. Most are B-cell origin.
  • R-CHOP (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin, Oncovin/vincristine, Prednisolone) is the standard regimen for DLBCL and most aggressive B-cell NHL — but it is not the treatment for every NHL:
    • indolent disease is often observed
    • gastric MALT is treated by H. pylori eradication
    • and Burkitt lymphoma needs an intensive short-course regimen with CNS prophylaxis, not R-CHOP.
  • (For relapsed/refractory DLBCL, anti-CD19 CAR-T therapy — axicabtagene/tisagenlecleucel — and bispecific antibodies are now established options.)

Burkitt's Lymphoma
  • Highly aggressive — a medical emergency (doubling time ~24 h) with the highest tumour lysis risk of any lymphoma, which can occur spontaneously before chemotherapy
  • admit, hydrate, rasburicase, and treat urgently with an intensive short-course regimen (not R-CHOP)

Follicular lymphoma — when to treat, and transformation
  • Watch and wait is standard for asymptomatic, low-bulk disease. Starting chemotherapy immediately does not improve overall survival, so the patient is observed with regular clinical review rather than treated.
  • Treat when there is a reason to: B symptoms or other symptomatic disease, bulky nodal masses, compression of or threat to an organ, marrow failure from marrow infiltration, or steady progression.
  • First-line treatment is rituximab + chemotherapy (anti-CD20 antibody on a chemotherapy backbone), followed by rituximab maintenance, which prolongs progression-free survival — a benefit in overall survival has not been shown.
  • FL is indolent but not curable with standard therapy: expect a relapsing–remitting course over many years, with treatment given in episodes.
  • Transformation to DLBCL is the feared event.
    • Suspect it when one node suddenly grows rapidly out of keeping with the rest, the LDH rises, or new B symptoms appear — then re-biopsy, targeting the most FDG-avid site on PET-CT
    • Transformed disease is treated as an aggressive lymphoma, not as FL
Tumour Lysis Syndrome
  • Massive cell death after chemo → ↑K⁺, ↑phosphate, ↓Ca²⁺, ↑uric acid → renal failure, arrhythmia
  • Prevention: IV fluids plus allopurinol for standard-risk patients, or rasburicase for high-risk disease (bulky/high-grade lymphoma such as Burkitt, high LDH, renal impairment)
  • Rasburicase is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency — it causes severe haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia — and is not given alongside allopurinol — so check G6PD status before giving it
  • Monitor U&Es, calcium, phosphate and urate before treatment and repeatedly through the first days in high-risk patients
  • Do not correct an asymptomatic hypocalcaemia while the phosphate is high — calcium-phosphate deposition worsens the kidney injury; treat only symptomatic hypocalcaemia
  • Escalate for renal replacement if there is refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguric AKI or fluid overload (BSH)
Ann Arbor Staging

Suffix:
  • A = no B symptoms
  • B = B symptoms present
  • E = limited extranodal extension contiguous with an involved nodal site (e.g. stage IIE) — this is NOT stage IV
  • S = splenic involvement (the spleen is lymphoid tissue, so this is not stage IV either)
Ann Arbor stage is then grouped into limited (early) stage and advanced stage — the split that actually decides how they are treated, and the grouping introduced by the modern Lugano revision of Ann Arbor, which also made PET-CT the staging and response standard.
  • The full staging criteria, the bulk and extranodal modifiers, and the International Prognostic Index (IPI) are set out in Risk Scores & Criteria — Haematology & Oncology.
Response Assessment
Staging tells you how much disease there is; response assessment tells you whether treatment is working.
  • PET-CT is used for both — a scan part-way through treatment shows early whether the disease is responding — and in Hodgkin lymphoma that interim scan is a decision point: a negative scan allows bleomycin to be dropped and treatment continued as AVD, a positive scan prompts escalation — and a scan at the end shows whether remission has been achieved
  • This is why PET-CT rather than CT alone is the modern standard in Hodgkin lymphoma
  • A residual mass on CT after treatment is often fibrosis rather than active disease, and a persistently positive scan is biopsied before anyone is called refractory, because infection and inflammation take up tracer too
Late Effects, Survivorship and Fertility
Most people with Hodgkin lymphoma are cured, and most are young when they are treated — so the long-term consequences of the treatment become the dominant clinical problem, often decades later.
  • This is why modern protocols use less radiotherapy, smaller fields and PET-guided de-escalation
  • and why survivors need lifelong follow-up rather than discharge at five years.
Second malignancies
  • Secondary AML and MDS — driven by alkylating agents and topoisomerase-II inhibitors. These appear relatively early, within the first decade, and are often heralded by an unexplained cytopenia or a dysplastic marrow.
  • Solid tumours arising within the radiotherapy field — these appear much later and the risk continues to rise for decades: lung (compounded by smoking), thyroid, breast, stomach and sarcoma.
  • Breast cancer after mediastinal radiotherapy in women treated young is the classic answer.
    • The excess risk is large enough that these women are entered into a dedicated early breast-screening programme, beginning years before population screening would start.
Cardiovascular, pulmonary and endocrine late effects
  • Cardiovascular disease — anthracycline (doxorubicin) cardiomyopathy compounded by mediastinal radiotherapy
    • which accelerates coronary disease and causes valve disease and constrictive pericarditis.
    • With second cancers, this is a leading cause of late death.
  • Arrange a baseline echocardiogram with LVEF before the first anthracycline dose, and manage conventional cardiovascular risk factors — especially smoking, blood pressure and lipids — aggressively and lifelong.
  • Pulmonary toxicity — bleomycin pneumonitis and fibrosis.
    • A new dry cough or exertional breathlessness during or after treatment is bleomycin until proven otherwise — stop the bleomycin and discuss urgently with the treating team; severe or non-resolving disease needs corticosteroids
    • Lung function with DLCO is followed from baseline, and the patient carries a lifelong caution against high inspired oxygen that any future anaesthetic or ITU team must know about
  • Thyroid dysfunction — the thyroid sits inside a neck or mediastinal radiotherapy field, and hypothyroidism is common, easily missed and trivially treated. Check TFTs annually for life.
  • Infection risk after splenic irradiation or splenectomy — vaccination and antibiotic prophylaxis as for any hyposplenic patient
    • plus a supply of emergency standby antibiotics and clear advice to seek medical help immediately with any fever: overwhelming post-splenectomy infection kills in hours (BSH).
Fertility — the conversation happens before the first cycle
  • Chemotherapy — particularly alkylating regimens — and pelvic radiotherapy can cause infertility and premature ovarian insufficiency.
    • ABVD carries a substantially lower gonadotoxic risk than alkylating regimens, but the risk is never zero and depends on the patient's age.
  • Fertility preservation must be discussed before the first cycle of chemotherapy. Once treatment has started the opportunity is largely gone — this is both an exam point and a recurring real-world failure.
  • Sperm banking for men, offered to every man whose treatment could affect fertility and arranged before starting. Counts may already be low at diagnosis, which is a reason to bank rather than not to.
  • Oocyte or embryo cryopreservation for women, with ovarian tissue cryopreservation in selected cases — refer urgently to reproductive medicine so that preservation runs alongside, and does not delay, urgent treatment.
Also on the survivorship list:
  • persistent fatigue, which can outlast treatment by years
  • the psychological impact of a cancer diagnosis in early adult life
  • and the practical burden of lifelong surveillance in someone who considers themselves cured

Aetiology & Key Cytogenetics

Aetiology
  • Genetic change → clonal population
  • Triggers: benzene, alkylating agents (→ secondary AML), radiation, HTLV-1, Down's syndrome (10–20× risk; ALL and AML)
Key Cytogenetics
  • t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL: >95% CML, some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI)
  • t(15;17) → PML-RARα: APML (AML subtype) → blocks differentiation → target with ATRA
⚠ Tumour Lysis Syndrome
📷 Image placeholder — Tumour-lysis biochemistry — cell breakdown releases urate, K⁺ and phosphate (all raised) with a reciprocal fall in Ca²⁺, driving urate-crystal AKI.
Chemo lyses cells → ↑urate, ↑K⁺, ↑phosphate, ↓Ca²⁺ → AKI (urate crystals)
  • Lab TLS = ≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo
  • Prevention: allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — prevents urate formation) OR rasburicase (urate oxidase — breaks down existing urate to allantoin) + IV hydration — never give both together
  • Check G6PD status before rasburicase — it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (severe oxidative haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia); use allopurinol and hydration instead
  • Where rasburicase is indicated it is time-critical and should not sit unprescribed while results are chased (BSH)
  • Key distinction: allopurinol works upstream/preventatively; rasburicase works on already-formed urate
Acute Leukaemia: Presentation & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film / bone marrow in acute myeloid leukaemia — myeloblasts with an Auer rod (pink needle-like cytoplasmic inclusion), pathognomonic of AML.
Presentation (Marrow Failure)
  • Anaemia (↓RBC)
  • Bleeding/petechiae (↓platelets/thrombocytopenia)
  • Infection (↓neutrophils/neutropenia)
  • ± lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly
Non-blanching rash differentials: leukaemia, meningococcaemia, ITP, HSP, vasculitis, NAI
Investigations
  • FBC: ↓Hb, ↓platelets, WCC ↑ or ↓
  • Bone marrow aspirate + film = definitive
    • acute leukaemia is ≥20% blasts in marrow or peripheral blood by WHO criteria
    • <20% is MDS territory, except the AML-defining genetic abnormalities — t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16) and NPM1 mutation — which are AML at any blast count
  • Auer rods = AML (pathognomonic)
  • Immunophenotyping for lineage
  • LP in ALL (CNS risk)
  • MRD by flow cytometry guides relapse risk and de-escalation
⚠ UK red flags
  • Offer a very urgent FBC (within 48 hours) for:
    • unexplained pallor or persistent fatigue
    • unexplained fever
    • persistent or recurrent infection
    • generalised lymphadenopathy
    • unexplained bruising/bleeding/petechiae
    • hepatosplenomegaly
  • And in a child or young person also for persistent or unexplained bone pain, the limp or refusal to weight-bear so easily written off as growing pains or a sports injury (NICE)
  • A child or young person with unexplained petechiae or hepatosplenomegaly needs immediate specialist assessment — same day, not a 48-hour FBC
  • Then act on the result:
    • blasts on the film, a new pancytopenia, or a WCC >100 is a same-day haematology referral, not a count to repeat next week
    • and any fever in a neutropenic patient is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise — IV antibiotics within 1 hour, before the neutrophil count is back
  • For the acute complications see the Neutropenic Sepsis and Oncological Emergencies topics (leukostasis, tumour lysis)
AML & ALL: Management
AML
  • Age: predominantly older adults — median ~70y at diagnosis, with about 40% aged 75 or over
  • Hallmark: Auer rods (pathognomonic)
  • ↑ risk after MDS or myeloproliferative disease
  • Chemo: cytarabine + an anthracycline (daunorubicin) — the “7+3” regimen, but only for patients fit for intensive induction (see the fitness fork below)
  • Allogeneic transplant for intermediate/high-risk cytogenetics
    • Patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy receive lower-intensity therapy (e.g. venetoclax + azacitidine) rather than intensive induction
    • Started on a dose ramp-up with tumour lysis prophylaxis and monitoring, because venetoclax itself causes tumour lysis
    • It is fitness, not age, that decides
ALL
  • Age: children (<5y) and >45y
  • Associations: Down's syndrome, ionising radiation
  • The CNS is a sanctuary site: diagnostic LP, and intrathecal methotrexate given as CNS-directed prophylaxis to every patient — not only those with proven CNS disease (intensified if CSF blasts are present)
  • High tumour burden → the highest tumour lysis risk of the four leukaemias at induction: hydrate and give allopurinol or rasburicase
  • Commonest childhood cancer
  • Chemo: vincristine, dexamethasone, asparaginase, daunorubicin; 2-year maintenance
  • Philadelphia+ ALL: add TKI (imatinib)
  • B-ALL monoclonals: rituximab (anti-CD20), blinatumomab (CD19/CD3)
  • Relapsed/refractory B-ALL: anti-CD19 CAR-T — tisagenlecleucel in children and young adults, with an adult CAR-T option now also commissioned (NICE)
APML subtype
  • Younger than other AML — median ~40y; t(15;17)/PML-RARα
  • Presents with DIC and life-threatening haemorrhage → start ATRA immediately on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation, alongside aggressive blood-product support
  • ATRA improves the coagulopathy — it is cytotoxic chemotherapy (blast lysis) that worsens the DIC, not ATRA
  • ATRA + arsenic trioxide makes APML the most curable AML subtype
  • Complication: differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnoea, hypoxia, oedema, weight gain, pulmonary infiltrates) → dexamethasone, hold ATRA if severe
AML: the decisive fork — fitness, not age
  • The decision point is performance status and comorbidity, not the year of birth.
    • AML is overwhelmingly a disease of older people, so most patients diagnosed with it are not candidates for intensive induction — assess ECOG performance status, cardiac / renal / hepatic reserve and frailty before choosing a pathway
    • Age alone never makes the decision, and neither does age alone rule a fit 75-year-old out
  • Fit for intensive therapy → induction with “7+3” → remission reassessed on marrow → consolidation chemotherapy ± allogeneic stem cell transplant
    • 7 days of continuous cytarabine + 3 days of an anthracycline — daunorubicin or idarubicin
    • The transplant decision is driven by cytogenetic / molecular risk group
    • favourable risk → consolidation chemotherapy alone
    • intermediate / adverse risk → allogeneic SCT in first remission if a donor and the fitness exist
  • For the frailest, best supportive care (transfusion, antimicrobials, hydroxycarbamide for count control) is a legitimate, actively chosen pathway — not a failure to treat.
Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia (CML)
📷 Image placeholder — Massive splenomegaly — the enlarged spleen crossing the midline that is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
Key Facts
  • Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL in >95%
  • Age ~65; middle-aged
  • Three phases: Chronic → Accelerated → Blast crisis
    • Chronic: ~5 years if untreated, often incidental ↑WCC — on a TKI most patients remain in chronic phase indefinitely
    • Blast crisis: ≥20% blasts in blood or marrow by WHO criteria; some older criteria use ≥30%; usually transforms to AML, often fatal
Presentation
  • Insidious onset: fever, weight loss, sweats
  • Massive splenomegaly
  • Blood film: leucocytosis with myeloid precursors, basophilia
Management
  • Imatinib (TKI — blocks BCR-ABL): first-line; 2nd-generation TKIs (dasatinib, nilotinib) are alternative first-line, and ponatinib is used for the resistant T315I mutation
    • Response is tracked by BCR-ABL1 transcript level (RT-qPCR)
    • a confirmed sustained rise or loss of response means check adherence and send kinase-domain mutation analysis before switching TKI, not simply escalate the dose
  • Allogeneic SCT for TKI-resistant or advanced-phase disease; interferon is now reserved for pregnancy (where TKIs are avoided) rather than for advanced disease
Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film in CLL — abundant mature lymphocytes with fragile "smudge / smear cells", the classic film finding.
Key Facts
  • Commonest leukaemia overall
  • Elderly patients (>55y); clonal mature B-cells; indolent but incurable
  • Blood film: smudge/smear cells
  • Immunophenotype: CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23
  • Diagnosis is made on peripheral-blood flow cytometry alone — a clonal mature B-cell lymphocytosis (≥5 ×10⁹/L) with that CD5/CD19/CD23 phenotype is enough.
    • No bone marrow is needed to diagnose CLL.
    • The rule “marrow aspirate = definitive” in the Investigations section above belongs to the acute leukaemias; do not generalise it to CLL
Presentation & Complications
  • Often asymptomatic — incidental lymphocytosis on routine bloods
  • Later: marrow failure features, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly
  • AIHA (warm antibody — cross-ref haemolytic anaemia)
  • Richter's transformation → high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL)
  • Recurrent infection from progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia — the commonest and most under-taught complication, and the leading cause of CLL-related death (see below)
Infection — what actually kills CLL patients
  • The clone is a useless B-cell clone: it expands while normal antibody production collapses, producing progressive hypogammaglobulinaemia
    • a secondary immunodeficiency that deepens as disease advances and is deepened further by treatment
  • Low IgG → failed opsonisation → recurrent infection with encapsulated organisms
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae (recurrent pneumonia, sinusitis, otitis)
    • Purine analogues such as fludarabine add T-cell depletion, so herpes-zoster reactivation and opportunistic infection appear on top
  • Infection accounts for roughly half of all CLL-related deaths — more than Richter's transformation and more than marrow failure
    • Recurrent chest infections in an older patient with a lymphocytosis are a CLL story, not bad luck
  • Vaccinate: annual influenza vaccine and pneumococcal vaccination (antibody responses are blunted but still worthwhile) — and no live vaccines in these immunocompromised patients
  • Immunoglobulin replacement is considered for recurrent or severe bacterial infection despite prophylactic antibiotics, in a patient with a low IgG
    • It cuts infection frequency rather than prolonging life, so it is a reserved therapy, not a routine one
When to treat
  • Early, asymptomatic CLL is watched, not treated — treating earlier does not help the patient live longer
    • Watch-and-wait means clinical review and an FBC, and is an active decision rather than nihilism
  • Treatment starts when the disease declares itself:
    • marrow failure (falling haemoglobin or platelets because of the CLL)
    • bulky or rapidly enlarging nodes or spleen
    • B symptoms
    • a lymphocyte doubling time of under 6 months (rate of change, not absolute count)
    • or an autoimmune cytopenia that will not settle on steroids
  • Never treat for a number alone — a high lymphocyte count on its own is not an indication
Management
  • Watch-and-wait (early/asymptomatic disease)
  • Symptomatic/progressive: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) — now largely second-line
  • Modern first-line: targeted agents — a BTK inhibitor (ibrutinib, acalabrutinib) or the BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax, usually with obinutuzumab
    • Venetoclax is started on a weekly dose ramp-up with hydration, urate-lowering cover and tumour lysis bloods around each dose increase — the tumour lysis rule is not confined to cytotoxic chemotherapy
Prognosis & Outcomes
The framing that makes this memorable:
  • the two chronic leukaemias are usually lived with, while the two acute leukaemias are survived or not
  • and within the acute pair the dominant modifier is age and fitness, not the label on the diagnosis
LeukaemiaOutcome pictureWhat drives it
ALL — adultsRoughly 40–50% five-year survival — far worse than in childrenMore adverse cytogenetics (Philadelphia-positive disease is commoner in adults) and poorer tolerance of intensive protocols
ALL — childrenExcellent — taught in full, with the prognostic factor lists, in Paediatric CancersSee that note rather than learning two versions of the same figures
AMLThe worst of the four overall, and it falls steeply with age: long-term survival is a realistic aim in fit younger adults given intensive induction, but is uncommon in the older, unfit majority treated non-intensivelyFitness for intensive therapy and cytogenetic risk group; secondary AML (post-MDS, post-alkylating agent) does worse
APMLThe exception — the most curable AML subtype, once the early DIC has been survivedDifferentiation therapy; early death from haemorrhage is the main threat, so the first days matter most

Exam trap:
  • “What is the prognosis of leukaemia?” has no single answer — the examiner is testing whether you split it first by which leukaemia and then by age/fitness
  • The steepest gradient in the whole topic is childhood versus adult ALL; the second steepest is the young-fit versus older-unfit AML fork

HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferative Disorder:
Myeloproliferative Disorders: Overview
📷 Image placeholder — JAK-STAT pathway schematic — how JAK2 V617F (and CALR/MPL) drive constitutive kinase signalling, contrasted with BCR-ABL in CML.
What are MPDs?

  • Uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line — cells still mature (contrast acute leukaemia where blasts fail to differentiate).

    Unifying genetics of the BCR-ABL-negative MPNs (PV, ET, MF): JAK2, CALR or MPL driver mutations → constitutive JAK-STAT signalling
  • CML is the BCR-ABL-positive MPN
  • All can transform to AML
Three classical types
• PV — erythroid line ↑
• ET — megakaryocyte line ↑
• Primary myelofibrosis — HSC → marrow fibrosis

Cross-ref CML — 4th classical MPN but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator
