Polycythaemia Vera (PV)
📷 Image placeholder — Ruddy plethora — the red, congested facial complexion and conjunctival plethora of polycythaemia vera; a recognisable clinical sign.
Features
  • Aquagenic pruritus after contact with water, classically a warm bath or shower — the hallmark
  • Conjunctival plethora, ruddy complexion, hypertension, splenomegaly
  • Hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, DVT, Budd-Chiari). ⚠ Symptomatic hyperviscosity (visual loss, TIA/stroke, chest pain) needs urgent venesection, not routine outpatient booking
  • Haemorrhage (abnormal platelet function)
  • Headache, visual disturbance, gout, angina
Investigations
  • ↑Haematocrit
  • JAK2 V617F+ with a raised haematocrit = confirmed (diagnostic thresholds Hct >0.52 men, >0.48 women — not the same as the <0.45 venesection target). If V617F-negative but PV still suspected (raised Hct with a low EPO), test JAK2 exon 12
  • Low ESR (high viscosity paradox)
  • Low EPO — separates from secondary polycythaemia
Management
  • Venesection (PCV <0.45) — first-line. The resulting iron deficiency is therapeutic — do not give iron supplements, which cause rebound erythrocytosis
  • Aspirin 75 mg od (antithrombotic) — but with platelets >1000–1500 ×109/L check von Willebrand factor activity first: acquired von Willebrand syndrome develops at extreme counts and aspirin then causes bleeding, so withhold it and cytoreduce until the count falls (BSH)
  • Cytoreduction if high-risk (age ≥65 or prior thrombosis — also consider for poor venesection tolerance, progressive splenomegaly, or progressive leucocytosis/thrombocytosis) (BSH): hydroxycarbamide first-line; interferon alfa — pegylated interferon alfa-2a in younger patients and in pregnancy, whereas ropeginterferon alfa-2b is the licensed agent for PV without symptomatic splenomegaly but is not recommended in pregnancy (MHRA); busulfan is leukaemogenic and reserved for elderly/palliative use
  • Ruxolitinib (JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor) if hydroxycarbamide-resistant or intolerant. Anagrelide is a platelet-specific agent used in ET, not in PV.
  • ⚠ Hydroxycarbamide and busulfan are teratogenic — interferon alfa is the agent of choice in pregnancy
Myelofibrosis
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film in myelofibrosis — teardrop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) with a leucoerythroblastic picture (nucleated red cells + immature myeloid cells).
Pathophysiology
📷 Image placeholder — Bone marrow trephine with a reticulin/silver stain showing dense marrow fibrosis — the reason for the "dry tap" on aspiration in myelofibrosis.

Stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release TGF-β (and PDGF) → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis. Can arise de novo (primary) or evolve from PV/ET.

Features
  • Anaemia (fatigue — commonest symptom); bleeding
  • Hypermetabolic: weight loss, night sweats
  • Massive hepatosplenomegaly → portal hypertension (extramedullary haemopoiesis). ⚠ Acute left-upper-quadrant or pleuritic shoulder-tip pain ± a friction rub = splenic infarction — usually self-limiting, managed with fluids and analgesia, but image to exclude rupture
Investigations
  • Anaemia; WCC/plt high early, fall late
  • Film: leucoerythroblastic + teardrop poikilocytes
  • ↑Urate, ↑LDH; Dry tap → trephine biopsy (the classic pairing)
Management

Transfusions, allopurinol, and a JAK inhibitor — ruxolitinib (shrinks spleen, eases symptoms); newer options include fedratinib and momelotinib (momelotinib is useful when anaemia is prominent). Allogeneic BMT = only cure.

Essential Thrombocythaemia (ET)
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film in essential thrombocythaemia — a markedly increased platelet count, some abnormally large (giant platelets).
Features

Isolated ↑platelets with a normal or near-normal Hb and a normal or mildly raised WCC (a mild leucocytosis is common and is itself a thrombosis risk factor).

Platelets abnormal in size/function → thrombosis > bleeding, with microvascular symptoms — erythromelalgia (burning red hands and feet), ocular migraine and TIA, all of which respond to low-dose aspirin.
Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) first.

Management

Aspirin for all patients unless contraindicated — but with platelets >1000–1500 ×109/L check von Willebrand factor activity first: acquired von Willebrand syndrome develops at extreme counts and aspirin then causes bleeding, so withhold it and cytoreduce until the count falls.
Cytoreduction only if high-risk — age >60, platelets >1500 ×109/L, or previous thrombosis or haemorrhage (BSH): hydroxycarbamide first-line; anagrelide second-line; interferon alfa in younger patients and in pregnancy; busulfan is leukaemogenic and reserved for elderly/palliative use.
⚠ On hydroxycarbamide, monitor the FBC (weekly at first, then about 3-monthly) with renal function and LFTs, and hold or reduce the dose for cytopenias; painful leg ulcers mean stopping the drug, and long-term use raises non-melanoma skin cancer risk — advise sun protection and skin self-examination (BNF).
⚠ Hydroxycarbamide and busulfan are teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy and in those planning conception (effective contraception required in both sexes), and switch to interferon about 3 months before conception; interferon alfa is the cytoreductive agent of choice in pregnancy.

In MPN pregnancy give low-dose aspirin throughout and LMWH for at least 6 weeks postpartum.

Exam Pearls
JAK2: ~95% PV, ~50% ET/MF; CML uses BCR-ABL — not JAK2
Venesection + aspirin = PV backbone; aspirin alone = ET backbone
Teardrop poikilocytes + dry tap = myelofibrosis — the signature pairing
EPO low in PV (marrow autonomy); EPO high in secondary polycythaemia — the key discriminator
Aquagenic pruritus after contact with water is a classic PV clue (present in ~40%) — check the haematocrit. Suggestive, not diagnostic
All MPNs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis may be primary, or arise as post-PV / post-ET myelofibrosis. ET = diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck = relative polycythaemia
HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia:
Myelodysplastic Syndrome: Overview
📷 Image placeholder — Spectrum diagram — isolated cytopenias → MDS (dysplasia, <20% blasts) → AML (≥20% blasts); MDS as the pre-leukaemic middle ground.

The defining paradox: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia — the clonal cells proliferate but die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood (marrow is full; periphery is empty)
MDS = group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders → ineffective haematopoiesis → progressive marrow failure

Sits on a spectrum: cytopenias → MDS → AML
MDS is the pre-leukaemic middle ground
Key cut-off: <20% blasts = MDS · ≥20% blasts = AML — unless an AML-defining genetic abnormality is present (t(15;17), t(8;21), inv(16), NPM1), which makes it AML at any blast count

Cross-ref MPN: MPN = over-production of mature cells; MDS = ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output (overlap MDS/MPN entities such as CMML show both)
Aetiology & Risk Factors
Risk Factors
  • Elderly — median onset >70 years; mostly primary/idiopathic
  • Therapy-related — prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy (key secondary cause — cross-ref leukaemia aetiology)
  • Benzene exposure (environmental)
Clinical Features
Often incidental — asymptomatic abnormal FBC
  • but an unexplained cytopenia or pancytopenia needs a very urgent FBC and urgent haematology referral rather than watchful repeat testing in primary care (NICE). Symptoms arise from one or more cytopenias — anaemia is the commonest and is often the only one
  • full pancytopenia is present in a minority at diagnosis:
CytopeniaFeatures
AnaemiaFatigue, pallor, shortness of breath
NeutropeniaRecurrent/severe infections
ThrombocytopeniaPurpura, bleeding — avoid aspirin, NSAIDs and other antiplatelets; significant or mucosal bleeding needs an urgent FBC and haematology review
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film dysplasia in MDS — a pseudo-Pelger–Huët (bilobed) neutrophil and hypogranular neutrophils, the named examinable findings.
FBC & Blood Film
  • One or more cytopenias (anaemia commonest and often the only one) — the anaemia is often macrocytic (raised MCV — the classic film clue). Exclude the reversible causes first: B12/folate, thyroid, liver, alcohol and drugs (BSH)
  • Blood film: dysplastic cells, blasts <20%
  • Pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells (acquired bilobed/hypolobated "pince-nez" neutrophils — the inherited Pelger–Huët anomaly is a benign mimic) and hypogranular neutrophils — named dysplasia findings, examinable
  • Ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria ringing the nucleus on Prussian-blue stain) — the MDS-RS subtype (often SF3B1-mutated), examinable
Bone Marrow (Definitive)
📷 Image placeholder — Bone marrow — hypercellular with dysplastic changes; and a Prussian-blue stain showing ring sideroblasts (iron granules encircling the nucleus).
  • Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy = confirms: hypercellular, dysplastic lines, blast %
  • Cytogenetics drives prognosis — isolated del(5q) = good prognosis; complex karyotype and monosomy 7/del(7q) = poor prognosis (isolated del(5q) is also the lenalidomide-responsive subtype)
  • IPSS-R score (Revised International Prognostic Scoring System) guides treatment intensity
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Risk-stratified treatment algorithm — low-risk (IPSS-R): supportive transfusion, EPO/ESA, luspatercept for transfusion-dependent ring-sideroblast anaemia, del(5q)→lenalidomide; high-risk: azacitidine (hypomethylating) → allogeneic SCT (only cure).
Low-Risk / Supportive
  • Watchful waiting — this means active monitoring, not discharge: regular FBC surveillance, with a repeat marrow if counts fall, transfusion need rises, or blasts climb — the triggers for re-scoring risk and changing treatment
  • Transfusions — RBC for symptomatic anaemia on a restrictive threshold, one unit at a time with reassessment; patients on a regular programme have an individualised threshold and target set rather than a fixed number (NICE)
  • EPO/ESA (for anaemia in selected patients — lower-risk, low transfusion burden, low serum EPO). ⚠ Do not over-correct: keep the Hb in the target range and avoid exceeding 120 g/L, which raises thrombotic risk (MHRA)
  • Luspatercept — licensed for transfusion-dependent anaemia in lower-risk MDS with ring sideroblasts / SF3B1, after failure of or ineligibility for an ESA; it is not the subject of a positive NICE recommendation, so NHS access in England is not routine (NICE)
  • Infection management — ⚠ neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency: empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation, before results and without waiting for the neutrophil count (see the Neutropenic Sepsis topic)
  • Iron chelation — for transfusional overload; considered in lower-risk patients on a long-term transfusion programme once ferritin exceeds ~1000 µg/L or about 20 units have been given, with ferritin monitored on treatment (BSH) (cross-ref haemochromatosis/thalassaemia)
Targeted & High-Risk
  • Isolated del(5q) → lenalidomide (thalidomide analogue — the targeted exam fact), licensed for transfusion-dependent anaemia in lower-risk disease; accepted for use in Scotland but not recommended by NICE for use in England — the drug–subtype pairing is still what is examined. ⚠ Teratogenic — the UK Pregnancy Prevention Programme applies; it also causes marked early neutropenia/thrombocytopenia — FBC weekly for the first 8 weeks, then at least monthly (BNF)
  • Higher-risk MDS: hypomethylating agent (azacitidine) for patients not eligible for allogeneic SCT — improves survival and delays AML transformation, but is not curative. Fit patients: intensive AML-type chemotherapy ± allogeneic SCT
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant = only cure (reserved for the fit — it is fitness and comorbidity, not chronological age, that decide; reduced-intensity conditioning extends it into the early 70s in selected patients)

5q- syndrome → lenalidomide
MDS is pre-leukaemic — classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy

HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / Von Willebran:
The decisive fork: platelet-type vs coagulation-type bleeding.
  • VWF sits at the platelet–vessel interface → mucocutaneous bleeding (gums, nose, periods) + a prolonged PFA closure time.
  • Factors VIII/IX sit deep in the cascade → deep bleeding (joints, muscles) + prolonged APTT with normal platelet function.
  • VWD is the bridge: VWF carries factor VIII, so severe VWD can lower VIII and prolong APTT.
  • Cross-ref DIC — acquired, consumptive, mixed clotting/bleeding.
The Two Disorders at a Glance
📷 Image placeholder — Diagram contrasting the two bleeding patterns — platelet/mucocutaneous (VWD: bruising, gum bleeding, epistaxis, menorrhagia, prolonged PFA closure time) vs deep/coagulation (haemophilia: haemarthrosis, muscle haematoma, prolonged APTT).
Von Willebrand Disease (VWD)
  • Commonest inherited bleeding disorder
  • Mostly autosomal dominant
  • Deficiency/dysfunction of VWF
  • Bleeding type: mucocutaneous
Haemophilia A & B
  • X-linked recessive — predominantly males; carrier females can have factor levels in the mild haemophilia range and do bleed (menorrhagia, postpartum), so they need their own levels checked
  • A = factor VIII deficiency; B = factor IX (Christmas disease)
  • Bleeding type: deep (haemarthroses, muscle)
VWF has two jobs: (1) platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall; (2) carrier and stabiliser of factor VIII. That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, ↑APTT).
Von Willebrand Disease

VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

TypeDefectNotes
1Partial ↓ VWF quantity~80% of cases; mildest; autosomal dominant
2Qualitative / abnormal VWF
Mostly autosomal dominant (2N is recessive)
  • 2A loss of large multimers
  • 2B ↑platelet binding + thrombocytopenia
  • 2M ↓platelet binding
  • 2N ↓factor VIII binding (mimics haemophilia A, affects both sexes)
3Total absence of VWFAutosomal recessive; severe — mimics haemophilia
Clinical Features & Investigations
Features — mucocutaneous
  • Gum bleeding on brushing, epistaxis
  • Menorrhagia — often presenting complaint
  • Prolonged bleeding after dental/surgical procedures
  • Easy bruising
  • Positive family history (AD)
Investigations
  • ↑PFA-100 closure time — the skin bleeding time is obsolete and no longer performed in the UK; note a normal PFA does not exclude VWD
  • APTT ±↑ (raised if VIII secondarily low)
  • PT normal; platelets normal — except type 2B, where they are low
  • ↓VWF antigen + activity
  • ↓Factor VIII (moderately)
Reduced VWF activity on a ristocetin-based assay (VWF:RCo / GPIbM) alongside VWF antigen — the VWF panel is what makes the diagnosis.
  • Ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation (RIPA) is a subtyping test
  • In type 2B low-dose RIPA is INCREASED, not reduced
Management
Acute bleeding / pre-procedure
  • Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases endogenous VWF; first-line for type 1
  • VWF concentrate (± factor VIII) — type 2/3 or severe bleeds
  • Tranexamic acid — antifibrinolytic for minor/mucosal bleeding
Menorrhagia — the options, not a fixed ladder
  • A levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first treatment to consider where it is suitable [NICE]
  • Tranexamic acid, and combined hormonal contraception or a cyclical progestogen, are the alternatives — and are often used alongside it
  • NSAIDs such as mefenamic acid, standard for heavy periods in the general population, are avoided here: they add a platelet defect to the existing bleeding disorder
  • Hysterectomy is a last resort, and the plan is agreed with the haemophilia centre
⚠️ Desmopressin — who it does not suit
  • Type 2B — do not use. The abnormal VWF already binds platelets too avidly; releasing more worsens the thrombocytopenia. (That is what the “2B” in the subtype list actually means.)
  • Type 3 — ineffective. There is no stored VWF to release, so there is nothing for it to do. Same logic as haemophilia B.
  • Establish the response first. A test/trial dose with paired levels shows whether this patient actually responds — do not assume it from the subtype alone.
  • Tachyphylaxis — stores deplete, so repeated doses work progressively less well.
  • Hyponatraemia — it is an ADH analogue. Restrict fluids and monitor sodium; unrestricted drinking has caused seizures, especially in young children.
Haemophilia A & B
📷 Image placeholder — X-linked recessive inheritance pedigree — carrier mother × unaffected father giving affected sons and carrier daughters; explains why haemophilia is almost exclusively male.
Haemophilia A — Factor VIII
  • X-linked recessive; males affected, females usually carriers — but carriers can have low factor levels and bleeding symptoms, and are described as having haemophilia when the level is low
  • Most common of the two
  • Desmopressin useful in mild disease
Haemophilia B — Factor IX (Christmas disease)
  • X-linked recessive; clinically identical to A
  • “Christmas disease” — named after Stephen Christmas, first patient described
  • Desmopressin not effective
Severity Grading

Moderate1–5%Bleeds with minor trauma
Mild5–40%Bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery
Clinical Features & Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — Haemarthrosis — a swollen, warm, painful knee from bleeding into the joint; the hallmark clinical sign of haemophilia (recurrent bleeds → chronic arthropathy).
Features — deep bleeding
  • Haemarthroses — the hallmark (knees, ankles, elbows)
  • Muscle haematomas
  • Prolonged post-surgical/traumatic bleeding
  • Haematuria, GI bleeding
  • Retroperitoneal haematoma
  • Intracranial haemorrhage (severe disease)
Investigations
  • ↑APTT
  • PT, TT, PFA closure time, platelets, VWF — all normal
  • ↓Factor VIII (A) or ↓Factor IX (B) — confirms diagnosis
  • Bethesda assay — detects inhibitor antibodies
Management
Factor replacement
  • IV recombinant factor VIII or IX concentrate — on demand or prophylaxis
  • Severe disease: prophylaxis from early childhood to protect joints — factor VIII roughly alternate days or 3×/week, factor IX around twice weekly (factor IX has the longer half-life); less often with extended half-life products
  • Desmopressin — mild haemophilia A only (releases stored VIII); ineffective in B
  • Tranexamic acid — adjunct for mucosal bleeding
Complications & modern therapy
  • Inhibitor antibodies — develop against infused factor; treatment fails
  • Emicizumab (Hemlibra) — bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
    • But it is prophylaxis only: a breakthrough bleed still needs factor, or a bypassing agent if there is an inhibitor
    • It does nothing in haemophilia B
  • Chronic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses
  • Historically: HIV/HCV from plasma-derived products
Gene therapy
A single-dose AAV vector delivering the clotting-factor gene.
  • For haemophilia B, etranacogene dezaparvovec is approved for NHS use under a managed-access arrangement and is given at a small number of specialist centres [NICE]
  • The haemophilia A product, valoctocogene roxaparvovec, has been withdrawn from the market by its manufacturer for commercial reasons and is no longer available
  • Gene therapy is not a permanent cure — expression wanes over years, and transaminitis needing steroid cover is common
  • Emicizumab and factor prophylaxis remain the mainstay
The Acute Bleed, Inhibitors & Living With It
🚑 Treat first. Factor replacement is not delayed for imaging, for a scan slot, or for a specialist to call back.
  • In a known haemophiliac with a suspected significant bleed, the factor goes in and then you investigate
  • The patient — or their parent — is usually an expert in their own condition and carries a treatment plan: ask them and follow it, and contact the haemophilia centre urgently
🚨 The bleeds that kill or maim
  • Intracranial — the leading cause of bleeding death. Any head injury, or headache/vomiting/drowsiness without one, gets factor first, then CT head. A normal initial examination does not exclude it
  • Throat and neck — airway compromise
  • Iliopsoas / retroperitoneal — a large volume bleeds silently into the abdomen; presents as groin or hip pain with the hip held flexed, and can mimic appendicitis or a hip problem
  • Compartment syndrome from a limb or forearm bleed
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding
🩺 How much, and what else
  • The target factor level rises with the seriousness of the bleed — a joint bleed needs a moderate rise, a life-threatening or intracranial bleed needs a level close to normal, held for longer
  • Tranexamic acid as an adjunct for mucosal and dental bleeding — but not for haematuria: it stabilises clot in the renal tract and can obstruct the ureter, causing hydronephrosis and anuria [BNF]
  • Renal-tract bleeding is managed with factor, hydration and observation
  • Analgesia: paracetamol and opioids are fine; aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs are not
Haemarthrosis
Factor first — on suspicion, without waiting for imaging — then rest, ice, compression and elevation, plus analgesia and early physiotherapy.
  • The joint is not routinely aspirated (risk of further bleeding and infection; reserved for suspected septic arthritis or an exceptionally tense joint, under factor cover)
  • The aim is to prevent the next one, because repeated bleeds into one joint produce chronic arthropathy

Inhibitors — when the factor stops working

🧬 An inhibitor is an alloantibody against the infused factor, and it is the most serious complication of treatment.
  • It is far commoner in severe haemophilia A than in B
  • It typically appears early — within the first several dozen exposures, i.e. in young children rather than after decades of uneventful treatment.
🔍 How you suspect one
  • A dose that used to work stops working — this is the clinical signature
  • A bleed fails to respond to adequate replacement
  • No expected rise in the post-infusion factor level — the recovery study is the objective version of the same observation
  • The mixing study is the screening step that flags an inhibitor before it is quantified — failure to correct on mixing points to an inhibitor rather than a deficiency (coagulation screen)
💉 How a bleed is treated once one exists
  • More factor is not the answer at high titre — it is neutralised.
    • The acute bleed is treated with a bypassing agent instead: recombinant factor VIIa, or activated prothrombin complex concentrate (FEIBA)
    • In a patient already on emicizumab, rFVIIa is preferred — aPCC with emicizumab has caused thrombotic microangiopathy and thrombosis
  • Eradicating the inhibitor is a separate goal: immune tolerance induction (repeated regular factor exposure to retrain the immune system) is the established approach and succeeds in most children with haemophilia A
  • Emicizumab has changed this picture: because it mimics factor VIII rather than replacing it, it provides prophylaxis whether or not an inhibitor is present

Living With It

🚫 Avoid
  • Aspirin and non-selective NSAIDs — they add a platelet defect to a factor defect. Agree any exception with the haematologist
  • Intramuscular injections without cover — including vaccinations, which are given subcutaneously or under factor cover with firm pressure afterwards. Vaccination itself is encouraged, not avoided
  • Contact sports are a discussion, not a blanket ban — activity protects joints and muscle bulk
🏥 Plan ahead
  • Dental work is planned with the centre — tranexamic acid mouthwash ± desmopressin or factor cover often makes extraction safe without admission
  • Surgery needs a written haemostatic plan agreed in advance — what to give, when, and for how many days afterwards
  • Care runs through a designated haemophilia comprehensive care centre: home therapy, an alert card, physiotherapy and 24-hour advice
  • New spontaneous bleeding in an older patient with no lifelong history is a different disease — consider acquired haemophilia (bruising & bleeding)

HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminated Intravasc:
The decisive fork: consumption.
  • Massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced — giving the paradox of clotting and bleeding simultaneously
  • Factors used up → PT/APTT/TT prolong; fibrinogen consumed → low; platelets consumed → thrombocytopenia
  • Red cells sheared through intravascular fibrin strands → schistocytes; secondary fibrinolysis → ↑FDPs/D-dimer
  • DIC is always secondary — there is no primary DIC
Overview
📷 Image placeholder — DIC mechanism diagram — trigger exposes tissue factor → widespread cascade activation → consumption of platelets/factors + secondary fibrinolysis → simultaneous microvascular thrombosis and haemorrhage.

What is DIC?
  • Widespread intravascular fibrin generation from massive coagulation cascade activation
  • Core paradox: too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage
  • Always secondary to an underlying trigger — never primary
Mechanism chain
  • Trigger → tissue factor exposed → coagulation cascade fires
  • Fibrin + platelet consumption → secondary fibrinolysis → FDPs
  • FDPs themselves worsen bleeding by inhibiting fibrin polymerisation
  • Haemorrhage + microvascular thrombosis
Aetiology
📷 Image placeholder — Trigger summary — anything exposing tissue factor: Sepsis (commonest, Gram-negative), Trauma/burns, Obstetric (amniotic-fluid embolism, HELLP, abruption), Malignancy/APML, Transfusion reaction.

Unifying mechanism: anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor — endothelial damage, monocyte TF expression driven by cytokines, or direct TF release.

Category Examples
Sepsis (commonest) Gram-negative sepsis especially; cytokine-driven TF expression on monocytes
Trauma / tissue destruction Burns, major surgery, crush injury, fat embolism, severe acute pancreatitis
Obstetric Amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, retained products of conception
Malignancy Advanced solid tumours; APML (acute promyelocytic leukaemia) — classic haematological trigger
Transfusion reaction ABO-incompatible transfusion
Vascular Aortic aneurysm, haemangioma
APML link:
  • Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is the classic leukaemia trigger for DIC — promyelocytes release procoagulant granules
  • ATRA rapidly improves the coagulopathy of APML and is started immediately on clinical suspicion, before genetic confirmation, alongside aggressive blood-product support
  • It is cytotoxic chemotherapy (blast lysis) that can transiently worsen DIC
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Purpura fulminans — retiform purpura with digital/skin necrosis from microvascular thrombosis; a striking clinical sign of severe DIC.
Bleeding (haemorrhagic end)
  • Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites — exam buzzword
  • Venepuncture / cannula sites, IV lines
  • Nose, mouth, gums
  • GI bleeding, haematuria
  • Wound/surgical site bleeding
Thrombosis (thrombotic end)
  • Microvascular occlusion → end-organ ischaemia
  • AKI (renal cortical necrosis)
  • Delirium / reduced GCS (cerebral ischaemia)
  • Purpura fulminans — digital/skin necrosis
  • Respiratory failure (ARDS pattern)

Severity ranges from subclinical (lab abnormalities only) to complete haemostatic failure.

  • Factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, low in DIC. This is the key discriminator
  • The third mimic is dilutional coagulopathy after massive transfusion or fluid resuscitation: PT/APTT prolong and fibrinogen falls
  • D-dimer is not markedly raised and there are no schistocytes — the history of large-volume replacement is the clue
Putting a number on it — the validated DIC score.
  • DIC is a clinicopathological diagnosis: the clinical picture plus a recognised trigger makes the diagnosis, and the score does not replace that
  • It gives you an objective, repeatable measurement of how decompensated the haemostatic system is
  • Three things govern its use:
    • it is only valid when a recognised precipitant is present (do not apply it to a patient with no DIC-associated illness)
    • it is built entirely from the four routine labs you have usually already sent (platelets, PT prolongation, fibrinogen, D-dimer/FDPs)
    • it is scored serially, not once — a rising score signals decompensation, a falling score suggests the coagulopathy is resolving as the trigger comes under control
  • Full components, point bands and the threshold for overt DIC are tabulated in Risk Scores & Criteria → Haematology & Oncology
  • Interpretation of the individual tests: Investigations → Haematology → Coagulation & Thrombosis
Management
📷 Image placeholder — DIC treatment ladder — treat the underlying cause (the only curative step); supportive products only if bleeding/pre-procedure (platelets >50×10⁹/L, FFP for factors, cryoprecipitate to keep fibrinogen >1.5 g/L); anticoagulation dosed by phenotype.
Priority 1: Treat the underlying cause — this is the only thing that reverses DIC
  • Antibiotics plus source control for sepsis, deliver in obstetric cases, and in suspected APML start ATRA at once, before genetic confirmation
  • Everything else is supportive
Supportive — only if bleeding or pre-procedure
  • Platelets → keep >50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding; if not bleeding but at high bleeding risk, the threshold falls to >20 ×10⁹/L (BSH)
  • FFP → replaces all clotting factors — initial dose 15 mL/kg in the bleeding patient with PT/APTT >1.5× normal (BSH)
  • Cryoprecipitate → replaces fibrinogen (target >1.5 g/L — but >2 g/L in ongoing obstetric haemorrhage)
  • Red cells → for anaemia / blood loss
  • Treat the patient, not the numbers alone
  • Product indications and thresholds are set out in Investigations → Haematology → Transfusion — not repeated here
Monitoring the response
  • Recheck FBC, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer after products are given and as the trigger is treated — in the actively bleeding or unstable patient that means hours, not days
  • At minimum the DIC score is repeated daily while it remains in the overt range
  • The trend matters more than any single value: a falling platelet count together with a falling fibrinogen across serial samples is the powerful dynamic clue that consumption is still winning
  • A single normal fibrinogen early on can mislead — it is an acute-phase reactant and may start high before it falls
  • Improving numbers after a transfusion tell you the product arrived, not that the disease has stopped — the only real endpoint is control of the precipitant
Anticoagulation — a three-step ladder
  • 1. Not bleeding, critically ill → give prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis
  • DIC is a prothrombotic state and these patients sit at high thrombotic risk; withholding thromboprophylaxis purely because the clotting screen is deranged is the commonest real-world error
  • 2. Thrombosis predominates (purpura fulminans, digital or organ ischaemia, overt VTE, with little or no bleeding) → therapeutic-dose anticoagulation, with LMWH preferred over unfractionated heparin
  • UFH reserved for when a short half-life and reversibility are needed — high bleeding risk, severe renal impairment
  • 3. Bleeding dominates → hold anticoagulation; in major or uncontrolled bleeding activate the major haemorrhage protocol and involve haematology early
  • Support with blood products and press on with treating the trigger
The exam trap lives on the middle rung:
  • therapeutic heparin is not the answer for the bleeding patient — do not reach for heparin reflexively
  • Do not confuse that with prophylactic-dose LMWH, which the non-bleeding critically ill patient should still be getting
Tranexamic acid — usually the wrong answer
  • Not routine in DIC, and harmful in the thrombotic phenotype: shutting off fibrinolysis while thrombin generation continues leaves microvascular fibrin undissolved — a recognised route to fatal thrombosis
  • Narrow exception: hyperfibrinolysis-predominant DIC in which bleeding persists despite treating the trigger and replacing products — a specialist decision, not a ward reflex
  • Avoid in APML patients on ATRA — thrombotic events are reported with this combination
Read the context, not the drug:
  • "give tranexamic acid early" is the rule for traumatic haemorrhage and for postpartum haemorrhage
  • Obstetric haemorrhage keeps its tranexamic acid even when DIC has developed
  • The caution below applies to DIC outside those two settings (Investigations → Haematology → Transfusion), where early hyperfibrinolysis is destroying clot the patient needs
  • DIC is the opposite problem — the two situations pull in opposite directions
Exam Pearls
DIC is always secondary — the most important management step is identifying and treating the underlying cause.
The DIC pentad: ↓plt, ↑PT/APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer, schistocytes. All five together = DIC until proven otherwise.
Treat the patient, not the numbers — only replace products (platelets, FFP, cryo) if actively bleeding or pre-procedure.
Sepsis = commonest trigger. APML = classic leukaemia link. Obstetric causes (amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP, abruption) are also high-yield.
vs Liver disease: factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, low in DIC. vs TTP/HUS: thrombocytopenia + schistocytes but normal coagulation screen.
Score it serially, not once:
  • the validated DIC score measures a diagnosis you have already made clinically
  • only valid when a recognised precipitant is present
  • earns its keep by showing the trajectory across days
The trend beats the value:
  • repeat FBC, PT/APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer
  • falling platelets and falling fibrinogen across serial samples is the powerful dynamic clue
  • control of the precipitant is the only real endpoint
Tranexamic acid is not a DIC drug:
  • harmful in the thrombotic phenotype and reserved for hyperfibrinolysis-predominant bleeding
  • avoid it in APML patients on ATRA
  • "Give TXA early" belongs to traumatic and postpartum haemorrhage, not to DIC generally
Anticoagulation ladder:
  • prophylactic-dose LMWH for VTE prophylaxis in the critically ill non-bleeding patient
  • therapeutic-dose anticoagulation (LMWH preferred over unfractionated heparin) when thrombosis predominates
  • hold it when bleeding dominates. Do not reach for therapeutic heparin reflexively — and do not withhold prophylaxis just because the clotting screen looks bad

Principle: Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes.
  • One unit at a time, then reassess
  • This does not apply to active major haemorrhage — do not wait for a trigger Hb: activate the major haemorrhage protocol, give empirical red cells with FFP (± platelets and cryoprecipitate), give tranexamic acid early in traumatic haemorrhage, keep fibrinogen >1.5 g/L and platelets >50×10⁹/L, and stop the bleeding (BSH)
Product Indication Key Facts
Red Cells
O neg = universal donor		 Anaemia / acute blood loss
  • Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L
    ACS: transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L
    Infuse over 90–120 min
  • Stored at 2–6°C
  • Each unit must be completed within 4 h of leaving controlled-temperature storage
FFP
AB = universal donor		 Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal) Contains all clotting factors. Universal donor = AB (no anti-A or anti-B). Large volume — avoid in fluid overload.
Cryoprecipitate Low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion
  • Concentrated: fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
  • Precipitate formed when FFP is thawed at 1–6°C → hence "cryo"
  • Standard adult dose 2 pools (10 donor units), raising fibrinogen by roughly 1 g/L
Platelets
  • Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding
  • Prophylactic if <10×10⁹/L. Not routinely given in TTP, HIT, ITP or chronic marrow failure — in the microangiopathies they feed the process
  • Serious bleeding overrides this
 Stored at 20–24°C (NOT cold — cold causes aggregation). 1 adult dose ↑ platelet count ~20–30×10⁹/L.
PCC
Prothrombin Complex Concentrate		 Emergency warfarin reversal (major bleed, ICH, emergency surgery) Fastest reversal — within 1h. Contains factors II, VII, IX, X. Always give with IV vitamin K (factor VII short half-life → INR creeps back up).
Special Products
📷 Image placeholder — Irradiated vs CMV-negative decision aid — irradiated (T-cell depleted) prevents TA-GvHD in the immunocompromised/Hodgkin/stem-cell recipients; CMV-negative for intrauterine/neonatal/pregnancy.
CMV-negative
CMV is leucocyte-transmitted, and since universal leucodepletion standard UK components are "CMV-safe". CMV-seronegative components are now reserved for intrauterine transfusion, neonates up to 28 days, and elective (non-emergency) transfusion in pregnancy — they are no longer routinely required for transplant recipients, HIV or other immunocompromised patients, who receive standard leucodepleted components.
Irradiated
Donor T-lymphocytes are inactivated by irradiation so they cannot proliferate (they are not removed). Prevents TA-GVHD (Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease) — fatal in immunocompromised patients (haematology, stem cell transplant).
Transfusion Thresholds & Warfarin Reversal
📷 Image placeholder — Warfarin-reversal algorithm — stop warfarin → IV vitamin K (always) → PCC (factors II/VII/IX/X, reversal <1h) for major bleed/ICH; FFP only if PCC unavailable.
Transfusion Thresholds
Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70 → target 70–90 g/L
ACS: transfuse if Hb <80 → target 80–100 g/L
Restrictive strategy (lower threshold) → fewer reactions, less fluid overload, better outcomes than liberal.
Warfarin Reversal
1. Stop warfarin
2. Vitamin K (phytomenadione) 5 mg IV — works in 4–6h (oral takes 24h). Always give (BNF).
3. PCC 25–50 units/kg — major bleed/ICH/emergency surgery. Reversal within 1h. Give WITH vitamin K, and recheck the INR afterwards (BNF).
4. FFP — older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload.
Why K with PCC? Factor VII has a short half-life — without vitamin K, new factors won't be synthesised and INR will rebound.
Giving a Transfusion Safely — Consent, Prescription & Bedside Checks
Almost every fatal transfusion incident is an identity error, not a biological surprise. Each step below exists to prove that this unit belongs to this patient.
1 · Before you start
  • Valid consent — explain the indication, the expected benefit, the alternatives (iron, tranexamic acid, treating the cause) and the risks, and document the discussion.
    • Give the patient the patient information leaflet
    • A refusal (e.g. a Jehovah's Witness) must be recorded, together with any advance decision
  • Prescribe on the transfusion chart — each unit written separately with the component, the volume or number of units, the rate/duration, and any special requirements (irradiated, CMV-negative) flagged so the laboratory can meet them.
  • Sampling — positive patient identification first: ask the patient to state their name and date of birth, then check the wristband.
    • Hand-write the tube label at the bedside, next to the patient, before leaving them
    • Never pre-label, never label at the desk — that is how "wrong blood in tube" happens
  • Baseline observations — pulse, BP, temperature and respiratory rate, taken within 60 minutes before the unit is started.
Grouping, the antibody screen, electronic vs serological crossmatch, sample validity and the emergency O-negative pathway are taught in Investigations → Haematology → Transfusion.
2 · The bedside check
  • Done at the patient's side, immediately before the unit is connected — never at the fridge, never in the corridor, never in advance.
  • Ask the patient to state name and date of birth where they are able to, then check that against the wristband and against the compatibility label attached to the unit.
  • Match every one of: surname, first name, date of birth, hospital number, donation/unit number, component and group, expiry date, and confirmation that any special requirement has been met.
  • Inspect the pack — leaks, clots, clumps or discolouration mean it goes back to the laboratory, not into the patient.
An unconscious or unidentified patient still gets a wristband check — the emergency identification number on the band is their identity for transfusion purposes.
3 · The observation schedule
When What is recorded Why that moment
Within 60 min before starting each unit Pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate Baseline — without it you cannot tell a reaction from the patient's normal
15 min after the start of EVERY unit ★ Pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate The severe early reactions — ABO haemolysis, bacterial sepsis, anaphylaxis — declare themselves in the first few minutes
Within 60 min of finishing each unit Pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate Picks up circulatory overload and later-onset reactions
Throughout Direct visual observation of the patient A deteriorating patient is seen before the next set of numbers is due — the most useful part of the whole schedule

Schedule per BSH guidance on the administration of blood components. Local policy may add observations — it may not take these away.

4 · Practical rules at the bedside
⌚
The 30-minute rule
A unit that has been out of controlled-temperature storage for more than 30 minutes cannot be returned to the blood fridge — it must be transfused or discarded. Collect the unit only when you are ready to start.
⏳
The 4-hour rule
Each unit must be completed within 4 hours of leaving controlled-temperature storage (JPAC). The limit is bacterial proliferation once the pack warms — it is not the shelf life of the component.
💧
Saline only
0.9% sodium chloride is the only fluid that may share the line. No drugs, no glucose, and no calcium-containing fluid such as Hartmann's — calcium overrides the citrate anticoagulant and clots the line.
💉
Blood giving set
A dedicated blood administration set with an integral 170–200 µm filter — a standard fluid giving set will not do. Change the set at least 12-hourly.
👀
Somewhere observable
Transfuse only where the patient can be directly observed and staff can respond. Avoid overnight transfusion unless it is clinically necessary, because reactions get missed.
🏠
Safety-net at discharge
Counsel the patient, verbally and in writing, to seek urgent help if they become unwell in the next 24 hours — fever, rash, breathlessness or dark urine.
Transfusion Reactions — Recognition & Management
📷 Image placeholder — ABO/RhD compatibility grid — which donor group each recipient can receive, showing O-negative as universal red-cell donor and AB as universal FFP donor; ABO mismatch causes acute haemolytic reactions.
STOP the transfusion — universal first step for every reaction
Reaction Cause Features Management
Febrile non-haemolytic Anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release Fever and chills — mild = a rise of 1–2°C to below 39°C with no other features
  • STOP and assess; paracetamol; may restart cautiously at a slower rate only if mild and the patient is stable
  • Rigors, a temperature ≥39°C or a rise ≥2°C is a moderate reaction — do not simply restart; exclude bacterial contamination and haemolysis first (BSH)
Minor allergic Reaction to donor plasma proteins Urticaria, pruritus — no systemic compromise Stop temporarily; antihistamine; can restart
Anaphylaxis Allergy to donor plasma proteins; classically severe IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibodies (rare — often no antibody is found) Hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema — rapid onset STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (500 micrograms) into the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 min if no response; ABC; high-flow O₂; IV fluids; if severe IgA deficiency is confirmed, flag it and use washed or IgA-deficient components in future
Acute haemolytic ★ ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error) Fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine — onset within minutes
  • STOP immediately
  • Keep IV access open with 0.9% saline and resuscitate aggressively to maintain urine output
  • Check patient ID + bag label
  • Call for senior/critical care help and telephone the transfusion laboratory at once (another patient may be about to receive the swapped unit)
  • Return unit + giving set with fresh clotted and EDTA samples for DAT, repeat group and crossmatch
  • Monitor for AKI and DIC
TRALI Donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; hypoxia; HYPOtension; fever — within 6h STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics
TACO Volume overload (too fast / pre-existing HF/renal failure) Pulmonary oedema; HYPERtension; raised JVP; orthopnoea — cardiogenic STOP; sit upright; O₂ + IV furosemide; if transfusion must continue afterwards, restart slowly one unit at a time
Bacterial contamination / sepsis Contaminated unit — especially platelets, which are stored at room temperature High fever, rigors, shock — soon after starting the unit STOP; cultures from the patient AND the unit; broad-spectrum antibiotics; resuscitate
Delayed haemolytic Anamnestic alloantibody response (prior sensitisation by transfusion or pregnancy) Falling Hb, jaundice, positive DAT — days to ~2 weeks later, often after the patient has gone home Supportive; identify the antibody so future units are crossmatched against it

After a Reaction — Escalation, Workup & Reporting
Universal first steps for any suspected reaction:
  • STOP the transfusion · keep the line open with 0.9% saline through a new giving set · assess ABC · recheck the patient's identity against the bag label · inform the transfusion laboratory and keep the unit
  • Only a mild febrile or minor allergic reaction may be cautiously restarted
Sending the workup
  • Return the unit and its giving set to the laboratory, with fresh clotted and EDTA samples from the patient.
  • The laboratory then performs the DAT, a repeat group and crossmatch and a haemolysis screen; take blood cultures from patient and unit if febrile.
  • The full sequence — what each test proves and how the results are read — is set out in Investigations → Haematology → Transfusion.
Do not discard the bag. Without the unit and the giving set the laboratory cannot separate an identity error from an antibody, and the incident cannot be closed.
Reporting — who must be told
  • Hospital transfusion team (transfusion practitioner plus haematology registrar) — same day; they advise on further components and lead the local investigation.
  • SHOT — Serious Hazards of Transfusion, the UK haemovigilance scheme. Professionally mandated, confidential reporting of adverse events, adverse reactions and near misses, including wrong blood in tube.
  • MHRA via SABRE — statutory reporting of serious adverse reactions and serious adverse events under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005. SABRE = Serious Adverse Blood Reactions and Events; the same portal is used to submit the SHOT report.
  • Traceability — the fate of every component issued must be recorded and those records kept for 30 years under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005. That is why the transfusion tag goes back to the laboratory.
  • Local incident report (Datix or equivalent), plus a duty of candour conversation with the patient.
Why haemovigilance earns its place:
  • SHOT reports consistently identify TACO as the commonest cause of transfusion-related death, and most serious incidents are avoidable human error rather than component failure
  • Reporting is what makes those errors visible — and TACO is the one that is largely preventable: do a pre-transfusion TACO risk assessment on everyone, particularly those over 50, under 50 kg, or with heart failure, renal impairment or a low albumin, and mitigate — one unit at a time, transfused slowly, with a prophylactic diuretic considered (SHOT)
Acute vs Delayed — the Complication Timeline

The reactions in the table above nearly all happen while you are standing there. A separate group appears once the patient has gone home — those are the ones that get missed.

MINUTES
Acute haemolytic (ABO) and anaphylaxis — precisely what the 15-minute observation set exists to catch.
< 6 HOURS
Febrile non-haemolytic, minor allergic, bacterial sepsis, TRALI, TACO.
DAYS – 2 WEEKS
Delayed haemolytic reaction; post-transfusion purpura (~5–12 days); TA-GvHD (~1–2 weeks — prevented by irradiation).
WEEKS – YEARS
Red cell alloimmunisation; iron overload; transfusion-transmitted infection.
📆
Delayed haemolytic reaction
An alloantibody from an earlier transfusion or pregnancy, below the detection threshold at crossmatch, is boosted by re-exposure.
  • Falling Hb, jaundice and a positive DAT days to ~2 weeks later
  • Supportive — but the antibody must be identified and recorded so every future crossmatch avoids that antigen
🧲
Iron overload
Each unit of red cells delivers roughly 250 mg of iron and there is no physiological route to excrete it, so regularly transfused patients accumulate it in heart, liver and endocrine organs. Monitoring and chelation are covered under Thalassaemia.
🎯
Red cell alloimmunisation
Antibodies form against donor red cell antigens the patient lacks (Rh, Kell, Kidd, Duffy).
  • Usually silent at the time, but it makes future units harder and slower to crossmatch, sets up delayed haemolytic reactions, and matters enormously in girls and women of childbearing age (haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn)
  • If an RhD-negative girl or woman of childbearing potential is inadvertently given RhD-positive red cells or platelets, give anti-D immunoglobulin and take specialist transfusion advice
🟣
Post-transfusion purpura
Rare. Profound thrombocytopenia ~5–12 days after transfusion, classically in a previously pregnant woman who is HPA-1a negative; platelet-specific alloantibodies destroy her own platelets as well as the donor's. Treat with IVIg — further platelet transfusions are largely ineffective.
🦠
Transfusion-transmitted infection
Now very rare in the UK: donor selection and testing put the residual risk of HIV or hepatitis C well below one per million donations, so bacterial contamination of a component is the commoner infective hazard. Universal leucodepletion was introduced as a precaution against variant CJD transmission.
Exam Pearls
Universal donors: RBC = O negative; FFP = AB (no anti-A or anti-B antibodies).
PCC + vitamin K together for warfarin reversal — K prevents INR rebound when PCC factors wear off.
Anaphylaxis during transfusion → IgA deficiency (anti-IgA antibodies react with IgA in donor blood).
Thresholds: Non-ACS <70 → target 70–90; ACS <80 → target 80–100. Restrictive strategy → better outcomes.
Products: FFP → PT/APTT >1.5; Cryo → fibrinogen <1.5; PCC → warfarin emergency. Platelets stored at 20–24°C (not cold!).
TRALI = hypotension + non-cardiogenic oedema → supportive, NO diuretics.
TACO = hypertension + cardiogenic overload → furosemide.
Acute haemolytic = ABO incompatibility (human error) → loin/back pain + dark urine within minutes → STOP + check identity immediately.
Label the tube at the bedside, by hand, after the patient states their name and date of birth — pre-labelling is the classic route to "wrong blood in tube".
The delayed four (+1): delayed haemolytic reaction, iron overload, alloimmunisation, transfusion-transmitted infection — plus post-transfusion purpura at ~5–12 days.
Observations: pulse, BP, temperature and RR within 60 min before starting, 15 min after the start of every unit, and within 60 min of finishing — with visual observation throughout.
High fever, rigors and shock minutes into a platelet transfusion → bacterial contamination (platelets are stored warm) → cultures from patient and unit, plus broad-spectrum antibiotics.
Reporting: SHOT = UK haemovigilance (professional, includes near misses); MHRA via SABRE = statutory, under the Blood Safety and Quality Regulations 2005; component fate traceable for 30 years.
30-minute rule — out of controlled storage for >30 min and it cannot go back.
  • 4-hour rule — the unit must be finished within 4 h of leaving controlled storage
  • Only 0.9% saline shares the line, through a 170–200 µm blood giving set
Irradiated → prevents TA-GVHD (T-cell mediated, fatal in immunocompromised).
CMV-negative → intrauterine transfusion, neonates up to 28 days, and elective transfusion in pregnancy only — leucodepletion makes standard components CMV-safe for everyone else (JPAC).

Neutropenic Sepsis: Overview

MEDICAL EMERGENCY — commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)

Definition (the diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call):
Neutrophils 0.5 ×10⁹/L or LOWER (≤0.5) in a patient on anticancer treatment PLUS either temp >38°C or other signs/symptoms consistent with clinically significant sepsis
⚠ Signs may be blunted — without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign. Patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead. Maintain a low threshold to treat.
Aetiology
📷 Image placeholder — An indwelling central venous catheter (Hickman line / PICC) — the usual portal of entry for coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (Staph epidermidis) in cancer patients.
Common Organisms
  • Commonest: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients
  • Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas — this is why piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover
Emergency Response — The Sequence
📷 Image placeholder — Door-to-needle algorithm — IV Tazocin within 1 hour (before cultures) → septic screen → 48h reassess (meropenem ± vancomycin) → 4–6 days unresponsive (antifungals); antibiotics are never delayed for investigations.
Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
StepActionNote
1IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediatelyWithin 1 hour ("door-to-needle") — before cultures if needed
2Cultures + septic screenBlood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
348h reassessStill febrile/unwell → escalate: meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
44–6 days unresponsiveInvestigate fungal infection → empirical mould-active antifungal (liposomal amphotericin B, or an echinocandin such as caspofungin) — fluconazole is inadequate, it lacks Aspergillus cover
De-escalation (bedside shorthand): switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h; typical total course 10–14 days — but see the NICE criteria below, which tie the switch to a reassessed low risk rather than apyrexia alone, and tie stopping to the sepsis having responded rather than to a fixed course length
Risk Stratification — Who Actually Needs to Stay In
Risk assessment happens AFTER the first dose — never instead of it.
  • Every patient with suspected neutropenic sepsis gets IV empiric antibiotics within 1 hour
  • Only once that dose is in, and the patient has been observed and found stable, do you ask the second question: does this person need to stay in hospital?
  • There is no low-risk patient who is "too well for the first dose"
Assessing risk
  • Low risk — suitable for early oral switch or ambulatory care
  • High risk — admit, continue IV antibiotics, inpatient monitoring
  • Components (each carries its own weighting; the weighted total is the index):
    • burden of illness (no/mild symptoms scores higher than moderate symptoms)
    • absence of hypotension
    • absence of COPD
    • solid tumour, or haematological malignancy with no previous fungal infection
    • absence of dehydration requiring IV fluids
    • outpatient status at onset of fever, and age <60.
Low risk — the ambulatory / outpatient pathway
  • 1. IV antibiotics first (piperacillin-tazobactam, within the hour), then
  • 2. A defined period of observation confirming clinical stability — the patient must be seen not to be deteriorating before anyone talks about home, then
  • 3. Oral ciprofloxacin + co-amoxiclav — the standard UK oral regimen.
    • Ciprofloxacin gives the Gram-negative/Pseudomonal cover
    • co-amoxiclav adds the Gram-positive (streptococcal/staphylococcal) and anaerobic cover that ciprofloxacin lacks.
  • Clinical criteria:
    • haemodynamically stable, no organ dysfunction
    • no severe focal infection (pneumonia, tunnel infection, perianal sepsis)
    • able to swallow and absorb tablets (no significant mucositis, no vomiting)
    • and not already taking quinolone prophylaxis (if they are, oral ciprofloxacin is not a rescue).
  • Social criteria:
    • a responsible adult at home, a working telephone, transport, and lives close enough to return to the treating unit quickly
    • Ambulatory care is a social decision as much as a microbiological one.
  • Return advice — explicit, written, with the 24-hour acute oncology number: come straight back (do not ring the GP, do not "see how it goes") if:
    • the fever returns or rises, rigors
    • vomiting or unable to keep tablets down
    • new or worsening pain, diarrhoea, breathlessness
    • drowsiness or confusion, or simply feeling worse.
NICE: "Consider outpatient antibiotic therapy for patients with confirmed neutropenic sepsis and a low risk of developing septic complications, taking into account the patient's social and clinical circumstances and discussing with them the need to return to hospital promptly if a problem develops."
⚠ The score does not outrank the doctor.
  • A validated risk score ≥21 in someone with profound neutropenia expected to last >7 days (e.g. AML induction, allograft conditioning), significant comorbidity, uncontrolled cancer or an unsafe home situation is still managed as an inpatient
  • Escalate the decision — outpatient management of neutropenic sepsis is a consultant-level/acute-oncology decision, not an F1's
The Central Venous Access Device (Hickman / PICC / port)
The two reflexes to unlearn (NICE)
  • 1. Do NOT remove the central venous access device as part of the initial empiric management of suspected neutropenic sepsis
  • Most episodes are not line-related, the line is the patient's lifeline for chemotherapy, blood products and antibiotics, and re-siting one in a neutropenic thrombocytopenic patient is not free.
  • 2. Do NOT offer empiric glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin) merely because a line is present — only if there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications
NICE — the "do nots" of initial empiric therapy
  • Do not remove central venous access devices as part of initial empiric management
  • Do not offer empiric glycopeptide antibiotics to patients with a central venous access device unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications
  • Do not offer an aminoglycoside (gentamicin/amikacin), either as monotherapy or in dual therapy, for initial empiric treatment unless there are patient-specific or local microbiological indications
    • beta-lactam monotherapy with piperacillin-tazobactam had lower mortality, fewer adverse events and fewer superinfections than aminoglycoside-containing combinations
    • and these are patients you do not want to make nephrotoxic
When the line DOES come out
  • Tunnel or pocket infection — erythema/tenderness/pus tracking along the subcutaneous tunnel or over an implanted port (as opposed to simple exit-site redness, which can often be treated through the line)
  • Candidaemia / fungaemia — the line is a biofilm reservoir; remove it
  • Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia (also Pseudomonas, and other difficult organisms by local policy) — risk of metastatic seeding
  • Persistent bacteraemia or persistent fever despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy — repeat cultures still positive after 48–72 h on an agent the organism is sensitive to
  • Plus the obvious: septic thrombophlebitis, endocarditis, or haemodynamic instability attributable to the line
How you decide the line is the source
  • Paired cultures — take blood from a peripheral vein AND from each lumen of the line, labelled clearly (this is why the septic screen specifies both)
  • Differential time to positivity — the line culture flagging positive ≥2 h before the peripheral culture with the same organism points to the line as the source
  • Look at it — inspect the exit site and palpate the tunnel/port pocket at every review; a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus in one bottle only is often a contaminant
Beyond the First 48 Hours — Reassess, Switch, Stop, Discharge
Neutropenic sepsis is not a "give Tazocin and walk away" diagnosis. The patient is reassessed daily — response to treatment and risk of septic complications, by a healthcare professional competent in managing complications of anticancer treatment, using a validated risk scoring system.
DecisionNICE criterionTrap
IV → oral switchAfter 48 hours of treatment, in patients whose risk of developing septic complications has been reassessed as low (competent professional, validated scoring system)The criterion is a reassessed risk, not simply "apyrexial for 48 hours". A patient can be afebrile and still high risk.
Stopping antibioticsDiscontinue empiric antibiotic therapy in patients whose neutropenic sepsis has responded to treatment — irrespective of neutrophil countDo not keep antibiotics running until the neutrophils recover. Count recovery is not the endpoint; resolution of the sepsis is.
DischargeOnly after the risk of septic complications has been reassessed as low, taking account of the patient's social and clinical circumstances, with explicit advice to return promptly if a problem developsDischarging on a falling temperature chart alone, with no risk reassessment and no return advice.
⚠ Reconcile the two rules you will be taught.
  • The familiar bedside shorthand is "oral once apyrexial 48 h, 10–14 days in total"
  • NICE's actual wording ties the 48-hour IV→oral switch to a reassessed low risk (not to apyrexia alone), and ties stopping to the sepsis having responded (not to a fixed course length and not to the neutrophil count)
  • If a question offers both, the NICE criterion is the safer answer
Daily review — what you are actually looking for
  • Response: temperature trend, observations/NEWS2, lactate and CRP trend, oxygen requirement, whether a source has declared itself
  • Microbiology: chase cultures at 24–48 h and rationalise to the narrowest effective agent once an organism and sensitivities are known
  • Counts: neutrophil trajectory tells you how long the risk window has left — it does not tell you when to stop antibiotics
  • New problems: line site, mouth (mucositis), perineum, abdomen (see complications), diarrhoea (C. difficile after broad-spectrum cover)
  • Persisting fever at 4–6 days → think invasive fungal disease, an undrained collection, a line, drug fever, or the tumour itself
And then — what happens to the next chemotherapy cycle?
  • An episode of febrile neutropenia is a dose-limiting toxicity. It changes the next cycle; the oncology team must document what and why.
  • Delay — the next cycle waits until the counts have recovered to the threshold specified by the regimen protocol and the infection has resolved
  • Dose reduction — reduce the dose of the myelosuppressive agent(s) for subsequent cycles
  • Secondary G-CSF prophylaxis — G-CSF from the next cycle onwards ("secondary" = after an episode has already happened; "primary" = from cycle 1 in a regimen with a high baseline risk of febrile neutropenia)
  • How you choose:
    • in curative-intent, dose-sensitive treatment (e.g. lymphoma, germ-cell tumours) the priority is to preserve dose intensity — add secondary G-CSF rather than cut the dose
    • In palliative treatment, where the aim is control with tolerable toxicity, dose reduction or delay is usually the better trade.
  • Also revisit prophylaxis (antibacterial/antifungal/antiviral) and make sure the patient still has, and understands, their alert card and 24-hour hotline number.
Complications & Deterioration
Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) — the classic UK finals trap
  • Fever + right iliac fossa pain + diarrhoea in a profoundly neutropenic patient
  • The reflex answer is appendicitis; the right answer is typhlitis
  • RIF pain in a neutropenic patient is typhlitis until proven otherwise.
Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)
  • Who: profound, prolonged neutropenia — AML induction, allogeneic transplant conditioning, taxane-containing regimens; typically in the nadir window
  • Mechanism: chemotherapy-damaged mucosa + no neutrophils → bacterial/fungal invasion of the bowel wall → oedema, ischaemia, necrosis.
    • Favours the caecum (Greek typhlon = caecum) because of its distensibility and relatively poor blood supply.
  • Presentation: fever, RIF pain and tenderness, watery or bloody diarrhoea, abdominal distension, nausea/vomiting.
    • Signs are muted — peritonism may be minimal or absent even with a perforation, because there are no neutrophils to make peritonitis.
  • Investigation: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast is the test — circumferential caecal wall thickening, pericaecal fat stranding/fluid, ± mucosal enhancement, ± pneumatosis intestinalis or free gas (perforation).
    • Ultrasound may show the thickened bowel wall
    • Send stool for C. difficile and cultures, blood cultures, FBC/clotting/lactate
  • Management is MEDICAL:
    • bowel rest (nil by mouth), IV fluids and electrolyte correction, NG decompression if ileus
    • broad-spectrum antibiotics with anaerobic and Gram-negative cover (piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem; add metronidazole if the chosen regimen lacks anaerobic cover)
    • consider antifungal cover, correct coagulopathy and transfuse platelets, stop the offending chemotherapy, consider G-CSF, and review with serial examination and repeat imaging.
    • Involve surgery early — for an opinion, not automatically for an operation.
  • Surgery is reserved for: perforation, full-thickness necrosis, uncontrolled GI haemorrhage (despite correction of coagulopathy/platelets), or clinical deterioration despite maximal medical therapy.
⚠ Why you do NOT rush to theatre.
  • A laparotomy in a patient with no neutrophils, low platelets and a friable oedematous bowel carries very high mortality: the wound will not heal, an anastomosis will not hold, and you have removed the only barrier they had left
  • Most cases settle with bowel rest and antibiotics as the neutrophil count recovers — count recovery is the treatment
  • Operate for a hole or dead bowel, not for pain
Deterioration → septic shock
  • Because the inflammatory signs are blunted, neutropenic patients can look deceptively well and then decompensate abruptly — treat any hypotension, tachycardia, rising lactate, oliguria or new confusion as shock, not as "he's just tired".
  • Sepsis Six within the hour, then reassess: fluid resuscitation, repeat lactate, urinary catheter and hourly urine output, senior review.
  • Septic shock = hypotension persisting despite adequate fluid resuscitation and requiring vasopressors, with a raised lactate → refer to critical care early. Do not titrate fluids on the ward for hours first.
  • Escalate to the acute oncology / haematology team in parallel — and agree the ceiling of care explicitly with the patient and the treating oncologist.
    • Neutropenic sepsis in a patient on curative-intent treatment is usually fully reversible and warrants full escalation
    • that conversation should happen early, not at 3 a.m.
Things not to do to a neutropenic patient
  • No PR (digital rectal) examination and no rectal thermometers
    • mucosal trauma in a neutropenic, often thrombocytopenic patient can seed bacteraemia and precipitate perianal sepsis
    • Use tympanic, oral or axillary temperature; inspect the perineum visually instead.
  • No suppositories or enemas, for the same reason; avoid unnecessary IM injections.
  • Remember perianal sepsis presents without pus — no neutrophils means no abscess to feel; pain and induration alone are enough to act on.
  • Avoid NSAIDs and paracetamol given "prophylactically" — masking fever in a neutropenic patient hides the one sign you have.
Prophylaxis
Prevention Strategy
  • Anticipated neutrophils 0.5 or lower → fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected period of neutropenia (NICE)
  • G-CSF (filgrastim) — shortens the duration of neutropenia, but is not routinely offered to prevent neutropenic sepsis (NICE)
    • reserve it for regimens where G-CSF is an integral part of the protocol, or where it is needed to maintain dose intensity
Exam Pearls
Escalation ladder: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days)

Malaria = protozoan Plasmodium infection via female Anopheles mosquito

The returning-traveller fever — suspect in anyone with fever who lives in or has travelled to an endemic area
The decisive fork:

  • Falciparum — most severe, no dormant stage, RBC sequestration → complications (cerebral, AKI, DIC) → admit every case: oral artemether-lumefantrine if uncomplicated, IV artesunate if any severity feature

    Vivax/Ovale — usually milder but relapsing — hypnozoites in liver → need primaquine for radical cure (after G6PD testing)
  • Vivax can still cause severe disease (ARDS, severe anaemia, splenic rupture), so assess severity whatever the species
Protective host factors (cross-ref Sickle Cell): sickle-cell trait, G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia, HLA-B53, Duffy-negative (specifically blocks vivax)
Life Cycle
Step-by-Step
  • Mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (hepatocytes) → merozoites
  • vivax/ovale only: some hepatocytes form dormant hypnozoites → relapse weeks/months/years later
  • Hepatocyte ruptures → merozoites enter RBCs → replicate → rupture every 48h (72h for P. malariae; 24h for P. knowlesi) → haemolysis + pyrogen release → cyclical fever → more merozoites
  • Falciparum: infected RBCs adhere to small-vessel endothelium → sequestration/occlusion → cerebral malaria, AKI, etc.

  • Rapid antigen tests (RDTs) — an adjunct to the film, never a replacement: a negative RDT does not exclude malaria (less sensitive at low parasitaemia and for non-falciparum species), and antigen can stay positive for weeks after cure, so it cannot be used to judge response (BSH)
  • Parasitaemia >2% in a non-immune patient = severe/complicated malaria → parenteral artesunate. >10% = hyperparasitaemia, a severity criterion in its own right and a marker of very high risk
  • FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), LFTs, glucose, clotting (DIC screen)
Management
📷 Image placeholder — Treatment decision tree — uncomplicated falciparum (oral artemether-lumefantrine) vs severe/complicated (admit + IV artesunate), with severity criteria (parasitaemia >2%, cerebral, AKI, ARDS, hypoglycaemia, acidosis, DIC).
Uncomplicated Falciparum Malaria (Oral)
  • Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet) — first-line
  • Atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone)
  • Quinine + doxycycline (clindamycin instead of doxycycline in pregnancy and in children)
  • Non-falciparum: chloroquine (an ACT where chloroquine-resistant vivax is likely — Indonesia, Papua New Guinea), then primaquine for vivax/ovale radical cure after G6PD testing
Severe/Complicated Malaria
  • IV artesunate = treatment of choice (over IV quinine)
  • Admit all falciparum (risk of rapid deterioration). Malaria is notifiable — notify the health protection team on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation, and the laboratory sends the film to the reference laboratory (UKHSA)
  • Manage severe malaria in a high-dependency or intensive care environment — with regular blood glucose monitoring (hypoglycaemia is common and easily missed) and cautious fluids (pulmonary oedema/ARDS risk)
  • IV artesunate for severe malaria — >2% parasitaemia in a non-immune patient already mandates parenteral treatment; >10% = hyperparasitaemia (routine exchange transfusion no longer recommended)
  • ⚠ Follow parenteral treatment with a full oral course once the patient can swallow and has had ≥24 h of artesunate (artemether-lumefantrine, or quinine + doxycycline/clindamycin) — artesunate's short half-life means monotherapy risks recrudescence. If IV artesunate is not immediately available, start IV quinine rather than delay treatment, and switch when it arrives
  • Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis — typically 1–3 weeks after treatment, i.e. after discharge.
    • Check FBC weekly for ~4 weeks after IV artesunate, and warn the patient to return if pale, breathless, jaundiced or passing dark urine
    • A falling Hb with raised LDH and bilirubin and low haptoglobin is haemolysis — some patients need transfusion
Relapse Prevention (Vivax/Ovale)
  • Primaquine — clears hypnozoites from the liver. In a patient with vivax/ovale infection this is radical cure; the same drug given to an asymptomatic exposed traveller is terminal prophylaxis
  • Tafenoquine — single-dose alternative for radical cure of vivax (also requires quantitative G6PD testing first — long half-life makes screening essential)
  • Check G6PD status first — primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. If G6PD-deficient, do not simply omit radical cure — seek specialist advice, as a modified regimen under supervision may be used, otherwise the hypnozoites remain and the patient relapses
Prophylaxis
  • Bite avoidance: nets, DEET, covering up
  • Chemoprophylaxis per region: Malarone / doxycycline / mefloquine
  • ⚠ No chemoprophylaxis is fully protective — breakthrough malaria occurs. A history of taking prophylaxis, even with perfect adherence, never excludes malaria: still send films
  • ⚠ Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy and in children under 12; primaquine is contraindicated in pregnancy.
    • Advise pregnant women not to travel to a malarious area; if travel is unavoidable, mefloquine may be used — including in the first trimester where falciparum risk is high — or chloroquine + proguanil (with folic acid 5 mg daily) depending on region, and where mefloquine resistance is documented there is no safe effective option, so advise against travel (UKHSA)
    • In treatment, clindamycin replaces doxycycline as the quinine partner drug

The decisive fork:
  • ↓ Production vs ↑ Destruction — with sequestration (hypersplenism, portal hypertension) as the third, quieter mechanism
  • Is the marrow failing to make platelets, are they made but consumed/destroyed, or are they simply pooled in a big spleen?
↓ Production (marrow fails)
  • B12/folate deficiency
  • Liver failure (↓thrombopoietin and splenic pooling)
  • Leukaemia/MDS
  • Drugs (valproate, methotrexate, isotretinoin — marrow suppression; antihistamines and PPIs are reported causes but act by an idiosyncratic/immune mechanism)
  • Alcohol
Usually other cytopenias + abnormal marrow
↑ Destruction (platelets consumed)
  • ITP — immune (anti-GPIIb/IIIa)
  • TTP — microangiopathic (ADAMTS13↓)
  • HIT — immune (anti-PF4/heparin)
  • HUS — microangiopathic (Shiga toxin)
  • DIC — consumptive
  • Sepsis — consumptive/immune (often via DIC)
Isolated low platelet count; normal/active marrow
Drug-induced immune — hapten-type:
  • The drug binds platelet glycoprotein and a drug-dependent antibody destroys it
  • Quinine, vancomycin, abciximab (historical — no longer marketed), sulfonamides
  • Treatment is to stop the drug — note this is a different mechanism from the marrow-suppressing drugs listed opposite
Bleeding pattern: Thrombocytopenia → mucocutaneous/platelet-type bleeding — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia. (Deep joint/muscle bleeding = factor deficiency.)
Clinical Features by Count
Platelet countRisk
