  • High risk of spontaneous bleeding — ICH, GI bleed
  • Review the drug chart: stop antiplatelets and anticoagulants, avoid NSAIDs, and avoid IM injections
📷 Image placeholder — Petechiae and purpura on the lower limbs — the mucocutaneous (platelet-type) bleeding pattern of thrombocytopenia
ITP (Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura)
Mechanism & Demographics
  • Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies (usually IgG) → platelet destruction
  • Children: acute, post-viral, self-limiting
  • Adults: chronic, women; can be 2° to SLE / CLL / HIV
  • Isolated thrombocytopenia — clotting normal
The three phases
  • Newly diagnosed — under 3 months
  • Persistent — 3 to 12 months
  • Chronic — beyond 12 months
  • The phase matters because it drives how aggressively you escalate, and because children usually remit spontaneously where adults usually do not (paediatric ITP)
Investigations
  • Isolated thrombocytopenia with a normal film — ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion; antiplatelet antibody testing is not routinely recommended (poor sensitivity and specificity). Screen for secondary causes (HIV, hepatitis C)
  • Bone marrow: ↑ megakaryocytes — not routine in typical ITP; reserve for atypical features or older adults (e.g. exclude leukaemia/MDS before immunosuppression)
When do you actually treat?
  • Not every low count needs treating.
  • A newly diagnosed adult who is asymptomatic or has only minor mucocutaneous bleeding, with a platelet count that is above roughly 30 ×109/L, is generally observed rather than started on steroids
  • Treatment is for bleeding, a count persistently below about 20 ×109/L, or to cover a procedure
  • You are treating bleeding and bleeding risk, not a number on a screen
  • When steroids are given, the course is short — a matter of weeks including the taper, not months. Prolonged prednisolone causes more harm than the thrombocytopenia in most patients
  • IVIg is the option when the count must rise fast — active bleeding or an urgent procedure. It works by saturating splenic Fc receptors, so the effect is temporary
Management
  1. Oral prednisolone — 1st line, as a short course
  2. IVIG — if urgent (pre-procedure / active bleed); raises count fast
  3. TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag / romiplostim) or rituximab — preferred 2nd line
  4. Splenectomy — now usually deferred (≥12 months) given infection/thrombosis risk; vaccinate first (pneumococcal, Hib, meningococcal, annual influenza) and give lifelong penicillin V afterwards
TTP (Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura)
📷 Image placeholder — Schematic — ADAMTS13 deficiency → uncleaved ultra-large vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi (consumption) + RBC shearing (MAHA/schistocytes).
Mechanism: ADAMTS13 deficiency (inherited or autoimmune) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi in small vessels → consumption (thrombocytopenia) + RBC shearing (MAHA)
Causes
  • Idiopathic, post-infection; SLE, HIV, tumours
  • Drugs: ciclosporin, OCP, clopidogrel, penicillin, aciclovir
Classic Pentad
  • Fever
  • Neurological signs
  • Thrombocytopenia
  • MAHA (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia)
  • Renal failure
Management
  • Plasma exchange — urgent, first-line (replaces ADAMTS13); start it within 4–8 hours of suspecting TTP and never delay it for the ADAMTS13 result — send the sample first, then treat (BSH)
  • Steroids + rituximab
  • Caplacizumab — anti-vWF nanobody, NICE-recommended add-on for acute acquired (immune) TTP alongside plasma exchange + immunosuppression
  • NEVER transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleed — fuels more thrombosis
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film: schistocytes (red-cell fragments) of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia — the hallmark shared by TTP, HUS and DIC (absent in ITP/HIT)
HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia)
📷 Image placeholder — Timeline — platelet count falling 5–10 days after starting heparin with new thrombosis; the timing is the diagnostic clue (4T score).
Mechanism: Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies → platelet activation → paradoxical thrombosis AND thrombocytopenia
Key Clinical Rules
  • Platelet fall typically 5–10 days after starting heparin
  • The timing is the diagnostic clue (4T score)
  • Paradoxical thrombosis, not just bleeding
Management
  • Stop ALL heparin immediately — LMWH and unfractionated heparin, line and cannula flushes, and heparin-bonded catheters
  • Switch to a non-heparin anticoagulant: argatroban or danaparoid (UK-licensed); fondaparinux or a DOAC are used off-licence, DOACs typically once the patient is stable.
    • Anticoagulation must be continued, not simply stopped, even if no thrombosis has been found
    • Where the risk of HIT is appreciable, check the platelet count every 2–3 days from day 4 to day 14 of heparin and act on a fall of ≥30% (BSH)
  • NOT warfarin acutely — it depletes protein C faster than factor II, deepening the prothrombotic state and precipitating venous limb gangrene and skin necrosis
    • Start a vitamin K antagonist only once the platelet count has recovered (≥150 ×109/L), at a low dose, overlapped with the non-heparin agent for at least 5 days
  • NOT platelet transfusion — it adds substrate to an ongoing thrombotic process
Platelets In, and Platelets In Pregnancy
🛑 Four conditions in which you do not routinely give prophylactic platelets.
  • This note already tells you never to transfuse in TTP and HIT — those are two members of a set of four, and the reasoning is the same each time: the platelets are being destroyed or consumed, so transfused ones are destroyed too, and in the microangiopathies they feed the process.
  • Chronic bone marrow failure — repeated transfusion drives alloimmunisation and refractoriness; save them for bleeding
  • Autoimmune (immune) thrombocytopenia — the antibody destroys donor platelets as fast as the patient’s own
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia — adding platelets to a prothrombotic state
  • Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura — classically described as “fuel on the fire”
  • The rule is about prophylactic transfusion. Serious bleeding changes the calculation in any of them — you treat the haemorrhage in front of you.
📎 The numeric transfusion ladder — the prophylactic threshold, the higher targets before surgery and before neurosurgery or eye surgery — is set out in Transfusion.
Before acting on any isolated low count, exclude EDTA-induced platelet clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) by checking the film or repeating in citrate (blood count & film).

A low platelet count in pregnancy is common and usually benign — but the differential contains two obstetric emergencies, so it is never ignored.

Four conditions where prophylactic platelets are not routinely given: chronic marrow failure, ITP, HIT and TTP. Serious bleeding overrides the rule.
Treat the bleeding, not the number. A newly diagnosed adult with a modestly low count and no significant bleeding is observed; steroid courses are short, and IVIg is for when the count must rise fast.
Drugs cause thrombocytopenia two different ways: marrow suppression, and hapten-type immune destruction (quinine, vancomycin, abciximab, sulfonamides) — the treatment for the latter is to stop the drug.
In pregnancy, gestational thrombocytopenia is commonest and needs nothing — but hypertension, proteinuria, deranged LFTs or schistocytes mean pre-eclampsia/HELLP or a microangiopathy instead.
The fork: ↓ production vs ↑ destruction.

HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia:
Pancytopenia — Overview
Definition:
  • Reduction in all three cell lines — anaemia + neutropenia/leucopenia + thrombocytopenia
  • It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is always to find the cause
  • Note that aplastic anaemia's "no abnormal cells" describes it at presentation: it carries a long-term risk of clonal evolution to MDS/AML and of PNH-clone expansion, so these patients need lifelong monitoring — regular FBC, with periodic repeat PNH clone testing and marrow morphology/cytogenetics
The decisive fork: Hypocellular marrow (production failure) vs Cellular marrow (ineffective / destruction / infiltration) — decided by bone marrow biopsy.
Anaemia

Fatigue, pallor, SOB

Thrombocytopenia

Bruising, bleeding, petechiae — cross-ref Thrombocytopenia

Neutropenia

Infections — ⚠ neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency: neutrophils ≤0.5 ×109/L with a temperature above 38°C or any clinical sign of sepsis (NICE).

  • That definition is written for patients on anticancer treatment, but febrile neutropenia from any cause of marrow failure is managed identically — and treat on suspicion if the count is falling steeply
  • Give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour — take cultures but do not wait for them, for the neutrophil count, or for a fever to be documented
  • Cross-ref Neutropenic Sepsis

Aetiology — Organised by the Marrow Fork
CategoryHypocellular marrow (↓ production)Cellular marrow (ineffective / destruction / infiltration)
Primary marrowAplastic anaemiaMDS, Acute leukaemia, Myelofibrosis
Infiltration—Myeloma, Lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma — the marrow is packed with infiltrate and therefore hypercellular, but depleted of normal haematopoiesis; often a leucoerythroblastic film
Nutritional—B12 / folate deficiency (megaloblastic — ineffective haematopoiesis)
Drugs / toxins
  • Chemotherapy, radiation, chloramphenicol, carbimazole, methotrexate, alcohol — also carbamazepine, phenytoin, sulfasalazine, clozapine, azathioprine and trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole
  • The first treatment is always to stop the culprit drug and recheck the FBC
—
InfectionViral (parvovirus B19 — classically pure red cell aplasia, true pancytopenia mainly in the immunocompromised; EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis), overwhelming sepsis (normo-/hypercellular marrow, often with haemophagocytosis); in a returning traveller add malaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) and disseminated TB — take a travel history
Destruction / pooling—Hypersplenism (including Felty's — RA + splenomegaly + neutropenia), SLE / autoimmune; PNH — complement-mediated haemolysis affects red cells only, so when PNH causes true pancytopenia it is via the associated marrow failure / aplastic-anaemia overlap
Cross-refs: MDS, Leukaemia, Myelofibrosis, Myeloma, Lymphoma, B12 deficiency are all structured notes — pancytopenia is the unifying presentation pointing at all of them.
Aplastic Anaemia — the Prototype Hypocellular Cause
Definition: Hypocellular ("empty") marrow replaced by fat — pancytopenia with no abnormal cells (no blasts, no dysplasia). This is the contrast with leukaemia/MDS.
Causes
  • Idiopathic / autoimmune — commonest
  • Drugs (see table above)
  • Viral (EBV, hepatitis, parvovirus)
  • Radiation
  • Inherited — Fanconi anaemia is the commonest (others: dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman–Diamond). Suspect an inherited cause in any young patient and confirm with chromosome breakage testing before giving immunosuppression or standard-intensity conditioning
Management
  • Supportive: irradiated and leucodepleted red cell and platelet transfusions — irradiation is mandatory once ATG is given and for all transplant candidates, to prevent fatal transfusion-associated GvHD; avoid family-member donations in potential transplant recipients (alloimmunisation); minimise transfusion generally. Infection control and prophylaxis
  • Severity first: severe AA = marrow cellularity <25% plus 2 of 3 — neutrophils <0.5, platelets <20, reticulocytes <20 (or <60 by automated count) (×109/L); very severe = as above with neutrophils <0.2. Non-severe AA is managed supportively if transfusion-independent — but transfusion-dependent non-severe disease is treated like severe disease with immunosuppression (BSH); the treatments below are for severe/very severe disease
  • Allogeneic stem cell transplant — first-line and potentially curative in patients under ~35–40 with an HLA-matched sibling donor; it is donor availability and fitness, not age alone, that decides
  • Immunosuppression where there is no matched sibling or the patient is older: horse (equine) ATG + ciclosporin — horse ATG is superior to rabbit first-line — with eltrombopag (TPO-receptor agonist) — horse ATG + ciclosporin with eltrombopag is the standard first-line immunosuppressive regimen for severe/very severe disease (BSH), though European approval is still required before it is used routinely upfront in the UK; eltrombopag is separately established here for refractory disease
📷 Image placeholder — Bone marrow trephine: hypocellular ("empty") marrow largely replaced by fat spaces with few haematopoietic cells — the picture of aplastic anaemia (contrast the hypercellular marrow of MDS/leukaemia)
Investigations — Workup Sequence
📷 Image placeholder — Megaloblastic film — hypersegmented neutrophil (≥6 lobes) with oval macrocytes, the reversible B12/folate cause to exclude before bone-marrow biopsy.
FBC + Reticulocytes

Confirm all three lines down. Low reticulocytes → production failure.

Blood Film — the Highest-Yield Early Clue
  • Blasts → leukaemia
  • Dysplasia / pseudo-Pelger–Huët cells → MDS (the inherited Pelger–Huët anomaly is a benign mimic)
  • Teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic picture → myelofibrosis / infiltration
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis → B12/folate deficiency
  • Schistocytes → microangiopathy
📷 Image placeholder — Blood film: leucoerythroblastic picture with teardrop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) — immature red/white precursors + teardrop cells suggest marrow infiltration / myelofibrosis (the "dry tap" cause)
Haematinics

B12 and folate — exclude the reversible nutritional cause, but send these in parallel, not in sequence: pancytopenia with blasts on the film, or with fever/neutropenia, warrants same-day haematology referral — and a new unexplained pancytopenia is itself a same-day referral, not a count to repeat next week.

Do not wait for the result. ⚠ If both are low, or B12 status is uncertain, treat B12 first — folate given alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate subacute combined degeneration of the cord.

Bone Marrow Aspirate + Trephine = the Decisive Test
  • Cellularity (empty vs full)
  • Blasts, dysplasia, infiltration, fibrosis
  • Dry tap → suggests myelofibrosis — also hairy cell leukaemia, marrow infiltration, or a technically failed aspirate; this is exactly why the trephine is mandatory
Supporting Tests

LFTs

  • virology (HIV, hepatitis, EBV, CMV, parvovirus)
  • autoantibodies (SLE)
  • LDH (cell turnover marker)
  • high-sensitivity flow cytometry for a PNH clone (FLAER-based, on granulocytes and monocytes — more sensitive than red-cell CD55/CD59, which is confounded by transfusion and haemolysis) — PNH is an aplastic-anaemia overlap

Exam Pearls
Pancytopenia is a pattern (all 3 lines ↓), never a final answer — always name the cause.
Bone marrow biopsy is the decisive investigation; blood film + reticulocytes are the best first clues.
The fork: hypocellular marrow → aplastic anaemia / drugs / radiation; cellular marrow → MDS, leukaemia, megaloblastic, infiltration.
Always check B12/folate — cheap and fully reversible — but in parallel with the rest of the workup, never as a reason to delay referral.
Aplastic anaemia = empty marrow, no abnormal cells; MDS = full marrow + dysplasia; leukaemia = full marrow + ≥20% blasts — the three-way discriminator.
Dry tap → suggests myelofibrosis (also hairy cell leukaemia, infiltration, or a failed aspirate); teardrop cells + massive splenomegaly strongly support it — the trephine (reticulin/collagen fibrosis) plus JAK2/CALR/MPL confirms it.
Two emergencies inside pancytopenia: neutropenic sepsis (IV antibiotics within 1 hour) and bleeding — an emergency at any platelet count.
  • The prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold is <10 ×109/L if stable, <20 if septic/febrile, <50 before invasive procedures — but that ladder is for reversible marrow failure
  • In chronic bone marrow failure such as aplastic anaemia prophylactic platelets are not routinely given (alloimmunisation and refractoriness) — transfuse for bleeding (NICE)
  • Cross-ref both notes

Definition: Raised Hb / haematocrit / red cell count. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is to classify the cause.
Two-step decisive fork:
1. True (↑ red cell mass) vs Relative (↓ plasma volume)
2. If true → EPO low (Primary / PV) vs EPO high (Secondary)
Why it matters: ↑ Hct → hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT/PE) — the complication that makes it worth diagnosing and treating. ⚠ Thrombosis also occurs at unusual sites — Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein), portal, splenic and mesenteric veins, cerebral venous sinus: any splanchnic or cerebral venous thrombosis should prompt a JAK2 V617F test even when the FBC looks normal.

Polycythaemia Vera — Primary Cause
Cross-ref: full PV detail lives in the Myeloproliferative Disorders note. Summary below.
Key Features
  • Clonal marrow; JAK2 V617F ~95%, plus JAK2 exon 12 ~3%
  • Low EPO
  • Aquagenic pruritus — itch on contact with water at any temperature, classically after a warm bath or shower; present in ~40% of PV, so suggestive rather than diagnostic
  • Ruddy/plethoric complexion, conjunctival plethora
  • Splenomegaly, HTN, gout
  • Headache, visual disturbance, thrombosis
  • Low ESR (hyperviscosity)
Management
  1. Venesection — 1st line; target Hct <0.45 in all patients, male and female. Remove 450–500 mL per session, reduced to 250–300 mL with fluid replacement in the elderly or those with cardiovascular disease. ⚠ The resulting iron deficiency is therapeutic — do not give iron supplements, which cause rebound erythrocytosis
  2. Aspirin 75 mg od for all unless contraindicated. ⚠ Withhold aspirin if platelets >1000–1500 ×109/L until acquired von Willebrand disease is excluded (ristocetin cofactor activity) — cytoreduce first, then reintroduce once the count falls. ⚠ Assess and treat cardiovascular risk factors in every patient — blood pressure, lipids, diabetes and smoking (BSH)
  3. Cytoreduction if high-risk — age ≥65 or prior thrombosis (BSH)
    • Also consider it for poor tolerance of or a high venesection requirement, symptomatic/progressive splenomegaly, or progressive thrombocytosis/leucocytosis. Hydroxycarbamide first-line
    • Interferon alfa preferred in younger patients — in pregnancy the agent used is pegylated interferon alfa-2a
    • Ropeginterferon alfa-2b is not recommended in pregnancy and requires a pregnancy test before starting and effective contraception during treatment and for 8 weeks afterwards (MHRA). ⚠ Hydroxycarbamide is teratogenic — avoid in pregnancy and ensure contraception. ⚠ On hydroxycarbamide monitor the FBC regularly, and advise sun protection and skin self-examination — long-term use causes painful leg ulcers and non-melanoma skin cancer (BNF)
  4. Ruxolitinib — JAK1/JAK2 inhibitor, for patients resistant to or intolerant of hydroxycarbamide

Secondary Polycythaemia — EPO-Driven
Appropriate (Hypoxic) — EPO correctly raised
  • Chronic lung disease (COPD)
  • High altitude
  • Cyanotic heart disease (R→L shunt)
  • OSA
  • Heavy smoking (carboxyhaemoglobin)

Cross-ref COPD / OSA notes

Inappropriate (Tumour) — EPO secreted autonomously
  • Renal cell carcinoma — classic
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Cerebellar haemangioblastoma
  • Uterine fibroids
  • (Phaeochromocytoma — rarer reported cause)

Exogenous / other: testosterone replacement and anabolic steroids, recombinant EPO abuse (doping), post-renal-transplant erythrocytosis, SGLT2 inhibitors.

Congenital: high-affinity haemoglobin, Chuvash polycythaemia (VHL). ⚠ Always take a drug and testosterone history before an invasive workup — this is now one of the commonest reasons a raised Hct is referred.

Management of secondary and apparent: treat the underlying cause — O₂/CPAP for hypoxia, smoking cessation, resect tumour, stop or reduce testosterone/anabolic steroids (keep the haematocrit below 0.54) and stop EPO abuse, ACE inhibitor or ARB for post-transplant erythrocytosis. Venesection only if symptomatic hyperviscosity — it is not routine in secondary polycythaemia and has no role in apparent/relative polycythaemia, where the treatment is weight, alcohol, smoking and blood-pressure control plus review of diuretics (BSH). ⚠ In cyanotic congenital heart disease venesection is a specialist cardiology decision — routine venesection causes harmful iron deficiency.
Investigations — Workup Sequence
Step 1 — Confirm and classify

Confirm a persistently raised haematocrit — >0.52 in men, >0.48 in women (repeat over ~2 months); exclude a spurious result and assess for dehydration (relative polycythaemia). ⚠ This is the diagnostic threshold and is not the same as the <0.45 venesection target.

Step 2 — JAK2 V617F = the first-line confirmatory test

JAK2 V617F positive in ~95% of PV — a positive result in a patient with a sustained raised Hct essentially establishes PV.

Step 3 — If JAK2 V617F is negative

Test JAK2 exon 12 (~3% of PV, covering most of the remainder), and send serum EPO: a low/subnormal EPO supports PV (a WHO minor criterion), while a normal or high EPO steers towards a secondary cause — though a normal EPO alone excludes nothing.

Step 4 — If secondary suspected
  • ABG / SpO₂ — hypoxia
  • CXR / lung function — COPD
  • Sleep study — OSA
  • Abdominal imaging (CT/USS) — renal / hepatic tumour
Supporting in PV

Low ESR (high viscosity prevents sedimentation), ↑ urate (high cell turnover), splenomegaly on USS.

Exam Pearls
JAK2 + low EPO + aquagenic pruritus = PV until proven otherwise.
Polycythaemia = a pattern (↑ Hb/Hct) → classify: true vs relative, then EPO high vs low.
EPO LOW = PV (autonomous marrow); EPO HIGH = secondary (hypoxia or tumour) — the single decisive discriminator.
Danger in true polycythaemia: hyperviscosity → thrombosis. Treat PV with venesection (target Hct <0.45) + aspirin.
Relative polycythaemia = normal red cell mass, low plasma volume (dehydration, Gaisböck) — Hct raised but red cell mass is normal.
Secondary causes: appropriate (hypoxic — altitude, COPD, OSA, shunt) vs inappropriate (EPO-secreting tumour — renal cell carcinoma is classic).

Neutropenic Sepsis

The commonest life-threatening complication of chemotherapy. Defined as a temperature >38 °C (or other signs of sepsis) with a neutrophil count ≤0.5 ×10⁹/L, typically 7–14 days after chemotherapy.

Do not wait for the blood count or cultures. Give empirical IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour — first-line piperacillin–tazobactam (Tazocin) — alongside the Sepsis 6.
See the dedicated Neutropenic Sepsis › note for full detail (risk stratification, G-CSF, prophylaxis).
Malignant Spinal Cord Compression (MSCC)

Compression of the spinal cord or cauda equina by tumour — usually vertebral metastases. Commonest primaries: breast, lung, prostate, myeloma, renal.

🩺 Features
  • Back pain — often the first symptom; worse on lying flat, coughing or straining
  • Radicular pain, limb weakness, a sensory level
  • Bladder/bowel dysfunction (a late, ominous sign)
  • UMN signs below the level (LMN if cauda equina)
💊 Management
  • Dexamethasone 16 mg — a loading dose as soon as possible, then 16 mg daily — with PPI cover and daily blood-glucose monitoring.
    • Give it to a patient with neurological symptoms or signs, on clinical suspicion and before the MRI; stop it if MSCC is then excluded (NICE)
    • If a haematological malignancy is seriously suspected, steroids can render the biopsy non-diagnostic — but that is a reason to get urgent senior oncology or haematology advice, not to withhold: in a patient who already has a deficit, the cord takes priority
  • Reduce spinal loading until stability is assessed — nurse supine with neutral alignment, log-roll for turns, and position flat or partly elevated guided by comfort; get expert spinal advice and start the stability assessment within 24 hours, so immobilisation lasts no longer than it needs to (NICE)
  • Urgent whole-spine MRI — as soon as possible, and always within 24 h; sooner, and out of hours if needed, when the neurology is progressing (NICE)
  • Definitive: surgical decompression or radiotherapy; involve the MSCC coordinator
  • Time-critical — the neurological function the patient has when treatment starts is the best predictor of the function they keep: most patients still walking stay walking, while established paraplegia is usually permanent. Hours of delay cost function, not just comfort
New or progressive back pain in a patient with cancer is MSCC until proven otherwise.
Spinal cord disorders — cord syndromes & levels ›
📷 Image placeholder — Sagittal whole-spine MRI: vertebral metastasis compressing the spinal cord — the urgent decisive investigation in suspected MSCC
Superior Vena Cava Obstruction (SVCO)

Obstruction of the SVC impairs venous return from the head, neck and upper limbs.

It usually develops subacutely over days to weeks, so there is normally time to image and obtain a tissue diagnosis before treatment — the exceptions are stridor, airway compromise or cerebral oedema, which are immediately life-threatening.

Causes: lung cancer (especially small-cell), lymphoma, thymoma, mediastinal metastases; also central-line thrombosis.

Steroids are widely given and sit in UK acute oncology pathways, but the evidence for them is weak — the interventions that change the picture are stenting and tumour-directed treatment.

🩺 Features
  • Swelling & plethora of the face, neck and arms; distended neck/chest wall veins
  • Dyspnoea, cough, headache (worse bending forward)
  • Pemberton’s sign: facial congestion/cyanosis on raising the arms
  • Severe: stridor/airway compromise, cerebral oedema
💊 Management
  • Sit up; oxygen if hypoxic, titrated to target saturations; dexamethasone 8 mg twice daily with gastroprotection (defer until tissue is obtained if lymphoma is a serious possibility). Stridor or airway compromise: call anaesthetics and senior oncology immediately and secure the airway — that is the one situation where treatment precedes the biopsy
  • CXR (mediastinal mass) then CT chest with contrast; obtain tissue diagnosis before steroids if lymphoma is possible (steroids can render the biopsy non-diagnostic)
  • Endovascular stenting for rapid relief (severe cases)
  • Radiotherapy / chemotherapy per tumour type (chemo for small-cell & lymphoma); anticoagulate if thrombotic
📷 Image placeholder — Clinical appearance of SVC obstruction: facial and neck swelling/plethora with distended neck and chest-wall veins (Pemberton’s sign on arm elevation)
Tumour Lysis Syndrome (TLS)
📷 Image placeholder — Mechanism schematic — tumour-cell lysis releasing K⁺, phosphate and urate (all raised) with a reciprocal fall in Ca²⁺, driving AKI, arrhythmia and seizures.

Massive tumour-cell breakdown (usually within days of starting chemotherapy, occasionally spontaneous) releases intracellular contents and causes acute metabolic derangement → AKI, arrhythmia, seizures.

What actually determines risk — three things: what the tumour is, how much of it there is, and how well the kidneys are working.

Highly proliferative, chemosensitive haematological cancers lyse fastest.

Bulk is judged clinically (large nodal masses, hepatosplenomegaly, a packed marrow) and biochemically by the white-cell count and the LDH — both stand in for tumour burden and cell turnover, and a high LDH at presentation marks bulky, fast-dividing disease.

A raised baseline urate, dehydration or any pre-existing renal impairment pushes a patient up a band, because the kidney is what clears the urate, potassium and phosphate. Risk is assessed and prophylaxis started before the first dose of chemotherapy — not after the first abnormal result.

Risk bandTypical pictureProphylaxis
LowerMost solid tumours; low-burden, slowly proliferating disease; normal renal function and urateEncourage oral fluids and check the bloods; allopurinol added if there is any doubt about burden or renal function
IntermediateAcute leukaemia or aggressive lymphoma without extreme bulk; modestly raised WCC and LDH; preserved renal functionIV hydration + allopurinol
HighBurkitt’s and other high-grade lymphoma, ALL or AML with a high WCC, bulky chemosensitive disease, high LDH — or any of these with renal impairment or a raised baseline urateIV hydration + rasburicase — check G6PD status first; if deficient, rasburicase is contraindicated and the patient is managed with IV hydration + allopurinol and close monitoring instead (BSH)
🧪 Biochemistry
  • ↑ Potassium (arrhythmia risk)
  • ↑ Phosphate
  • ↑ Urate (uric acid)
  • ↓ Calcium (binds the raised phosphate)
⚠️ Who is at risk
  • High-grade lymphoma (Burkitt’s), acute leukaemias (ALL/AML)
  • Bulky, chemosensitive tumours; a high white-cell count and a high LDH — the two lab surrogates for tumour burden and cell turnover
  • Pre-existing renal impairment / dehydration
💊 Prevention & treatment
  • IV hydration is the backbone — generous potassium-free crystalloid started before chemotherapy and continued through the lysis window, aiming at a good urine output to carry urate and phosphate out through the kidney
  • Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — stops new urate forming) for prophylaxis in lower- and intermediate-risk patients; rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase — breaks down urate already formed) for high risk or established TLS, contraindicated in G6PD deficiency. They are used instead of one another, not together — see Leukaemia › for the lab-TLS definition and the allopurinol-versus-rasburicase rule
  • “Close monitoring” means a schedule, not a phrase: U&E, calcium, phosphate, urate, LDH and fluid balance before treatment, then repeated several times a day through the first days of chemotherapy in high-risk patients — not once on the morning round — stepping down as the numbers stabilise.
    • Continuous cardiac monitoring while the potassium is high
    • After rasburicase, urate samples must go into a pre-chilled tube on ice, or the enzyme keeps working in the bottle and reports a falsely low urate
  • Treat hyperkalaemia as an emergency — the “no calcium” rule above is about correcting a low calcium number, and does not override IV calcium gluconate to protect the heart when there are hyperkalaemic ECG changes; then insulin–dextrose ± salbutamol. Phosphate binders for rising phosphate; stop nephrotoxic drugs and avoid contrast where you can
  • Escalate early for renal replacement therapy — hyperkalaemia refractory to medical treatment, oliguric/anuric AKI or fluid overload not responding to fluids and diuresis, severe hyperphosphataemia with symptomatic hypocalcaemia, or refractory acidosis. TLS-driven AKI often needs dialysis sooner than other causes, so involve renal/critical care before the numbers are desperate
🚫 Four things not to do in TLS
  • Do not add potassium to the hydration fluid. The problem is too much potassium, not too little — hydrate with potassium-free crystalloid and check before hanging any bag with added K⁺
  • Do not alkalinise the urine. Urinary alkalinisation with bicarbonate is no longer recommended: it does make urate more soluble, but it drives calcium-phosphate precipitation in the tubules and can worsen the very AKI it is meant to prevent
  • Do not correct asymptomatic hypocalcaemia.
    • Giving calcium into a high-phosphate circulation risks calcium-phosphate deposition in the kidney and other tissues and worsens the AKI
    • Treat only symptomatic hypocalcaemia — arrhythmia, seizure, tetany — and treat the symptom, not the number
  • Do not wait for the biochemistry to declare itself. Risk-stratify and start prophylaxis before the first dose; once TLS is established you are firefighting
Leukostasis (Hyperleukocytosis)

When the circulating blast count is very high the blood itself stops flowing properly: blasts are large, stiff and adhesive, and once they plug the pulmonary and cerebral microcirculation the tissue behind them is ischaemic.

This is why blasts on the film, or a WCC >100, is a same-day haematology referral rather than a number to repeat in a week.

It is commonest in AML (especially the monocytic subtypes), CML in blast crisis and ALL — lymphoblasts are smaller and less adhesive, so ALL tolerates a higher count before symptoms appear.

Hyperleukocytosis is the count; leukostasis is the count plus symptoms. The diagnosis is clinical — you make it at the bedside in a patient whose blood film has already told you the answer.

🩺 Two symptom domains (plus one)
  • Pulmonary — dyspnoea, tachypnoea and hypoxia, often out of proportion to an unimpressive early chest film; can progress to respiratory failure
  • CNS — headache, visual change or blurring, tinnitus, dizziness, confusion, drowsiness and, untreated, coma; fundoscopy may show engorged retinal veins and haemorrhages
  • Priapism — the classic third presentation, and an emergency in its own right
  • Intracranial haemorrhage and other end-organ ischaemia (limb, myocardial) are the feared complications
💊 Management
  • Immediate haematology involvement — early mortality is high and the clock is the blast count
  • IV hydration, and urgent cytoreduction under haematology — hydroxycarbamide, with apheresis in selected symptomatic patients, to bring the count down quickly
  • Cytoreduction only buys time — the definitive treatment is prompt induction chemotherapy for the underlying leukaemia, started without delay
  • Concurrent TLS prophylaxis (hydration + urate-lowering, with the monitoring schedule above) — cytoreduction lyses exactly the cells that cause TLS
  • Correct coagulopathy and give platelets as needed — platelets do not meaningfully raise viscosity, so do not withhold them
Hold the red cells.
  • Transfusing red cells before the white count has come down raises whole-blood viscosity and can precipitate or worsen leukostasis — correct the anaemia after cytoreduction unless the patient is haemodynamically compromised
  • Avoid diuretics and do not let the patient become dehydrated — haemoconcentration raises viscosity too
Practice point.
  • There is no UK national guideline for leukostasis; what is written here is standard practice distilled from review literature, and the count at which centres reach for apheresis varies
  • Beyond the WCC >100 referral trigger used across these notes, no thresholds are quoted here for that reason
Hypercalcaemia of Malignancy
📷 Image placeholder — ECG in hypercalcaemia — a shortened QT interval, the key cardiac clue and arrhythmia-risk marker.

The commonest life-threatening metabolic complication of cancer. Mechanisms: PTHrP (squamous-cell lung, breast, renal), osteolytic bone metastases (breast, myeloma), and tumour 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma).

🩺 Features — “stones, bones, groans, moans, thrones”
  • Polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration
  • Constipation, abdominal pain, nausea
  • Confusion, lethargy, low mood
  • Bone pain, renal stones; short QT, arrhythmia
💊 Management
  • Stop the contributors first — thiazide diuretics, calcium and vitamin D supplements — then aggressive IV fluids (0.9% saline) to rehydrate and promote calcium excretion. Loop diuretics are NOT first-line: they worsen the dehydration that drives the hypercalcaemia, and are used only for fluid overload once the patient is fully rehydrated
  • IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronic acid) once rehydrated
  • Denosumab if bisphosphonate-refractory / renal impairment; steroids for lymphoma-related
  • Treat the underlying malignancy
See also Hyperparathyroidism / Hypercalcaemia › (Endocrinology) for the full differential, work-up and follow-through.
Exam Pearls
Highest TLS risk
Burkitt’s lymphoma and acute leukaemias with a high white-cell count.
Neutropenic sepsis
IV piperacillin–tazobactam within 1 hour of presentation — never wait for the neutrophil count.
Spinal cord compression
Back pain + neurology in a cancer patient → urgent whole-spine MRI + high-dose dexamethasone.
SVCO
Facial/arm swelling, distended veins, dyspnoea; small-cell lung cancer; Pemberton’s sign; stenting for rapid relief.
Malignant hypercalcaemia
Fluids first, then a bisphosphonate. Commonly PTHrP-mediated (squamous lung) or myeloma bone disease.
LDH
A marker of cell turnover and tumour burden: a high LDH alongside a high white-cell count flags bulky, fast-dividing disease and moves the patient into a higher TLS risk band.
Leukostasis
Blasts on the film or WCC >100 with breathlessness or confusion. Hydroxycarbamide ± apheresis and prompt induction, with TLS cover — and hold the red cells until the count is down.
TLS — the four do-nots
No potassium in the hydration bag, no urinary alkalinisation, no calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcaemia, and no waiting for abnormal biochemistry before starting prophylaxis.
Tumour lysis biochemistry

  • ↑K, ↑phosphate, ↑urate, ↓calcium
  • Hydration is the backbone; allopurinol at low/intermediate risk, rasburicase at high risk or in established TLS — one or the other, never both (avoid rasburicase in G6PD deficiency)
HAEMATOLOGY__Full Blood Count (FBC) — In:
What it is

The Full Blood Count is the most commonly requested blood test.

An automated analyser counts and sizes the three cell lineages and derives red-cell indices. Always interpret the FBC as three separate lineages — red cells, white cells, platelets — then ask whether one, two, or all three are abnormal.

Sample: EDTA tube (purple/lavender top). Fill to the line — under-filling falsely lowers counts and can clump platelets. Analyse promptly; delays cause spurious results.
The three lineages at a glance
🔴 Red cells
Hb, RBC, Hct and the indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW). Answer: anaemia or polycythaemia? Then classify by MCV.
⚪ White cells
Total WCC plus the differential (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils). Always read the differential, not just the total.
🟣 Platelets
Count plus MPV. Check for pseudothrombocytopenia (EDTA-induced clumping) before acting on an isolated low value.
Adult reference ranges

Ranges vary between labs — always use your local reference range. Typical UK adult values:

A systematic read — every time
  1. Scan all three lineages first. Is the abnormality isolated (one line) or does it involve two/three lines?
  2. If anaemic → classify by MCV (microcytic / normocytic / macrocytic). This single step frames the whole differential.
  3. Check the reticulocyte count — is the marrow responding (high retics = blood loss/haemolysis) or failing (low retics)?
  4. Read the WCC differential, not just the total. A normal total can hide neutrophilia + lymphopenia.
  5. All three lines down = pancytopenia → think marrow (infiltration/failure), hypersplenism, B12/folate, or sepsis. This is never normal.
  6. Request a blood film for any unexplained or flagged result — morphology often gives the diagnosis.
Trend beats a single value. Compare with the patient's baseline. A platelet count of 140 that was 400 last week is more worrying than a stable 140.

HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Film — Abnormalities:
What it is

A peripheral blood film is a stained smear examined under the microscope — the single most useful next step for almost any unexplained FBC abnormality. It reports morphology that automated counters miss.

Requested when: unexplained anaemia, abnormal indices, cytopenia/cytosis, suspected haemolysis or haematological malignancy, or an analyser 'flag'. Always interpret alongside the FBC and clinical picture.
How to describe a film

Comment systematically on the three lineages: red cell size, shape and colour; white cell numbers and maturity; platelet number and morphology; then any extra features (parasites, rouleaux).

White cell & platelet clues
  • Blasts — acute leukaemia. Urgent haematology referral.
  • Left shift (immature neutrophils, toxic granulation) — severe infection/sepsis.
  • Hypersegmented neutrophils — B12/folate deficiency (megaloblastic).
  • Atypical/reactive lymphocytes — EBV, CMV, viral infection.
  • Smear (smudge) cells — CLL.
  • Auer rods — AML.
  • Platelet clumps — cause of spurious (pseudo)thrombocytopenia.

HAEMATOLOGY__Coagulation Screen (PT, APT:
What it is

Screens the clotting cascade. Sample: citrate tube (blue top) — fill exactly to the line (the citrate:plasma ratio matters; under/over-filling gives false results).

PT → extrinsic + common pathway (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen).
  • Basis of the INR, monitors warfarin.
    APTT → intrinsic + common pathway (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII …)
  • Monitors unfractionated heparin.
    TT → thrombin acting on fibrinogen; sensitive to heparin & low/abnormal fibrinogen
Which factor / cause?
PTAPTTSuggests
↑normalWarfarin (early), factor VII deficiency, mild liver disease, vitamin K deficiency (early)
normal↑Heparin, haemophilia A/B (VIII/IX), factor XI/XII, von Willebrand disease, lupus anticoagulant
↑↑DIC, liver failure, vitamin K deficiency (late), warfarin overdose, massive transfusion
normalnormalNormal screen — but does not exclude vWD or platelet-function disorders
Fibrinogen falls in DIC and consumption. TT is prolonged by heparin and by low/dysfunctional fibrinogen.
Correction on mixing (1:1 with normal plasma)
  • Corrects → factor deficiency (the missing factor is replaced).
  • Does NOT correct → an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor VIII inhibitor).
  • ↑PT + ↑APTT + ↓platelets + ↓fibrinogen + ↑D-dimer → DIC: treat the cause, supportive blood products.
  • Prolonged times with active bleeding → urgent haematology / major-haemorrhage pathway.
  • Isolated ↑APTT in a bleeding child/young adult → think haemophilia / vWD.
HAEMATOLOGY__D-Dimer:
What it is

A fibrin degradation product — released when cross-linked fibrin is broken down. It is a marker of active clot turnover, not of any specific site.

Its power is the negative result. A normal D-dimer in a patient with low or intermediate pre-test probability effectively rules out VTE (high sensitivity / high negative predictive value).
How to use it
  1. Assess pre-test probability first (e.g. Wells score).
  2. Low/intermediate probability → D-dimer. Negative → VTE excluded, no imaging.
  3. Positive → proceed to imaging (CTPA / Doppler USS).
  4. High probability → go straight to imaging; do not use D-dimer to rule out.
Age-adjusted cutoff (age >50): age × 10 µg/L (FEU). Improves specificity in older patients without losing sensitivity.
Non-specific — many causes

A raised D-dimer is not diagnostic of VTE:

VTE (PE/DVT)infection / sepsisrecent surgery / traumapregnancymalignancyliver diseaseinflammationincreasing ageDIC

Because so many things raise it, D-dimer is a rule-out, not a rule-in, test. A positive result only prompts further imaging.
HAEMATOLOGY__ESR & CRP:
Two markers of inflammation
  • CRP — an acute-phase protein made by the liver. Rises within 6–8 h, peaks ~48 h, falls fast when the stimulus resolves. Responsive and dynamic.
  • ESR — how fast red cells sediment; an indirect measure driven by fibrinogen and immunoglobulins. Rises and falls slowly (days–weeks).
What raises each
CRPESR
SpeedFast (hours)Slow (days)
Bacterial infection↑↑↑↑
Viral infectionusually normal/mild ↑variable
Raised byInfection, inflammation, tissue necrosis, malignancyAlso anaemia, pregnancy, age, myeloma (paraproteins), female sex
Very high ESR (>100) — think the classic triad: malignancy (esp. myeloma), giant cell arteritis / PMR, and serious infection (TB, endocarditis, abscess).
When they disagree
  • High ESR, normal CRP → classically SLE; also myeloma (paraprotein raises ESR but not CRP).
  • High CRP, normal ESR → very acute event (CRP rises first).
Both are non-specific — never diagnostic alone. Use to support a picture and to trend response to treatment. CRP is generally preferred for tracking acute infection.
HAEMATOLOGY__Iron Studies (serum iron, f:
The panel
  • Ferritin — body iron stores (but an acute-phase reactant).
  • Serum iron — circulating iron (fluctuates, diurnal).
  • TIBC / transferrin — capacity to carry iron (↑ when stores are low).
  • Transferrin saturation = iron / TIBC — the most useful single index of supply.
IDA vs ACD vs overload
FerritinSerum ironTIBCTransferrin sat
Iron deficiency↓↓↑↓
Chronic disease (ACD)normal/↑↓↓normal/↓
Iron overload↑↑↑↓/normal↑↑
TIBC is the discriminator between the two common causes of microcytic anaemia: high in iron deficiency, low in anaemia of chronic disease.
Ferritin pitfalls
Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant — it rises with infection, inflammation, liver disease and malignancy, and can be falsely normal despite true iron deficiency. A low ferritin is specific for deficiency; a normal/high one does not exclude it if CRP is up.
Iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or postmenopausal woman is GI blood loss until proven otherwise — investigate for GI malignancy (coeliac screen + upper/lower GI endoscopy).
HAEMATOLOGY__B12 & Folate:
Why they matter

Both are needed for DNA synthesis; deficiency causes a macrocytic, megaloblastic anaemia (hypersegmented neutrophils on film). B12 deficiency also causes irreversible neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration).

Deficiency causes
B12Folate
Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune, anti-IF antibodies)Poor diet, alcohol
Malabsorption (Crohn's, ileal resection, coeliac)Malabsorption (coeliac)
Vegan diet, metformin, PPIs↑ demand: pregnancy, haemolysis
—Drugs: methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin
Always treat B12 before folate. Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
Pitfalls
  • Serum B12 is an imperfect test — if clinical suspicion is high despite a borderline level, check MMA and homocysteine (raised in true deficiency).
  • Check anti-intrinsic-factor antibodies if pernicious anaemia is suspected (specific but insensitive).
HAEMATOLOGY__Reticulocyte Count:
What it is

Reticulocytes are immature red cells released from the marrow. The count reflects how hard the marrow is working — the key test for classifying anaemia as production vs loss/destruction.

Interpreting in anaemia
ReticulocytesMarrowCauses
HighResponding appropriatelyAcute blood loss, haemolysis, response to iron/B12/folate replacement
Low / inappropriately normalFailing to respondMarrow failure/infiltration, untreated haematinic deficiency, aplasia, CKD, ACD
In anaemia the marrow should pump out reticulocytes. A low/normal count in the face of anaemia is inappropriate and points to a production problem.

HAEMATOLOGY__Direct Antiglobulin Test (C:
What it detects

The direct antiglobulin test detects antibody and/or complement bound to the patient's own red cells — i.e. it identifies immune-mediated haemolysis.

Positive DAT → immune cause. Negative DAT with haemolysis → look for membrane (spherocytosis), enzyme (G6PD), mechanical (MAHA/valve) or PNH causes.
Why the DAT is positive
  • Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia — warm (IgG) or cold (IgM/complement).
  • Haemolytic transfusion reaction.
  • Haemolytic disease of the newborn (materno-fetal incompatibility).
  • Drug-induced immune haemolysis.
Two flavours of AIHA

AntibodyIgGIgM (+ complement)

First-line RxSteroidsKeep warm; treat cause; rituximab

What it is

Separates haemoglobin variants by charge (electrophoresis or HPLC) to diagnose haemoglobinopathies — sickle cell disease and the thalassaemias.

Normal adult: HbA (α₂β₂) ~97%, HbA₂ (α₂δ₂) <3.5%, HbF (α₂γ₂) <1%.

HAEMATOLOGY__LDH:
What it is

Lactate dehydrogenase is an intracellular enzyme released on cell turnover or damage — highly sensitive but very non-specific.

Think of cell turnover/breakdown

haemolysistumour lysislymphoma / leukaemiatissue infarction (MI, PE)liver diseasemuscle injurymegaloblastic anaemia

In haemolysis LDH rises alongside ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin and ↓ haptoglobin. In lymphoma LDH is a prognostic marker and tracks disease bulk/response.
A rapidly rising LDH with ↑K⁺, ↑phosphate, ↑urate after chemotherapy = tumour lysis syndrome.
HAEMATOLOGY__Haematinics:
What it means

'Haematinics' is the umbrella term for the nutrients needed for normal erythropoiesis — iron, vitamin B12 and folate. Checked together in the work-up of anaemia.

Anchor the request to the MCV: microcytic → iron studies; macrocytic → B12 & folate; normocytic → often mixed, check all three.

HAEMATOLOGY__Bone Marrow Aspirate & Trep:
Two complementary samples
  • Aspirate — liquid marrow; assesses cell morphology, differential, iron stores, and provides material for flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular tests.
  • Trephine — a core of bone; assesses cellularity, architecture, fibrosis and infiltration.
Taken from the posterior iliac crest under local anaesthetic. A 'dry tap' (no aspirate) itself suggests fibrosis or a packed marrow.
When it's done

Unexplained cytopenias/pancytopenia, suspected leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma, myelodysplasia or myelofibrosis, staging, and assessing marrow infiltration or response to treatment.

blasts (leukaemia)plasma cells (myeloma)dysplasia (MDS)fibrosis (myelofibrosis)infiltrationiron stores

What it is

HAEMATOLOGY__ADAMTS13 (TTP):
What it is

ADAMTS13 is the enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor multimers. Severe deficiency (<10%, usually autoantibody-mediated) causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

TTP is a haematological emergency. Pentad: MAHA (schistocytes), thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal impairment, fever — but do NOT wait for all five.
Interpretation
  • ADAMTS13 <10% → confirms TTP.
  • Send the sample before plasma exchange, but never delay treatment for the result.
  • The PLASMIC score estimates probability of severe deficiency at the bedside.
Treatment: urgent plasma exchange + steroids (± caplacizumab, rituximab). Platelet transfusion is generally contraindicated unless life-threatening bleeding.
HAEMATOLOGY__Anti-PF4 & 4T Score (HIT):
What it is

Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes cause platelet activation, a falling platelet count and paradoxical thrombosis, typically 5–10 days after starting heparin.

Pre-test probability (0–2 each; max 8)
T2 points
Thrombocytopenia>50% fall & nadir ≥20
TimingDay 5–10 (or ≤1 day if recent heparin)
ThrombosisNew confirmed thrombosis
oTher causeNone evident

0–3 low4–5 intermediate6–8 high

Low score (≤3) has a high negative predictive value — HIT is effectively excluded. Intermediate/high → send anti-PF4 antibodies (confirm with a functional assay, e.g. serotonin release).
If HIT is suspected: STOP all heparin immediately (including flushes/LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (e.g. argatroban, danaparoid, fondaparinux). Do not give platelet transfusions and do not start warfarin until platelets recover (risk of venous limb gangrene).
HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria Films (Thick & Thin:
The gold standard

Microscopy of Giemsa-stained films remains the diagnostic standard. Send three samples over 48–72 h before excluding malaria.

  • Thick film — concentrated; detects parasites and estimates parasitaemia (sensitive).
  • Thin film — species identification and parasite count (% infected red cells).
Speciation matters

Plasmodium falciparum is the dangerous species. Features on film: ring forms, multiply-infected cells, high parasitaemia; gametocytes.

Falciparum with any of: parasitaemia >2%, impaired consciousness, AKI, ARDS, shock, hypoglycaemia, acidosis, DIC → severe malaria: IV artesunate + HDU/ITU.
A single negative film does not exclude malaria — repeat as above. Rapid antigen tests (RDTs) complement but do not replace microscopy/parasite count.
HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Count & Film:
The full blood count (FBC) is the most commonly requested blood test. An automated analyser counts and sizes the three cell lines — red cells (haemoglobin & indices), white cells (count & differential) and platelets — giving a rapid overview of anaemia, infection/inflammation, bleeding risk and marrow function.
1When to order
  • Almost any acute or chronic illness — anaemia symptoms, infection, bleeding / bruising, weight loss.
  • Monitoring — chemotherapy, DMARDs / cytotoxics, pregnancy, chronic disease.
  • Pre-operative assessment and as part of a septic or malignancy screen.
2What it measures
🔴Haemoglobin (Hb)
Concentration of Hb — low = anaemia, high = polycythaemia. Haematocrit (Hct) is the % volume of red cells.
📏Red-cell indices
MCV = average cell size (micro/normo/macrocytic)
  • MCH = Hb per cell (low = hypochromic, e.g. iron deficiency), with MCHC the concentration
  • RDW = variation in size (raised early in deficiency, and in a dimorphic picture)
⚪White cells + differential
Total WCC plus the split: neutrophils (bacterial infection, steroids), lymphocytes (viral, CLL), monocytes, eosinophils (allergy, parasites), basophils.
🟣Platelets
Low (bleeding risk) or high (reactive vs myeloproliferative).
  • An isolated very low count in a non-bleeding patient may be EDTA-induced clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) — confirm on the film / repeat in citrate
  • Always check a film if very abnormal

Hb 130–170 g/L (M)Hb 120–155 g/L (F)WCC 4–11 ×10⁹/LNeutrophils 2.0–7.5Lymphocytes 1.0–4.0Platelets 150–400 ×10⁹/LMCV 80–100 fL

Isolated vs combined → thrombocytopenia ›, pancytopenia › (marrow failure, infiltration, myelodysplasia ›).

Neutropenic sepsis › Leukaemia ›
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Always read the FBC as three lines — red, white, platelet
  • One line down = focused work-up; two or three lines down (bi-/pancytopenia) points to a marrow problem
  • A grossly abnormal count or any flag → look at the film
A blood film is a stained drop of blood examined under the microscope.
  • It is requested when the analyser flags an abnormality, or clinically for unexplained anaemia, cytopenias, suspected haematological malignancy, haemolysis or possible malaria
  • The morphology of the cells points to the diagnosis

🧫Blasts
Large immature cells — acute leukaemia until proven otherwise (≥20% blasts defines it, WHO); urgent referral. Auer rods = AML.

🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Schistocytes + low platelets = microangiopathy (DIC, TTP/HUS)
  • Spherocytes = hereditary spherocytosis or AIHA (DAT sorts them)
  • Howell–Jolly bodies = hyposplenism
  • Auer rods = AML
  • Smear cells = CLL
The MCV (mean cell volume) is the single most useful FBC index for an anaemia — it sorts the causes into three groups. This is the entry point to the work-up detailed in the Anaemia › notes (and the Anaemia & Haematinics investigation tab).
1Classify the anaemia by MCV
🔻Microcytic (MCV <80)
Small cells
Causes → Thalassaemia, Anaemia of chronic disease (often normocytic), Iron deficiency (commonest), Lead poisoning, Sideroblastic — mnemonic TAILS. Thalassaemia ›
➖Normocytic (80–100)
Normal-sized cells
Causes → acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, renal failure, haemolysis, mixed deficiency. Anaemia ›
🔺Macrocytic (MCV >100)
Large cells
Megaloblastic (B12 / folate) vs non-megaloblastic → alcohol / liver, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia ›, reticulocytosis, drugs.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • A raised RDW flags a dimorphic picture — a combined micro + macrocytic deficiency can average out to a normal MCV, so check ferritin, B12 and folate together and look at the film
  • Full pattern-to-diagnosis detail is in the Anaemia & Haematinics tab
Reticulocytes are young red cells released from the marrow, still containing residual RNA. The reticulocyte count measures how hard the marrow is working — the key test for splitting anaemia into production failure vs increased loss / destruction.
1High vs low — and what it means
⬆️High reticulocytes
Marrow responding
Anaemia + high retic → haemolysis or acute blood loss (or the healthy response to treating a deficiency). Confirm haemolysis → haemolysis screen — ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin, ↑unconjugated bilirubin, blood film and DAT (immune vs non-immune). Haemolysis / blood loss ›
⬇️Low / inappropriately normal
Marrow not responding
Anaemia + low retic → production failure — haematinic deficiency, marrow failure / infiltration, CKD (low EPO), myelodysplasia ›. Marrow failure ›
💡 Interpret the count relative to the degree of anaemia — a ‘normal’ reticulocyte count is inappropriately low in someone who is very anaemic (the marrow should be pouring out reticulocytes).
  • The reticulocyte production index corrects for this
  • On the film, a reticulocytosis shows as polychromasia (blue-tinged young red cells)
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Anaemia + high reticulocytes = losing or destroying red cells (bleed / haemolysis); anaemia + low reticulocytes = not making them (deficiency, marrow, renal)
  • Reticulocytes also rise ~5–7 days after starting the correct treatment for a deficiency — a marker of response
Blood films for malaria — light microscopy of Giemsa-stained thick and thin films — remain the gold-standard diagnostic test. Any traveller returning from an endemic area with a fever has malaria until three films prove otherwise.
1Thick vs thin film
🩸Thick film
Sensitive screen. Many layers of lysed red cells concentrate the parasites — best for detecting a low parasitaemia and confirming infection.
🔬Thin film
Species & quantification. A single monolayer preserves cell shape — used to identify the species and calculate the % parasitaemia.
2When & how to test
  • Fever + travel to an endemic area (up to a year later for non-falciparum). Send FBC, film, LFTs, U&Es, glucose.
  • Send three films before excluding malaria — repeat at 12–24 h and again after a further 24 h [BSH]; one negative film does not rule it out (parasitaemia fluctuates).
  • Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) detect parasite antigen and support (but do not replace) microscopy.
3Species & severity
☠️P. falciparum
Most severeRing formshigh parasitaemia
Can deteriorate fast → cerebral malaria, AKI, ARDS, hypoglycaemia, DIC. Parasitaemia >2% and end-organ signs mark severe disease. Malaria ›
🔁P. vivax / ovale
Relapsinghypnozoites
Dormant liver stage → can relapse weeks–months later. Malaria ›
🕰️P. malariae / knowlesi
malariae: chronicknowlesi: SE Asia, can be severe
→ confirm the species on the thin film. Malaria ›

Falciparum malaria is a medical emergency that can deteriorate within hours. Never exclude malaria on a single negative film — repeat to three films (at 12–24 h then a further 24 h) — and quantify the parasitaemia, as it guides severity.

  • Falciparum = most dangerous; vivax/ovale = relapse from liver hypnozoites

HAEMATOLOGY__Anaemia & Haematinics:
Iron studies assess whole-body iron status using four measures: serum iron (iron in transit on transferrin), ferritin (intracellular storage protein — the single best marker of iron stores), TIBC / transferrin (iron-carrying capacity) and transferrin saturation (serum iron ÷ TIBC — the % of transferrin carrying iron).
1When to order
  • Work-up of anaemia — especially microcytic (low MCV).
  • Suspected iron deficiency (fatigue, pica, koilonychia, angular cheilitis) or iron overload (arthralgia, skin bronzing, deranged LFTs, diabetes, cardiomyopathy).
  • Monitoring iron replacement, CKD / dialysis, IBD, or work-up before IV iron.
💡 Take a fasting morning sample and before starting iron — serum iron has a diurnal rhythm and rises after intake, falsely lifting the saturation.
2The four markers
🩸Serum iron
Iron currently bound to transferrin. Fluctuates hour-to-hour and with intake — weak alone.
📦Ferritin
Iron stores. Low = highly specific for deficiency. But an acute-phase reactant — infection, inflammation, malignancy & liver disease raise it and can mask deficiency.
🚚TIBC / transferrin
Carrying capacity. Rises in deficiency (body makes more transferrin); falls in chronic disease / malnutrition.
⚖️Transferrin saturation
Iron ÷ TIBC = availability. Low in deficiency & chronic disease; high in overload.
📷 Image placeholder — blood film (iron deficiency): microcytic, hypochromic red cells with anisopoikilocytosis & pencil cells.
3Normal values (typical UK adult — check local lab)
Ferritin 30–300 µg/L (M)Ferritin 15–200 µg/L (F)Serum iron 10–30 µmol/LTIBC 45–70 µmol/LTransferrin sat 20–45%
Ferritin <30 µg/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency in either sex (BSG); <15 near-diagnostic. Ranges are lab-dependent.
