↑ raised ·  ↓ low ·  ↔ normal
⬇️Iron-deficiency anaemia
Ferritin ↓TIBC ↑Sat ↓
Confirm → find the source. Check coeliac › serology (tTG + total IgA) in all. ♂ & post-menopausal ♀ → bidirectional endoscopy. Pre-menopausal ♀ → treat menstrual loss + iron trial; scope GI if ≥50, GI symptoms, FHx bowel Ca, or refractory. Iron-deficiency anaemia › Colorectal Ca ›
🔥Anaemia of chronic disease
Ferritin ↑/↔TIBC ↓Sat ↓
Confirm → raised CRP + a chronic driver (a.k.a. anaemia of inflammation). Ferritin >100 with low sat favours it. Anaemia › CKD › IBD ›
🟤Haemochromatosis / overload
Ferritin ↑Sat ↑ >45–50%
Confirm → repeat fasting sat+ferritin (>50% ♂ / >45% ♀), then HFE genotype (C282Y/H63D), LFTs, MRI liver. Haemochromatosis ›
🧬Microcytosis, normal iron
Ferritin ↔TIBC ↔Sat ↔MCV ↓
Confirm → Hb electrophoresis (↑HbA2 = β-trait; α-trait is electrophoresis-normal → genetic testing); Mentzer <13. Thalassaemia trait ›
💠Sideroblastic anaemia
Ferritin ↑Sat ↑MCV ↓/dimorphic
Confirm → iron overload with anaemia (unlike haemochromatosis, which causes overload but no anaemia). Blood film (dimorphic ± basophilic stippling) and marrow → ring sideroblasts. Seek a cause — alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia, or congenital. Myelodysplasia ›
🔬 When ferritin is confounded (inflammation / CKD / HF, and IDA vs ACD unclear): soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) is raised in true iron deficiency and unaffected by inflammation; reticulocyte-Hb content also helps. Combined IDA + ACD is common (RA, IBD, CKD) — a normal ferritin can still hide deficiency.
🚩
Red flags & escalation. All men and post-menopausal women with unexplained IDA need bidirectional endoscopy (OGD + colonoscopy) [BSG]. The suspected-cancer (“2-week-wait”) pathway triggers at age ≥60, or younger with a positive FIT or alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, rectal bleeding, abdominal / rectal mass) [NICE]. A “normal” ferritin does not exclude deficiency when CRP is raised — use a higher cut-off (e.g. <100 µg/L in inflammation, CKD or heart failure).
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Learn the 4-way pattern: IDA (↓ferritin, ↑TIBC, ↓sat) · ACD (↑/n ferritin, ↓TIBC, ↓sat) · thalassaemia trait (normal iron, low MCV, high RBC, Mentzer <13) · haemochromatosis (↑ferritin, ↑sat)
  • Ferritin is the classic acute-phase-reactant trap; never start iron before sampling
Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) and folate are cofactors for DNA synthesis, so deficiency of either causes a megaloblastic (macrocytic) anaemia.
  • They are measured together to work up a raised MCV — and B12 additionally for neurological disease
  • Serum folate reflects recent intake; red-cell folate reflects body stores
1When to order
  • Work-up of macrocytic anaemia (high MCV).
  • Unexplained neuropathy, sensory ataxia, cognitive decline or glossitis (B12).
  • Malabsorption / risk: coeliac, Crohn’s (terminal ileum), post-gastrectomy or bariatric surgery, strict vegan diet, drugs (metformin, PPI → B12; methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin, alcohol, pregnancy, haemolysis → folate).
💡 Check B12 before giving folate — folate alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord.
2The markers
🧪Serum B12 (total)
Total cobalamin. Imperfect assay — a normal level does not exclude deficiency (falsely low in pregnancy / OCP; raised in liver / myeloproliferative disease / infection). [NICE] indeterminate zone ~180–350 ng/L, no hard cutoff.
🎯Active B12 (holoTC)
Holotranscobalamin — the metabolically available fraction; more specific. NICE accepts it first- or second-line, and prefers it first-line in pregnancy.
🥬Serum folate
The standard folate test. Reflects recent intake — labile. <7 nmol/L supports deficiency (grey zone ~7–10).
📦Red-cell folate
Reflects stores over ~120 days but is no longer routinely recommended (unreliable; also falsely low in B12 deficiency — methylfolate trap).
📷 Image placeholder — blood film (megaloblastic): oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils (≥6 lobes).
3Normal values (lab-dependent)
Serum B12 indeterminate ~180–350 ng/LActive B12 (holoTC) ~>35 pmol/LSerum folate <7 nmol/L = low
No single B12 cutoff (NICE): interpret against the clinical picture — if symptomatic with an indeterminate level, use MMA / active B12 and treat on clinical grounds. Ranges lab-dependent.
4Read the pattern → diagnosis
↑ raised ·  ↓ low ·  ↔ normal
⬇️Low B12 (± neuro)
B12 ↓MMA ↑Homocysteine ↑
Confirm cause → anti-intrinsic-factor Ab for autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) — ~50% sensitive, so a negative does not exclude it; coeliac serology; consider terminal-ileal disease, diet, metformin/PPI, nitrous oxide. Anaemia › Coeliac › Cord (SACD) ›
⬇️Low folate
Folate ↓Homocysteine ↑MMA ↔
Confirm → red-cell folate for stores. Causes: poor intake / alcohol, malabsorption (coeliac), ↑ demand (pregnancy, haemolysis), drugs (methotrexate, trimethoprim, phenytoin). Anaemia › Coeliac ›
🍺Macrocytosis, normal B12/folate
B12 ↔Folate ↔MCV ↑
Non-megaloblastic → alcohol / liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, reticulocytosis (haemolysis / bleeding), drugs. Alcohol / Liver › Hypothyroid › Myelodysplasia ›
🔬 Indeterminate B12 (~180–350 ng/L) or suggestive symptoms?
  • Use MMA (or active B12) — MMA & homocysteine rise before serum B12 falls
  • Both ↑ in B12 deficiency; only homocysteine ↑ in folate deficiency (MMA normal)
  • Caveats: MMA ↑ in renal impairment; homocysteine ↑ in renal failure, hypothyroidism, B6 deficiency
  • No test is gold-standard — treat symptomatic patients on clinical grounds
  • Nitrous-oxide misuse gives a functional deficiency with a normal serum B12 (NICE: test MMA regardless of the level)
🚩
Neurology can occur with a normal Hb and normal MCV. B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration (dorsal columns + corticospinal + peripheral nerves → sensory ataxia, ↓ vibration / proprioception, absent ankle jerks with up-going plantars) — damage may be irreversible, so treat promptly. Never give folate alone when B12 deficiency is possible.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Megaloblastic film = oval macrocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils
  • Autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) = autoimmune gastric atrophy → anti-IF (specific) / anti-parietal-cell (sensitive); linked to other autoimmune disease and ↑ gastric-cancer risk (NICE: endoscopic surveillance)
  • MMA↑ + homocysteine↑ = B12; homocysteine↑ alone = folate
Haematinics are the nutrients needed to build blood — iron, vitamin B12 and folate.
  • This tab is the one-look approach: how to pull the individual tests together and let the MCV steer the work-up of an anaemia
  • The detail for each test lives in its own tab —
1Start with the MCV
🔻Microcytic (MCV <80)
Iron studies first. ↓ferritin = iron deficiency; normal/↑ferritin with ↓TIBC = anaemia of chronic disease; normal iron studies → think thalassaemia trait.
➖Normocytic (80–100)
Mixed / early deficiency, anaemia of chronic disease, renal, haemolysis or acute bleeding. A combined micro + macrocytic deficiency can sit here with a normal MCV.
🔺Macrocytic (MCV >100)
B12 and folate. ↓ = megaloblastic; if both normal it is non-megaloblastic (alcohol/liver, hypothyroid, myelodysplasia, reticulocytosis).
💡 Always send an FBC + blood film and a reticulocyte count too — the film shows the cell shapes and the reticulocytes separate production failure (low) from haemolysis / bleeding (high). Film clues: pencil cells (iron deficiency); oval macrocytes + hypersegmented neutrophils (megaloblastic); target cells (thalassaemia, liver disease, post-splenectomy); and blasts — refer urgently to haematology (?acute leukaemia).
2When to send the panel
  • Any new anaemia — request the haematinics guided by the MCV (iron studies for micro; B12/folate for macro).
  • Symptoms despite a normal Hb (fatigue, restless legs, glossitis, neuropathy) — deficiency can precede anaemia.
  • Combined-deficiency risk — coeliac, IBD, bariatric surgery, pregnancy, the elderly or a restricted diet: send ferritin, B12 and folate together.
3Combined pattern → which tab
🔻Microcytic anaemia
MCV ↓Ferritin ↓ or ↔
Go to → iron studies (IDA vs ACD); if iron is normal, screen for thalassaemia.
🔺Macrocytic anaemia
MCV ↑B12 / folate ↓ or ↔
Go to → B12 & folate (megaloblastic vs non-megaloblastic).
🔀Dimorphic / combined
MCV ↔ (normal)RDW ↑Film two populations
Beware → mixed iron + B12/folate deficiency (e.g. coeliac) can normalise the MCV — check ferritin AND B12/folate and look at the film / RDW.
💥High reticulocytes (haemolysis / bleeding)
MCV ↔/↑Retics ↑
Confirm → haemolysis screen — blood film, LDH ↑, haptoglobin ↓, unconjugated bilirubin ↑, then DAT (Coombs) to split immune from non-immune; exclude overt bleeding. Anaemia ›
🚩
A normal MCV does not exclude deficiency. A combined microcytic + macrocytic picture can average out to a normal MCV with a raised RDW and a dimorphic film — so in the right context check ferritin, B12 and folate even when the MCV looks normal. And always replace B12 before folate.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • MCV drives the work-up: microcytic → iron studies (then Hb electrophoresis if iron is normal); macrocytic → B12 & folate
  • Interpret ferritin with CRP (acute-phase reactant), check B12 before folate, and use the reticulocyte count to separate underproduction from haemolysis / bleeding
Haemoglobin electrophoresis — now usually performed by HPLC or capillary electrophoresis — separates the different haemoglobins by their charge to identify and quantify normal and abnormal (variant) haemoglobins. It is the key test for the haemoglobinopathies: the thalassaemias (a quantity problem — too little globin chain) and the structural variants such as HbS (sickle), HbC and HbE.
1When to order
  • Microcytic anaemia with normal iron studies — especially a raised RBC count and a disproportionately low MCV (Mentzer index <13). Send with an FBC and blood film.
  • Newborn screening — the universal bloodspot screen offered to all babies (NHS Sickle Cell & Thalassaemia programme).
  • Antenatal screening — offered to all women; in low-prevalence areas the Family Origin Questionnaire (FOQ) triages who needs the lab test based on ancestry (African, Caribbean, Mediterranean, Middle-Eastern, South / South-East Asian) or a positive family history.
  • Pre-operative sickle screen in at-risk patients before a general anaesthetic (the acute solubility test → confirm with electrophoresis); unexplained haemolytic anaemia; or to confirm a positive sickle solubility test.
💡 Check iron studies alongside — iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and can mask β-thalassaemia trait. Re-test once iron-replete if the suspicion is high.
2The haemoglobins it measures
🅰️HbA (α₂β₂)
The main adult haemoglobin (~96–98%). Absent in sickle-cell anaemia and β-thalassaemia major.
2️⃣HbA₂ (α₂δ₂)
Normally 2–3.5%. ↑ >3.5% is the hallmark of β-thalassaemia trait (but falsely lowered by iron deficiency).
🍼HbF (α₂γ₂)
Fetal Hb — dominant at birth, normally <1% in adults. Markedly ↑ in β-thalassaemia major / intermedia and HPFH.
🧬Variant bands
Abnormal peaks — HbS (sickle), HbC, HbE, HbD etc. — identified and quantified by their position.
📷 Image placeholder — HPLC / electrophoresis traces: normal (HbA + small HbA₂) vs β-thal trait (↑HbA₂) vs sickle-cell anaemia (HbS peak, no HbA) vs HbSC.
3Normal adult pattern (lab-dependent)
HbA ~96–98%HbA₂ 2–3.5%HbF <1%
Newborns are HbF-predominant, so adult fractions settle by ~6–12 months — the newborn screen reports the qualitative pattern rather than adult percentages.
4Read the pattern → diagnosis
🩸Sickle-cell anaemia (HbSS)
HbS predominantHbA absentHbF ↑
Confirm → variant identified on HPLC + a positive sickle solubility test; family studies. HbSC disease shows HbS + HbC and no HbA. Sickle Cell Disease ›
🧬Sickle-cell trait (HbAS)
HbA predominantHbS ~30–40%HbA > HbS
Carrier → usually no anaemia; relevant for anaesthesia, altitude and antenatal / partner screening. Sickle cell trait ›
⬆️β-thalassaemia trait
HbA₂ ↑ >3.5%HbF ↔/↑MCV ↓RBC ↑
Confirm → the ↑HbA₂ is diagnostic once iron deficiency is excluded (it falsely lowers HbA₂); Mentzer <13. Thalassaemia ›
🍼β-thalassaemia major / intermedia
HbF ↑↑HbA ↓/absentHbA₂ ↔/↑
Confirm → severe microcytic anaemia from infancy; globin-gene genetic testing defines the genotype. Thalassaemia ›
🔎α-thalassaemia trait
Electrophoresis ↔ normalMCV ↓HbA₂ ↔
Not seen on electrophoresis → microcytosis with normal iron studies and normal HbA₂ — needs DNA / genetic analysis to confirm. Note the severe α-thals do show on HPLC: 3-gene deletion = HbH disease (HbH β₄ band + haemolytic anaemia); 4-gene = Hb Bart’s (γ₄) → hydrops fetalis (antenatal significance). Thalassaemia ›
🚩
Interpretation traps. Iron deficiency lowers HbA₂ and can hide β-thal trait — correct iron and repeat. A recent transfusion introduces donor HbA, so wait ~3 months or interpret with caution. The sickle solubility test confirms HbS is present but cannot distinguish trait from disease — always characterise with electrophoresis / HPLC.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • ↑HbA₂ = β-thalassaemia trait.
  • α-thalassaemia trait is electrophoresis-normal → needs genetic testing
  • HbSS = no HbA + high HbS/HbF; HbAS trait = HbA > HbS
  • Microcytosis + raised RBC + Mentzer <13 with normal iron points to a thalassaemia rather than iron deficiency
HAEMATOLOGY__Haemolysis:
Haemolysis is the premature destruction of red cells. The haemolysis screen is a panel that confirms haemolysis is happening, shows how the marrow is responding, and separates intravascular from extravascular destruction — before the cause is pinned down with the DAT and blood film.
1When to suspect / order
  • Anaemia with jaundice (unconjugated), dark urine, or splenomegaly.
  • A normocytic (or macrocytic) anaemia with a high reticulocyte count and no bleeding source.
  • Pigment gallstones, leg ulcers, or a known haemolytic disorder (sickle, thalassaemia, hereditary spherocytosis, G6PD).
2The markers
⬆️Reticulocytes ↑
The marrow’s response — young red cells pour out to replace those destroyed (polychromasia on the film). Caveat: may be low in a parvovirus-B19 aplastic crisis on a background of chronic haemolysis (HS, sickle).
🟡Unconjugated bilirubin ↑
Haem breakdown → pre-hepatic jaundice; drives pigment gallstones. It is not water-soluble — no bilirubinuria (‘acholuric jaundice’); urine darkens from urobilinogen (and free Hb in intravascular haemolysis).
🧪LDH ↑
Released from lysed red cells — a sensitive (but non-specific) marker of cell turnover.
🧽Haptoglobin ↓
Mops up free haemoglobin, so it falls (or is absent) in haemolysis — especially intravascular. Caveat: it is an acute-phase protein, so a ‘normal’ level with coexisting inflammation does not exclude haemolysis.
🔬Blood film
The key to the cause — spherocytes, schistocytes, sickle cells, bite & blister cells (G6PD), Heinz bodies (on a supravital stain), malaria parasites.
3Intravascular vs extravascular
💥Intravascular
Lysis within vessels.
Haptoglobin ↓↓/absentFree Hb / haemoglobinuriaHaemosiderinuria (chronic)
Chronic haemoglobinuria / haemosiderinuria with no ABO, G6PD or mechanical cause → suspect PNH → flow cytometry (CD55/CD59). See the DAT tab.
🫀Extravascular
Cleared by the spleen/liver.
SplenomegalyBilirubin ↑Haptoglobin ↓ (less marked)
💡 Examples: intravascular — ABO transfusion reaction, G6PD crisis, MAHA (DIC/TTP/HUS), PNH, malaria; extravascular — warm AIHA, cold AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis, haemoglobinopathies.
4Confirmed haemolysis → find the cause
➕DAT positive
Antibody on red cells
Immune → autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, transfusion reaction, haemolytic disease of the newborn (see the DAT tab). Haemolytic anaemia ›
➖DAT negative + film clue
SpherocytesSchistocytesBite cells
Non-immune → hereditary spherocytosis, MAHA (DIC ›/TTP/HUS ›), G6PD, sickle ›, thalassaemia ›, mechanical valve, PNH.
🚩
Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) until proven otherwise — TTP, HUS or DIC. With fever, AKI or new neurology, treat as TTP: a haematological emergency needing urgent haematology input and plasma exchange. Do not transfuse platelets in TTP unless there is life-threatening bleeding — it can worsen the thrombotic process.
📷 Image placeholder — haemolysis: jaundiced sclera and a film showing polychromasia with spherocytes (extravascular) or schistocytes (intravascular / MAHA).
🎓 Exam pearl. The haemolysis screen = ↑ reticulocytes, ↑ unconjugated bilirubin, ↑ LDH, ↓ haptoglobin, with a helpful film. Then the DAT splits immune from non-immune. Haemoglobinuria = intravascular.
The direct antiglobulin test (DAT / direct Coombs) detects antibody or complement bound to the surface of the patient’s own red cells. It is the single most important test for identifying immune haemolysis. (The indirect antiglobulin test detects antibodies free in the serum — used for crossmatching and antenatal antibody screening.)
1A positive DAT — immune haemolysis
🔥Warm AIHA (IgG)
IgG ± C3ExtravascularSpherocytes
Reacts at 37°C → idiopathic, or secondary to lymphoma › / CLL ›, SLE, drugs (e.g. methyldopa). Next: screen for a secondary cause — film + immunophenotyping ± CT (CLL/lymphoma), ANA/dsDNA (SLE) and a drug history. Warm AIHA ›
❄️Cold AIHA (IgM / C3)
C3 only on DATCold agglutininsExtravascular (C3, hepatic) ± intravascularAcrocyanosis
Reacts in the cold → Mycoplasma, EBV, or lymphoma ›.
Lab pearl: cold agglutinins clump red cells → a spuriously high MCV / low RBC and visible clumping on the film; warm the sample to 37°C and repeat.
Next: Mycoplasma / EBV serology if post-infective; if chronic or relapsing, screen for a lymphoproliferative disorder (serum electrophoresis / paraprotein ± marrow).
🩸Alloimmune
Transfusion reactionHDN
→ haemolytic transfusion reaction, or haemolytic disease of the newborn (anti-D / ABO).
2A negative DAT with haemolysis — non-immune
🧬Membrane / enzyme
Hereditary spherocytosis (osmotic fragility / EMA binding), G6PD deficiency (bite & blister cells, Heinz bodies). Pitfall: a G6PD level taken during an acute crisis can be falsely normal (the deficient old cells are already lysed) — repeat in steady state (~2–3 months).
🧾Haemoglobinopathy
Sickle-cell disease, thalassaemia — confirm on electrophoresis.
🔪Mechanical / MAHA
Prosthetic valve, DIC, TTP/HUS — schistocytes on the film.
🌙PNH
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — intravascular, thrombosis; confirm by flow cytometry (loss of GPI-anchored CD55/CD59; FLAER).
Sickle Cell Disease › Thalassaemia › DIC ›
⚠️ Interpret the DAT with the haemolysis screen.
  • A positive DAT can occur without haemolysis (incidentally in inpatients, after IVIG or a recent transfusion, or with hypergammaglobulinaemia), and ~5–10% of genuine AIHA is DAT-negative — a negative DAT does not fully exclude immune haemolysis (low-level or low-affinity IgG, or IgA)
  • If suspicion is high, ask the lab to extend the panel
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • DAT positive = immune (warm IgG vs cold IgM/C3); DAT negative = non-immune (membrane, enzyme, haemoglobinopathy, mechanical, PNH)
  • Direct Coombs = antibody on the cell (haemolysis work-up); indirect Coombs = antibody in serum (crossmatch / antenatal screen)
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is an enzyme present in almost all cells; it is released when cells are destroyed or turning over rapidly. It is sensitive but non-specific — always interpret it with the clinical picture and the rest of the bloods.
1Why LDH rises
🩸Haemolysis
Released from lysed red cells — very high LDH with a low haptoglobin and high reticulocytes supports haemolysis.
🧫High cell turnover / malignancy
High-grade lymphoma & leukaemia (a marker of tumour burden and prognosis) and tumour lysis syndrome.
💔Tissue infarction / injury
Ischaemia/infarction (e.g. PE, bowel ischaemia), rhabdomyolysis, liver disease.
🧪Ineffective erythropoiesis
Megaloblastic anaemia (B12/folate) — cells destroyed in the marrow raise LDH and bilirubin.
🔎Other high-yield associations
Pneumocystis (PJP) pneumonia in HIV (a classic clue), germ-cell tumours (a serum tumour marker alongside AFP / βhCG), and pleural fluid — a raised fluid LDH marks an exudate (Light’s criteria).
Lymphoma › Tumour lysis syndrome ›
⚠️ Spurious LDH.
  • A haemolysed sample (difficult venepuncture or delayed processing) leaks LDH — and K⁺ — from red cells in the tube, mimicking true haemolysis
  • If the LDH or K⁺ is unexpectedly high, check the sample was clean and repeat before acting
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • In haemolysis, LDH ↑ and haptoglobin ↓ move together
  • Beyond haemolysis, LDH is a prognostic marker in lymphoma and part of the tumour lysis syndrome picture (↑LDH, ↑urate, ↑K⁺, ↑phosphate, ↓Ca²⁺)
  • Because it is non-specific, a raised LDH is a clue, not a diagnosis
ADAMTS13 is the enzyme that cleaves von Willebrand factor (vWF) into normal-sized multimers. A severe deficiency (<10%) — usually from an autoantibody (immune TTP), occasionally inherited (congenital TTP) — leaves ultra-large vWF multimers that trap platelets into microthrombi, causing thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
1Recognise TTP
🩸The core two
MAHA (schistocytes)Thrombocytopenia
Unexplained MAHA + low platelets → is TTP until proven otherwise — a haematological emergency. Thrombocytopenia ›
🧠The pentad (classic, often incomplete)
+ AKI+ Neuro (confusion, seizures)+ Fever
Do not wait for the full pentad → it is present in a minority; the first two are enough to act.
2Testing
  • Send ADAMTS13 activity (and an inhibitor assay) before starting plasma exchange — but do not wait for the result to treat.
  • <10% activity confirms TTP; an inhibitor indicates immune TTP (iTTP) — the hereditary form is congenital TTP (cTTP).
  • The PLASMIC score estimates the probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency at the bedside.
💡 Normal coagulation (PT/APTT/fibrinogen) in TTP/HUS helps separate them from DIC, where clotting times are deranged and fibrinogen falls.
3TTP vs HUS vs DIC
🧠TTP
ADAMTS13 <10%Neuro prominentNormal clotting
→ ultra-large vWF; platelet microthrombi. TTP ›
💧HUS
AKI prominentOften E. coli O157Normal ADAMTS13
→ Shiga-toxin (typical, children) or complement (atypical).
Pitfalls: in STEC-HUS avoid antibiotics (may increase toxin release) and avoid platelet transfusion; atypical (complement) HUS → eculizumab.
🧬DIC
Deranged PT/APTTFibrinogen ↓D-dimer ↑
→ consumptive coagulopathy driven by sepsis, malignancy, obstetric causes. DIC ›
🚩
TTP is a medical emergency. Untreated it carries a very high mortality. Any MAHA (schistocytes) with thrombocytopenia and no other cause should prompt urgent haematology referral and ADAMTS13 testing. Treat immune TTP with urgent plasma exchange + corticosteroids, plus caplacizumab (anti-vWF) and rituximab (BSH). Never give platelet transfusions for the low count unless there is life-threatening bleeding (they can fuel the microthrombi).
🎓 Exam pearl. ADAMTS13 <10% = TTP. MAHA + thrombocytopenia + normal clotting = TTP/HUS (neuro → TTP, AKI → HUS); MAHA + thrombocytopenia + deranged clotting / low fibrinogen = DIC.
HAEMATOLOGY__Coagulation & Thrombosis:
The coagulation screen — PT, APTT, TT and fibrinogen — tests the clotting cascade to work up bleeding or abnormal bruising, an abnormal pre-operative check, or a sick patient with suspected DIC. Sample: a citrate (blue-top) tube filled exactly to the line — the citrate:plasma ratio matters, so under- or over-filling gives false results.
1The four tests
🩸PT / INR
Extrinsic + common pathway (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen).
  • The basis of the INR; monitors warfarin
  • Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so the PT rises first in warfarin, vitamin K deficiency and liver disease
⏱️APTT
Intrinsic + common pathway (factors VIII, IX, XI, XII). Monitors unfractionated heparin — LMWH is not reflected in the APTT (use an anti-Xa level if monitoring is needed).
🧵TT (thrombin time)
Thrombin acting on fibrinogen. Prolonged by heparin and by a low or dysfunctional fibrinogen.
🧪Fibrinogen
The final clot substrate. Falls in DIC / consumption; an acute-phase reactant, so a ‘normal’ level with inflammation can be misleading.
Typical adult ranges (check local lab): PT ~11–14 s · APTT ~24–38 s · TT ~14–19 s · fibrinogen ~1.5–4 g/L. The INR standardises the PT for warfarin monitoring.
2Read the pattern (PT vs APTT)
↑ PT · normal APTT→Warfarin (early), factor VII deficiency, early liver disease, early vitamin K deficiency.
normal PT · ↑ APTT→Heparin, haemophilia A/B › (VIII/IX), XI/XII, von Willebrand disease, lupus anticoagulant.
↑ PT · ↑ APTT→DIC ›, liver failure, late vitamin K deficiency, warfarin overdose, massive transfusion.
normal · normal→Normal screen — but does not exclude von Willebrand disease or a platelet-function disorder.
3Mixing study (1:1 with normal plasma)
✅Corrects
Factor deficiency — the missing factor is replaced by the normal plasma, so the time normalises. Next: factor assays — VIII/IX levels (haemophilia A/B) and vWF studies (vWF antigen, activity/ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII) for von Willebrand disease.
⛔Does NOT correct
An inhibitor is present — e.g. lupus anticoagulant or a factor VIII inhibitor — which also blocks the added factor. Next: an antiphospholipid screen (lupus anticoagulant) or refer to haematology for a factor inhibitor (acquired haemophilia).
4Sample & drug pitfalls
  • Wrong fill / contaminated sample — an under- or over-filled citrate tube, or blood drawn from a heparinised line, gives spuriously prolonged times; repeat from a clean stick.
  • DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) variably prolong the PT/APTT and are not reliably monitored by the screen — use a drug-specific anti-Xa level or dilute thrombin time.
  • Lupus anticoagulant paradox — prolongs the APTT in the tube but causes thrombosis, not bleeding, in the patient. Next: antiphospholipid work-up — lupus anticoagulant (dRVVT), anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, repeated ≥12 weeks apart; persistent positivity + a clinical event = antiphospholipid syndrome (anticoagulate).
  • Unprovoked / recurrent VTE — thrombophilia screen?
    • Test only if it will change management, and never during the acute clot or while on anticoagulant (heparin, warfarin and DOACs distort the assays) — defer to a steady state per haematology
    • Screen: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin + antiphospholipid antibodies
🚩
↑ PT + ↑ APTT + ↓ platelets + ↓ fibrinogen + ↑ D-dimer = DIC › — treat the underlying cause with supportive blood products. Prolonged times with active bleeding → activate the major-haemorrhage pathway and call haematology. An isolated ↑ APTT in a bleeding child or young adult → think haemophilia or vWD.
📷 Image placeholder — the coagulation cascade: the intrinsic (APTT) and extrinsic (PT) pathways converging on the common pathway (X → II → fibrin), annotated with which test covers which factors.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • PT = extrinsic (warfarin / INR); APTT = intrinsic (heparin)
  • A mixing study splits the two: corrects = factor deficiency, fails to correct = inhibitor
  • Remember the lupus anticoagulant paradox — a prolonged APTT that signals thrombosis, not bleeding
A D-dimer is a fibrin degradation product — released when cross-linked fibrin is broken down.
  • It marks active clot turnover, not any specific site
  • Its power is the negative result: with a low or intermediate pre-test probability, a normal D-dimer effectively rules out VTE (high sensitivity / negative predictive value)
  • It is a rule-out, not a rule-in, test
1Use it with a pre-test probability
Low / intermediate probabilitye.g. Wells score
Negative → VTE excluded, no imagingPositive → image (CTPA / Doppler USS ›)
High probabilitydo not use D-dimer to rule out
Go straight to imaging — a normal D-dimer cannot exclude VTE here
2Cutoffs
  • Age-adjusted cutoff (age >50): use age × 10 µg/L (FEU) instead of the fixed threshold — improves specificity in older patients without losing sensitivity.
  • Know your assay units — results are reported as fibrinogen-equivalent units (FEU) or D-dimer units (DDU), and the cutoffs differ; check the local reference range.
  • Pregnancy — the D-dimer is physiologically raised, so its rule-out value is limited; follow pregnancy-specific VTE pathways and image (Doppler / CTPA or V/Q) rather than relying on it.
3Why it rises (non-specific)
VTE (PE/DVT)Infection / sepsisSurgery / traumaPregnancyMalignancyLiver diseaseInflammationIncreasing ageDIC ›
Because so many things raise it, a positive result is not diagnostic of VTE — it only prompts imaging.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • D-dimer rules out, never rules in
  • A normal value with a low/intermediate pre-test probability excludes VTE and spares imaging; a positive value only mandates imaging; and in a high-probability patient it should not be sent at all — image directly
  • Don’t order a D-dimer you are not prepared to act on
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — antibodies against platelet factor 4 (PF4)–heparin complexes activate platelets, causing a falling platelet count and paradoxical thrombosis (not bleeding), typically 5–10 days after starting heparin. Score the pre-test probability with the 4Ts before testing.
1The 4T score
Each ‘T’ scores 0, 1 or 2 (max 8). The 2-point criteria:
📉Thrombocytopenia
>50% fall AND nadir ≥20 ×10⁹/L.
🕔Timing
Onset day 5–10 (or ≤1 day if heparin in the last 30 days).
🧱Thrombosis
New confirmed thrombosis (or skin necrosis / post-heparin reaction).
❓oTher cause
None evident for the thrombocytopenia.
0–3 low4–5 intermediate6–8 high
2Testing
Low score (≤3)→High negative predictive value — HIT is effectively excluded; do not test.
Intermediate / high (≥4)→Send anti-PF4 antibodies (immunoassay — sensitive, non-specific), then confirm with a functional assay (serotonin release / HIPA).
🚩
If HIT is suspected, act before the assay returns. STOP all heparin immediately (including flushes and LMWH) and start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, danaparoid or fondaparinux; a DOAC is an option once the patient is clinically stable). Do not transfuse platelets, and do not start warfarin until the platelet count recovers — early warfarin risks venous limb gangrene / skin necrosis. HIT is a prothrombotic emergency — screen for thrombocytopenia › and thrombosis.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • HIT = thrombocytopenia + thrombosis (not bleeding), 5–10 days into heparin
  • A low 4T score excludes it; intermediate/high → anti-PF4 then a functional assay
  • Management: stop heparin, start a non-heparin anticoagulant, avoid platelets and early warfarin
HAEMATOLOGY__Inflammation & Marrow:
ESR and CRP are two non-specific markers of inflammation. Use them to support a clinical picture and to trend the response to treatment — never as a diagnosis on their own.
1The two markers
⚡CRP
An acute-phase protein made by the liver. Rises within 6–8 h, peaks ~48 h, and falls fast when the stimulus resolves — responsive and dynamic, so best for tracking acute infection.
🐢ESR
How fast red cells sediment — an indirect measure driven by fibrinogen and immunoglobulins. Rises and falls slowly (days–weeks).
Reference values (check local lab): CRP normal <5 mg/L; the ESR upper limit rises with age — roughly age ÷ 2 (men) or (age + 10) ÷ 2 (women). Procalcitonin is a more bacteria-specific marker used in some antibiotic-stewardship protocols.
2What raises each
Speed of change→CRP fast (hours) · ESR slow (days–weeks)
Bacterial infection→CRP ↑↑↑ · ESR ↑
Viral infection→CRP usually normal/mild · ESR variable
CRP is raised by infection, inflammation, tissue necrosis and malignancy. ESR is also raised by anaemia, pregnancy, older age, myeloma (paraproteins) and female sex.
3Very high ESR (>100)
🧬Malignancy
Especially myeloma (paraproteins). Next: serum & urine protein electrophoresis (paraprotein / Bence Jones protein). Myeloma ›
👁️GCA / PMR
Giant cell arteritis or polymyalgia rheumatica. GCA / PMR ›
🦠Serious infection
TB, infective endocarditis, deep abscess.
The classic >100 triad — malignancy, GCA/PMR, serious infection.
4When they disagree
High ESR · normal CRP→Classically SLE; also myeloma (paraprotein raises ESR but not CRP).
High CRP · normal ESR→A very acute event — CRP rises first, before the ESR catches up.
🚩
In suspected giant cell arteritis (temporal headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms), a raised ESR/CRP supports the diagnosis — but do not delay high-dose steroids for the result or temporal-artery biopsy: untreated GCA threatens sight. GCA ›
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • CRP = fast, liver acute-phase, best for tracking acute infection; ESR = slow, driven by fibrinogen/immunoglobulins
  • High ESR + normal CRP → SLE or myeloma
  • ESR >100 → malignancy, GCA/PMR, or serious infection
  • Both are non-specific — support, don’t diagnose
A bone marrow examination takes two complementary samples — a liquid aspirate and a solid trephine core — usually from the posterior iliac crest under local anaesthetic. It is the key test for diagnosing and staging primary marrow disease.
1Two complementary samples
💧Aspirate
Liquid marrow. Assesses cell morphology, the differential and iron stores, and provides material for flow cytometry, cytogenetics and molecular tests.
🦴Trephine
A core of bone. Assesses cellularity, architecture, fibrosis and infiltration — the things a liquid aspirate cannot show.
A ‘dry tap’ (no aspirate obtained) is itself a clue — it suggests fibrosis or a packed marrow.
2When it’s done
  • Unexplained cytopenias / pancytopenia ›.
  • Suspected leukaemia, lymphoma, myeloma, myelodysplasia or myelofibrosis.
  • Staging, assessing marrow infiltration, or the response to treatment.
3What it shows → diagnosis
Blasts→Leukaemia › (≥20% blasts, WHO)
Plasma cells→Myeloma ›
Dysplasia→Myelodysplasia ›
Fibrosis / dry tap→Myelofibrosis ›
Infiltration→Lymphoma or metastatic carcinoma
Iron stores / ring sideroblasts→Iron deficiency (absent stores) or sideroblastic anaemia (ring sideroblasts on a Perls' / Prussian blue stain)
📷 Image placeholder — bone marrow: an aspirate smear (blasts, plasma cells, ring sideroblasts on Perls’ stain) alongside a trephine core (normal cellularity vs a fibrotic / infiltrated marrow).
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Aspirate = morphology, flow, cytogenetics & molecular; trephine = cellularity, architecture, fibrosis & infiltration
  • A dry tap → think fibrosis or a packed marrow
  • Blasts = leukaemia, plasma cells = myeloma, dysplasia = MDS, fibrosis = myelofibrosis
Flow cytometry (immunophenotyping) identifies cells by their surface CD markers. It is used to classify and diagnose leukaemias and lymphomas, confirm PNH, and detect minimal residual disease (MRD) on treatment.
1High-yield lineage markers
CD19, CD20→B cells (CD20 = target of rituximab)
CD3→T cells
CD13, CD33→Myeloid
CD34, TdT→Immature blasts / precursors
CD5 + CD23→CLL
CD10 (CALLA)→Common ALL, follicular lymphoma
Loss of CD55 / CD59 (FLAER)→PNH (GPI-anchored proteins absent)
2Worked example
Circulating blasts — flow panel
TdT +CD19 +CD10 +CD3 −CD13/33 −
Immature (TdT⁺) B-lineage (CD19⁺/CD10⁺) blasts → B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia ›
3What it is used for
  • Diagnose & classify acute leukaemias (lineage of the blasts) and lymphoproliferative disorders › (e.g. CLL).
  • Confirm PNH — loss of GPI-anchored CD55/CD59 on red cells and granulocytes (FLAER assay).
  • Minimal residual disease (MRD) — highly sensitive tracking of response to treatment.
🎓 Exam pearl. CD19/20 = B, CD3 = T, CD13/33 = myeloid, CD34/TdT = blasts, CD5+CD23 = CLL, CD10 = common ALL / follicular. PNH → loss of CD55/CD59. A classic vignette: TdT⁺ CD19⁺ CD10⁺ blasts = B-ALL.
HAEMATOLOGY__Transfusion:
Pre-transfusion (compatibility) testing.
  • A Group & Save (G&S) determines the patient’s ABO & RhD group and screens for atypical red-cell antibodies, holding the sample ready
  • A crossmatch then confirms specific donor units are compatible before they are issued
1Group & Save
  • ABO & RhD grouping of the patient’s red cells.
  • Antibody screen — an indirect antiglobulin test (IAT) for clinically significant alloantibodies (e.g. anti-K, anti-Kidd, anti-Duffy) from prior transfusion or pregnancy.
  • Sample validity — if transfused or pregnant in the last 3 months, the sample is valid only 72 h (new antibodies can appear).
2ABO / RhD compatibility
🩸Red cells
O RhD-negative = universal donor (emergency use); AB = universal recipient.
🧪Plasma / FFP
AB = universal donor (no anti-A or anti-B) — the mirror image of red cells.
♀️RhD in females
Give RhD-negative (and K/Kell-negative) blood to girls and women of childbearing potential to avoid anti-D (and anti-K) sensitisation, which cause haemolytic disease of the newborn. If an RhD-negative girl/woman does receive RhD-positive red cells or platelets, give anti-D immunoglobulin as soon as possible and discuss with haematology.
3Crossmatch
Electronic (computer)→Group known & antibody screen negative → units issued in minutes.
Serological (full)→If antibodies present or a relevant history → physical crossmatch, ~45 min.
Emergency→O RhD-negative if no time; group-specific once grouped; fully crossmatched when available.
4G&S or crossmatch?
  • Group & Save — transfusion unlikely but possible (many elective procedures).
  • Crossmatch — transfusion anticipated; the MSBOS (maximum surgical blood ordering schedule) guides how many units.
🚩
The greatest risk is misidentification, not the biology. ‘Wrong blood in tube’ and bedside ID errors are the leading cause of fatal ABO-incompatible transfusion → acute intravascular haemolysis. Positively identify the patient and label the tube at the bedside at sampling, and check identity again at administration.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • G&S = ABO/RhD group + antibody screen (sample saved); crossmatch = compatibility of specific units
  • Electronic crossmatch (group known + screen negative) is fast; a full serological crossmatch is needed if antibodies are present
  • Emergency = O-negative
  • The commonest fatal error is patient misidentification
Modern practice is a restrictive transfusion strategy — transfuse to the lowest safe threshold, give one unit at a time, then reassess. Restrictive thresholds mean fewer reactions, less circulatory overload and better outcomes than liberal transfusion.
1Red cell (Hb) thresholds
Most patients (non-ACS)→Transfuse if Hb <70 g/L → target 70–90 g/L.
Acute coronary syndrome→Transfuse if Hb <80 g/L → target 80–100 g/L.
One unit, then reassess the Hb and symptoms. Red cells are stored at 4°C, infused over 90–120 min, and used within 4 h of leaving the fridge.
2Other products & their triggers
🧪FFP
Clotting factor deficiency with bleeding — e.g. PT or APTT >1.5× normal. Contains all clotting factors; large volume — avoid in fluid overload.
🧊Cryoprecipitate
Low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC ›, liver failure, massive transfusion. Concentrated fibrinogen, VIII, vWF, XIII.
🟣Platelets
Active bleeding → transfuse if <30 ×10⁹/L; prophylactic if <10 ×10⁹/L. One dose ↑ count ~20–30. Stored at 20–24°C (not cold — cold aggregates them). Higher targets before procedures: >50 for surgery, >100 for neurosurgery/eye.
💊PCC
Emergency warfarin reversal (major bleed, ICH, emergency surgery). Factors II, VII, IX, X; reversal <1 h. Give with IV vitamin K.
3Warfarin reversal
  1. Stop warfarin.
  2. IV vitamin K — always give (works in 4–6 h).
  3. PCC for a major bleed / ICH / emergency surgery — reversal within 1 h; give with the vitamin K.
  4. FFP only if PCC is unavailable (large volume, slower, less complete).
Why K with PCC? Factor VII has a short half-life — without vitamin K the INR rebounds as the PCC factors wear off.
🚩
Restrictive thresholds do not apply to active major haemorrhage. Don’t wait for a trigger Hb — activate the major-haemorrhage protocol and give empirical red cells with FFP (± platelets and cryoprecipitate), give tranexamic acid early in traumatic haemorrhage, and treat the source.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • Non-ACS <70 → 70–90; ACS <80 → 80–100; restrictive wins
  • FFP → PT/APTT >1.5; cryo → fibrinogen <1.5; platelets prophylactic <10; PCC + vitamin K for warfarin
  • Platelets are stored at 20–24°C — not cold
Any suspected transfusion reaction → STOP the transfusion first.
  • Keep the line open with saline, recheck the patient’s identity against the unit, assess ABC, and inform the lab
  • The workup and management then depend on the type of reaction
🛑
Universal first step — STOP the transfusion. Maintain IV access with saline, re-check patient ID vs the bag label, assess airway/breathing/circulation, and escalate. Only a mild febrile or minor allergic reaction may be cautiously restarted.
1Recognise the reaction
🌡️Febrile non-haemolytic
Anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokines. Fever, chills, rigors (mild, rise ≥1°C). → slow/stop, paracetamol; may restart if stable.
🌰Minor allergic
Donor plasma proteins. Urticaria, pruritus; no systemic compromise. → stop temporarily, antihistamine; may restart.
⚠️Anaphylaxis
IgA deficiency + anti-IgA. Hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema — rapid. → STOP, IM adrenaline, ABC, IV fluids.
🩸Acute haemolytic ★
ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error). Fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine within minutes. → STOP, check ID + bag, DAT + re-crossmatch, supportive.
🫁TRALI
Donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak. Non-cardiogenic oedema, hypoxia, HYPOtension, fever (within 6 h). → STOP, O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics.
💧TACO
Circulatory overload (too fast / HF / renal failure). Cardiogenic oedema, HYPERtension, raised JVP, orthopnoea. → slow/stop, furosemide + O₂, sit up.
🦠Bacterial sepsis
Contaminated unit (esp. platelets — stored warm). High fever, rigors, shock soon after starting. → STOP, cultures (patient + unit), broad-spectrum antibiotics, resuscitate.
⏳Delayed haemolytic
Anamnestic alloantibody response (prior sensitisation). Falling Hb, jaundice, positive DAT — days to ~2 weeks later. → supportive; identify the antibody for future crossmatching.
2The workup (suspected haemolytic / severe reaction)
  • Return the unit + giving set to the lab with a clotted and EDTA sample.
  • DAT (direct Coombs) and a repeat group & crossmatch — confirm ABO incompatibility and detect the culprit antibody.
  • Haemolysis screen — FBC, LDH, haptoglobin, bilirubin, U&E, coagulation, and urinalysis (haemoglobinuria).
  • Blood cultures (patient and unit) if febrile / suspected sepsis.
3TRALI vs TACO — the key discriminator
🫁TRALI
Immune capillary leak; HYPOtension; non-cardiogenic oedema. O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics.
💧TACO
Volume overload; HYPERtension; cardiogenic oedema. Furosemide + O₂.
Both cause pulmonary oedema — the split is clinical (BP, JVP), not radiological. TACO is the commonest cause of transfusion-related death (SHOT). TRALI = leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO = too much fluid + high BP → diurese.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • STOP is the universal first step
  • Acute haemolytic = ABO/human error → loin pain + dark urine in minutes → DAT + re-crossmatch
  • Anaphylaxis → IgA deficiency
  • TRALI = hypotension + non-cardiogenic → no diuretics; TACO = hypertension + cardiogenic → furosemide
HAEMATOLOGY__Arterial Blood Gas (ABG):
An arterial blood gas (ABG) is a point-of-care test — usually from the radial artery — that reports three things within minutes: oxygenation (PaO₂, SaO₂), ventilation (PaCO₂) and acid–base status (pH, HCO₃⁻, base excess). Modern analysers add lactate, electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺), glucose, haemoglobin and carboxyhaemoglobin — making it the single most useful bedside test in the acutely unwell, breathless or deteriorating patient.
1When to take one
  • Respiratory distress / hypoxia — low SpO₂, breathlessness, or to assess type 2 respiratory failure (CO₂ retention) before / during NIV.
  • The critically unwell — shock, sepsis (lactate), major trauma, cardiac arrest, reduced consciousness of unclear cause.
  • Suspected metabolic disturbance — DKA, renal failure, poisoning / overdose, severe vomiting or diarrhoea.
  • Monitoring a response — lactate clearance in sepsis, CO₂ during NIV, or correction of a metabolic acidosis.
💡 A venous blood gas (VBG) is fine for a quick pH, HCO₃⁻, lactate and K⁺, and avoids an arterial stab.
  • Reach for an ABG when you need an accurate PaO₂ / PaCO₂ (oxygenation and ventilation)
  • A normal venous CO₂ helps exclude hypercapnia; a raised venous CO₂ should be confirmed on an ABG before acting
2Taking the sample (technique)
  • Radial artery is first-line (collateral flow via the ulnar artery); an Allen’s test is sometimes done first, though the evidence that it prevents ischaemic complications is weak.
  • Pre-heparinised syringe; it is more painful than venepuncture — warn the patient and consider local anaesthetic.
  • Apply firm pressure ≥5 min afterwards (longer if anticoagulated); analyse promptly and always record the FiO₂ / oxygen delivery — the numbers are meaningless without it.
3Normal values (breathing room air — check local lab)
pH 7.35–7.45PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa (35–45 mmHg)PaO₂ 10–13 kPa on airHCO₃⁻ 22–26 mmol/LBase excess ±2 mmol/LSaO₂ 94–98%Lactate <2 mmol/L
UK labs report in kPa; roughly kPa × 7.5 = mmHg. A PaO₂ should be ≈ 10 kPa below the FiO₂ in % (e.g. ~40 kPa on 50%).
4A systematic approach
👤1 · The patient & the FiO₂
Read the gas with the clinical picture and the oxygen they are on. Hypoxia on high-flow O₂ is far worse than the same PaO₂ on air.
🫁2 · Oxygenation
Is the PaO₂ adequate for the FiO₂? Marked hypoxia, or a PaO₂ far below expected, signals a gas-exchange problem.
⚖️3 · The pH
<7.35 = acidaemia; >7.45 = alkalaemia. This tells you the net disturbance even when compensation is present.
💨4 · Respiratory (PaCO₂)
CO₂ moves opposite to pH in a respiratory problem: ↑CO₂ with ↓pH = respiratory acidosis; ↓CO₂ with ↑pH = respiratory alkalosis.
🧪5 · Metabolic (HCO₃⁻ / BE)
HCO₃⁻ moves the same way as pH in a metabolic problem: ↓HCO₃⁻/BE with ↓pH = metabolic acidosis; ↑ with ↑pH = metabolic alkalosis. Base excess is HCO₃⁻’s quantitative partner: more negative than −2 = metabolic acidosis; above +2 = metabolic alkalosis.
🔄6 · Compensation & gap
Is the other system compensating, and is that compensation appropriate?
  • A single acute disorder rarely returns the pH fully to normal — a normal or over-corrected pH signals a mixed disturbance
  • Then calculate the anion gap for any metabolic acidosis (next tab)
5Worked example
Gas — 19-year-old, drowsy, breathing deeply, on air
pH 7.18PaCO₂ 3.1 kPaPaO₂ 13 kPaHCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/LBE −16Lactate 3Glucose 28
  • Patient / FiO₂ — acutely unwell, breathing hard, on air.
  • Oxygenation — PaO₂ 13 kPa on air is adequate; no gas-exchange problem.
  • pH 7.18 — acidaemia.
  • Respiratory? PaCO₂ is low (3.1) — a low CO₂ would raise the pH, so it is not driving the acidosis; the patient is blowing off CO₂ to compensate (Kussmaul breathing).
  • Metabolic? HCO₃⁻ 9 and BE −16 — a metabolic acidosis: this is the primary disorder.
  • Compensation & gap — appropriate respiratory compensation, with a raised anion gap from ketones (glucose 28).
High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis + respiratory compensation → DKA ›
🧭 Quick logic: find the pH problem → ask which value (CO₂ or HCO₃⁻) matches it → that is the primary disorder; if the other value has shifted to push the pH back toward normal, that is compensation. A pH that is fully normal in a sick patient is a clue to a mixed picture, not the absence of one.
Acid–base balance is a tug-of-war between the lungs (PaCO₂, an acid — fast control) and the kidneys (HCO₃⁻, a base — slow control).
  • The pH is set by their ratio
  • Four primary disorders result, and either system can partly compensate for the other
1The four primary disorders
↑ raised ·  ↓ low ·  ↔ normal
💨Respiratory acidosis
pH ↓PaCO₂ ↑HCO₃⁻ ↔/↑ (if chronic)
Hypoventilation → COPD, life-threatening asthma, opioids / sedatives, neuromuscular weakness, obesity hypoventilation. COPD › Respiratory failure ›
🌬️Respiratory alkalosis
pH ↑PaCO₂ ↓HCO₃⁻ ↔/↓ (if chronic)
Hyperventilation → anxiety / pain, PE, pneumonia, high altitude, early sepsis, salicylate toxicity (early). PE › Pneumonia ›
🧪Metabolic acidosis
pH ↓HCO₃⁻ ↓PaCO₂ ↓ (compensating)
Split by the anion gap → high-gap (lactate, ketones, urate, toxins) vs normal-gap (GI / renal HCO₃⁻ loss). See step 3. Acid-base balance › DKA › AKI ›
🧂Metabolic alkalosis
pH ↑HCO₃⁻ ↑PaCO₂ ↑ (compensating)
Loss of acid / gain of base → vomiting / NG suction, diuretics, hypokalaemia, Conn’s (mineralocorticoid excess). Electrolyte disturbance ›
2Compensation
  • Respiratory compensation for a metabolic problem is fast (minutes–hours) — the lungs blow off or retain CO₂ (e.g. Kussmaul breathing lowers PaCO₂ in DKA).
  • Metabolic (renal) compensation for a respiratory problem is slow (days) — the kidney retains or excretes HCO₃⁻ (a raised HCO₃⁻ in chronic CO₂ retention).
  • Compensation never fully corrects the pH and never over-corrects it — so the pH still points to the primary disorder. If both values are deranged in opposite directions and the pH is very abnormal, suspect a mixed disorder.
  • Is the compensation adequate?
    • For a metabolic acidosis the expected PaCO₂ ≈ 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 (±2) in mmHg (Winter’s formula; ÷7.5 for kPa)
    • A PaCO₂ higher than expected reveals a second, respiratory acidosis; lower than expected, a coexisting respiratory alkalosis
💡 Acute vs chronic respiratory acidosis: a near-normal pH with a high PaCO₂ and a high HCO₃⁻ = chronic (compensated) retention, e.g. stable COPD.
3The anion gap (for a metabolic acidosis)
Anion gap = Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻) — normal ~8–12 mmol/L (lab-dependent). It sorts a metabolic acidosis into two buckets:
⬆️Raised anion gap
Added acid.
  • Lactic acidosis (sepsis, ischaemia), ketoacidosis (DKA, alcohol, starvation), urate (renal failure), and toxins (methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylates)
  • Mnemonic MUDPILES / GOLD-MARK
  • Next: check lactate, glucose/ketones and U&E (renal function), and if a toxin is possible a salicylate level and the osmolar gap — this identifies the acid and directs treatment
↔️Normal anion gap
Lost bicarbonate (hyperchloraemic). GI loss (diarrhoea, high-output stoma), renal tubular acidosis, or large-volume 0.9% saline.
Correct for albumin: a low albumin lowers the measured gap (~2.5 mmol/L per 10 g/L below 40 g/L) and can mask a raised-gap acidosis. With suspected toxins, also check the osmolar gap (methanol, ethylene glycol).
🚩
A raised lactate (>2, and especially >4 mmol/L) in an unwell patient suggests tissue hypoperfusion — think sepsis or ischaemia and escalate.
📷 Image placeholder — acid–base map: a pH-vs-PaCO₂/HCO₃⁻ grid plotting the four primary disorders and their compensation lines.
🎓 Exam pearl.
  • CO₂ = respiratory, opposite to pH; HCO₃⁻ = metabolic, same as pH.
  • Always anion-gap a metabolic acidosis
  • Classic vignettes: DKA = high-gap metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation; prolonged vomiting = hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; aspirin overdose = early respiratory alkalosis then a high-gap metabolic acidosis (mixed)
The other half of the ABG is oxygenation — is enough oxygen reaching the blood, and why not? — plus the point-of-care extras (lactate, K⁺, glucose, Hb, CO-Hb) that change management immediately.
1Hypoxia & the two types of respiratory failure
1️⃣Type 1 respiratory failure
PaO₂ ↓ (<8 kPa)PaCO₂ ↔/↓
Oxygenation / V-Q problem → pneumonia, PE, pulmonary oedema, asthma, early COPD. Respiratory failure › Pneumonia ›
2️⃣Type 2 respiratory failure
PaO₂ ↓ (<8 kPa)PaCO₂ ↑ (>6 kPa)
Ventilatory failure → COPD, life-threatening asthma, sedation, neuromuscular weakness, chest-wall disease — the setting for NIV. COPD › Asthma ›
💡 The A–a gradient separates the causes of hypoxia.
  • On air, alveolar PAO₂ ≈ 20 − PaCO₂/0.8 (kPa), and the A–a gradient = PAO₂ − PaO₂ (normal <2 kPa, rising with age)
  • It is normal in hypoventilation and at altitude (the alveolar O₂ is itself low); raised with V/Q mismatch, shunt or diffusion defects (pneumonia, PE, oedema, fibrosis)
2SaO₂ vs PaO₂ — and where pulse oximetry misleads
  • The oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid: below a PaO₂ of ~8 kPa the SaO₂ falls steeply, so small drops in PaO₂ cause big desaturations.
  • Right shift (offloads O₂ to the tissues) — acidosis, high CO₂, fever, raised 2,3-DPG (the Bohr effect); left shift (holds O₂ on) — alkalosis, low CO₂, hypothermia, HbCO and fetal Hb.
  • Carbon-monoxide poisoning gives a falsely normal SpO₂ (the pulse oximeter cannot tell HbCO from oxyHb) — the ABG co-oximeter reveals the high carboxyhaemoglobin.
  • Methaemoglobinaemia tends to pin the SpO₂ around ~85% regardless of true oxygenation.
📷 Image placeholder — oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve: sigmoid SaO₂-vs-PaO₂ curve with the steep segment and right/left shifts labelled.
3The point-of-care extras
🔥Lactate
Marker of tissue hypoperfusion / anaerobic metabolism. >2 abnormal, >4 mmol/L = severe — a key sepsis and shock marker; also trends the response to resuscitation.
⚡Potassium (K⁺)
A near-instant result. Hyperkalaemia (renal failure, DKA, crush) or hypokalaemia (vomiting, diuretics) — confirm on a formal lab sample and get an ECG if high.
🍬Glucose
Immediate — flags DKA / HHS or hypoglycaemia in the collapsed patient.
🩸Haemoglobin
A rapid Hb for the bleeding or shocked patient while the formal FBC is pending.
🟥Carboxy- / met-haemoglobin
Co-oximetry detects CO poisoning (HbCO) and methaemoglobin — invisible to a standard pulse oximeter. Treat suspected CO poisoning with high-flow 100% O₂ via a non-rebreather mask (shortens the HbCO half-life); discuss hyperbaric O₂ in severe cases (coma, cardiac / neurological signs, pregnancy).
Electrolyte disturbances › Diabetic emergencies (DKA/HHS) ›
🚩
Two do-not-miss ABG signs. In a tiring asthmatic, a normal PaCO₂ is itself a life-threatening feature (they should be hyperventilating and blowing it off), and a rising / raised PaCO₂ signals near-fatal asthma with exhaustion → urgent senior / ICU input. In COPD receiving oxygen, watch for a rising PaCO₂ with a falling pH (target sats 88–92% in known retainers).
🎓 Exam pearl. Type 1 = low O₂, normal/low CO₂; Type 2 = low O₂, high CO₂. A normal SpO₂ does not exclude CO poisoning — check carboxyhaemoglobin. Use lactate to spot and track shock / sepsis.
